title: Ailean Mòr falls at Àth na Fala
body: The host of Dùn dhearg and the eastern households who never bowed come against the king at the ford below Dùn dhearg. Ailean Mòr holds the ford alone three days and three nights, and the dead of the host dam the river. On the third night he falls, worn down by the whole host; no one man overcame him, and age had not touched him. His kin, quarrelling already over the shares of the kingdom, did not come. He was four thousand six hundred and twenty-six years old, and had been king since the grove. The ford is called Àth na Fala after.

title: The Binding of the First Flame
body: Custody is declared over the vein, and the first flame is bound at Dùn ìseal: the undying flame of Brìde, kept over the stone of Crom Cruaich. The heirs of Ailean Mòr, gathered to part his kingdom, cannot part the vein, and swear it to no one of the blood. Its keepers, Òrd Bhrìde, are the first order on Dia-thìr to govern both rite and people, and they are older by centuries than any rìgh after Ailean.

title: Runners to every coast
body: The kin in the valley send runners in pairs from fires that do not trust each other to every coast of the island, to call in the king's blood who had not come.

title: Aodh Crom asks for a cord of the heirs
body: The eldest keeper of the slab, Aodh Crom, comes to the house of the knot-keeper Sìne nan Snaidhm by night and asks her for a new cord, to count the heirs, since none of them will believe another's count.

title: The knotting of the heirs begins
body: Sìne nan Snaidhm sits down at the door of the gathering-house below Dùn ìseal with a new cord of flax and wool of many colours, one colour for each child of the king with living heirs. No heir is to be heard on the shares who has not first been knotted at the door.

title: The heirs sit at Dùn ìseal
body: The kin of Ailean Mòr, come too late to the ford, stay on at Dùn ìseal after the Binding to part his kingdom. The knot-keeper Sìne nan Snaidhm ties a knot on a cord for every heir who stands up to claim: seven hundred and twelve. The eldest of them, Murchadh Mòr, is near two thousand nine hundred years old; the youngest who claims is a child in arms.

title: Ìomhar Dearg comes to the ford
body: Ìomhar Dearg, a son of Ailean Mòr, who had stayed three days in the valley under Dùn ìseal arguing for river-grazing, comes down out of the heather to Àth na Fala on the morning after the king fell, and finds the river dammed by the dead and his father on the west bank.

title: The spent host broken at the ford
body: Ìomhar Dearg's household crosses the ford and falls on the host of the east where it lies spent in the heather. Many are killed, many run, and some sit down and cover their heads. By evening Ìomhar holds the ford.

title: The greybeard found in the ford
body: The greybeard of the eastern households who gave the counsel of the third day is found at dawn face down in the shallows below the king's stone. Whether he fell or went in of his own will, nobody on the east bank will say.

title: Dùn dhearg taken and its halls burned
body: Ìomhar Dearg walks in through both gates of Dùn dhearg, where the households of the east had sworn they owed nothing to Dùn ìseal. No one will own the blow that felled the king. He has the halls within the double bank burned, and takes the people under his own hand.

title: The bier of spears
body: On the fifth day after the ford the king's body is laid on a bier lashed from the host's spears and carried up the valley road by twelve men of Dùn dhearg who had been in the river. Two grey sons of the king meet it at the lip of the valley and walk behind it. Ìomhar Dearg does not go with it.

title: The dead of the ford buried on the meadow
body: Ìomhar Dearg has the dead of the host drawn out of the river and buried in long trenches on the meadow, all together, since none can be told apart. The king's stone at the head of the ford is left standing, and he forbids anyone to move it.

title: The twelve bearers given cattle
body: The twelve bearers come back to Dùn dhearg with the poles of the bier. Ìomhar Dearg gives each a cow and a place within the bank, and sets the poles up at the inner gate.

title: The grey stone at the ford left standing
body: In his nine days at Dùn dhearg Ìomhar Dearg has the bank of the ford cleared but the grey stone left where it stands, and forbids anyone to move it.

title: The eastern households called down from the hills
body: Ìomhar sends riders round the eastern hills to the households who fled with their cattle: if they come down to him and to nobody else they keep their cattle and their lives. Most come. Those who do not are hunted.

title: The tidings at Dùn ìseal
body: Donnan, a herd-boy of the eastern hills who watched the ford from the ridge, comes over the tops to the spring below Dùn ìseal on the fourth evening after the battle. The first word said in the camps of the kin is a question: who holds the hill now?

title: The keening in the valley
body: Mairsile, an aged daughter of the king, begins to keen alone at her fire in the upper valley, and the whole valley of the kin takes it up fire by fire.

title: The bier at the gathering-house
body: The bier of spears comes up the valley road with two grey sons of the king behind it. Sìne nan Snaidhm gives the twelve bearers water at the spring. The keepers of the slab take the king from them at the door of the gathering-house.

title: The king laid in the earth
body: After three nights in the gathering-house Ailean Mòr is carried out before dawn and laid in the earth under a mound. The tellers of Dùn ìseal show a mound on the slope facing the vein; the reciters of the Mason's line, following Seathan Crom of Clann na Ceiste, show another. The two have never been reconciled.

title: Ìomhar Dearg comes up as lord of Dùn dhearg
body: Ìomhar Dearg rides up the valley road with his household in the cloaks of the east and stands in the door of the gathering-house as lord of Dùn dhearg. Aodh Crom bids him sit.

title: Two mounds shown for the king's grave
body: The knot-keepers of Dùn ìseal show a long low mound on the slope facing the vein as Ailean Mòr's grave; the reciters of the Mason's line tell of another, and of the lame reciter Seathan Crom who spoke to the grey sons on the third night. Sìne did not follow the bier and will not say.

title: The keepers bring down their fire
body: The nine keepers of the slab come down from Tobar dhìreach to Dùn ìseal with the fire of their hut in a covered pot. The reciters of the Mason's line hold that it came down from the mason's fire; the keepers say only that it is old and must not go out.

title: The heirs' first quarrel over the hill
body: The kin of Ailean Mòr meet in the gathering-house below Dùn ìseal and quarrel three days over the hill, which stands over the vein: by the eldest, by the living, by the dead, and by a gallery to each line. Eithne nic Ailein and Murchadh Mòr nearly come to blood on the first day.

title: Aodh Crom's asking
body: Aodh Crom, eldest of the keepers of the slab, asks the heirs to declare the keepers' charge, as the keepers had asked of Catrìona Mhòr, and to put the vein and the hill over it into no share, held by no one of the king's blood. Each line would sooner nobody had it than a cousin.

title: Gille-Brìde carries a coal of the First Flame home
body: Gille-Brìde of the line of Somhairle comes down from the high valleys, swears the Binding last of the king's blood, and asks for a coal of the flame. He carries it home in a clay pot and asks for nothing more, and no knot is tied for him.

title: The flame kept in the keepers' hut
body: After the Binding the First Flame is kept in the keepers' hut on the slope above the gathering-house at Dùn ìseal, fed with a little of the coloured coal each night.

title: Murchadh Mòr comes alone to the keepers' hut
body: On the night before the swearing Murchadh Mòr climbs alone to the keepers' hut and sits across the fire from Aodh Crom like a carrier, knees up, to tell him the hill will go to the fire and not to the man who feeds it, and to ask what the keepers want.

title: The youngest keeper asks who will hold the flame
body: On the night after the Binding, while the heirs drink in the valley, the youngest of the nine keepers sits down across the flame from Aodh Crom and asks who will hold it when he and the rest of them are gone.

title: Murchadh Mòr knotted first
body: Murchadh Mòr, eldest living son of the king, gives his line in two words, 'Ailean's son', and stands over the knot-keeper while she ties it. The knotting of his line takes the whole first day.

title: Fionn Beag sent home
body: Eithne nic Ailein sets her own knot-keeper, Fionn Beag of the lowlands, on the step to count after Sìne nan Snaidhm. After four days he tells her that the knot-keeper of Dùn ìseal has made no mistake, and Eithne sends him home.

title: Niall Òg's knot tied once
body: Niall Òg, a grandson of the king, gives his line through his mother and again through his father and says that he is owed twice. Sìne nan Snaidhm ties his knot once.

title: The knot-keeper refuses a cow
body: A steward of one of the lines of the dead brings Sìne nan Snaidhm a cow in milk to have doubtful cousins tied close to his lord's line. She sends him away, and two more after him, and the stewards begin to watch one another's lines at the door.

title: The knots of the dead
body: For the lines of the king's children who died before him, Sìne nan Snaidhm ties a hollow knot of black wool round nothing, and ties their heirs after it. By the end there are more hollow knots in the cord than knots for the king's living children.

title: Four lines protest Ìomhar's knot
body: When Ìomhar Dearg is knotted as a son of the king, four lines send their stewards to Aodh Crom to say they will not agree to Dùn dhearg being counted as one share when the shares are cut.

title: The youngest heir knotted
body: A great-great-grandchild of the king of the salt-shore line, a child in arms, is held up at the door and knotted, the youngest of all the heirs.

title: The cord laid on the floor
body: On the eleventh evening the cord of the heirs, Sreang nan Oighrean, is laid along the floor of the gathering-house from the hearth to the door and back, with lamps set beside it, and the heirs walk it looking at their own knots and counting their neighbours'.

title: The four rules put before the valley
body: As the sitting settles in for the winter, the heirs' quarrel sorts itself into four rival rules for the parting of the kingdom: the eldest to hold and feed the rest, the living to hold by nearness of blood, the dead's children to stand in their fathers' places, and the shares to be thrown for by lot.

title: Murchadh Mòr argues the eldest's rule
body: Murchadh Mòr holds, before the assembled heirs, that the eldest of the king's children should take the whole kingdom and feed the rest of the blood from his own hand, as a household divides no differently at a father's death.

title: Eithne argues the rule of the living
body: Eithne nic Ailein argues that the living should hold in the order of their nearness to the king's blood and no further back, so that the youngest living child stands level with the eldest.

title: The dead's children ask a place in the reckoning
body: The lines of the king's dead children, gathered behind an old man who had felt the hollow knot at the door, argue that a line does not end because its head died before the king, and ask a rule that does not forget them.

title: The youngest heirs ask the lot
body: Among the youngest and least-landed of the heirs a fourth rule is heard, that the shares be thrown for by lot and left to the ancestors to judge, since none of the other three rules gives them much to hope for.

title: Niall Òg carries words between the two fires
body: Niall Òg, owed twice over and feared by nobody's steward, begins carrying words straight between Murchadh Mòr's fire and Eithne nic Ailein's, each of them trusting him, of all the valley, to repeat the meaning and not soften it.

title: The grass of the valley fails to come back
body: The riverside grass, grazed to the earth by two winters of the sitting's horses and households, does not come green again with the spring, and does not for three years after.

title: Mairsile nic Ailein dies in the cold
body: Mairsile nic Ailein, the white-haired daughter who began the keening at the ford, dies in the valley in the second month of the year, when the short winter ration leaves her brazier low overnight; she is laid by the river as she had asked before her death.

title: Four lines protest the Red Share
body: Four lines with no claim on Dùn dhearg argue that Ìomhar Dearg's hold on it, won by the sword and not by any of the four rules, ought to be parted into whatever settlement the rest of the kingdom comes into; Eithne answers that no rule written after the fact can take back what is already held.

title: The clause against the name of rìgh
body: Through the summer the strongest lines come, fire by fire, to swear that none of the nine shall be called rìgh or take the word for a share, since the kingdom ended with Ailean Mòr; Murchadh Mòr swears it hardest, having watched what the word cost his father.

title: Aodh Crom proposes the four rules together
body: Aodh Crom, asked his mind though he holds no share, tells the heads of the strongest lines that no one of the four rules can be sworn alone, and sets out a settlement that gives each rule something: nine great shares for the eldest living lines, a portion out of all nine for the dead, and the lot within each share where an equal claim cannot be told apart.

title: The nine eldest lines agree to the settlement
body: The nine strongest lines of the king's blood, among them Murchadh Mòr, Eithne nic Ailein, Fionnghal nic Ailein of the western shore, Artair mac Ailein of the salt shore and Cormac mac Ailein of the east, agree to hold the nine great shares, with the portion of the dead set out of all nine and the Red Share of Ìomhar Dearg let stand.

title: The agreement to cut the cord at the handful
body: The nine lines agree that the cord of the heirs shall be laid on the gathering-house floor again and cut into nine lengths at the night of the handful, with the clause against the name of rìgh and the peace of the Hall's ground sworn once before the whole valley as it is cut.

title: The cord of the heirs laid twice round the gathering-house floor
body: On Oidhche an Dòrlaich the keepers bring the cord of the heirs down from its chest and lay it from the hearth to the door and back, with lamps set along its length. Nine plain, unmarked knives are laid out for the nine lines that will cut it.

title: Roinn na Rìoghachd
body: On the night of the handful the heirs swear the parting of the kingdom, Roinn na Rìoghachd. The island below the mountain is cut into nine great shares, earrannan mòra, for the nine eldest lines of the king's blood, and the lines of his dead children are given the portion of the dead, cuid nam marbh, out of all nine. No heir is to be called rìgh. The ground of the Hall is in no share. Dùn dhearg, which Ìomhar Dearg had taken with the sword after the ford, is let stand as his share, over the protest of four lines.

title: Murchadh Mòr cuts the cord first
body: Murchadh Mòr, eldest living son of the king and near two thousand nine hundred years old, cuts the cord in one stroke exactly where he had long meant to, and takes up the great share of the north, from Baile Mòr mhòr to the high passes.

title: Eithne nic Ailein's knife cuts through a knot
body: Eithne nic Ailein, youngest of the nine eldest lines, kneels long over her place on the cord and cuts through a knot rather than between two, leaving one heir's line divided between her share and the next.

title: Ciorstaidh cut through and claimed by two shares
body: Ciorstaidh of the salt shore, whose knot is cut through by Eithne's knife, answers the two lords quarrelling over her with "I'll take both." It is let stand: the first of the double oaths sworn that night.

title: Eleven knots cut through in one night
body: Where the nine knives cross the cord's thickest stretches, eleven knots in all are cut through rather than between. Eleven households find themselves sworn to two lords at once; most pay both oaths rather than contest them.

title: The western share sworn to Fionnghal nic Ailein
body: Fionnghal nic Ailein cuts her length of the cord clean and takes the western share, with its seat on the harbour at Ros dhomhain.

title: The salt shore sworn to Artair mac Ailein
body: Artair mac Ailein, who had argued least of the nine that summer, takes the share of the salt shore, seated at the western Baile ghorm.

title: The eastern share sworn to Cormac mac Ailein
body: Cormac mac Ailein takes the eastern share, seated at Caol shean, in which the silver of Muileann chiar will one day be found.

title: The four lesser shares sworn to Ùna, Coll, Gormlaith and Tadhg
body: The last four of the nine cut their lengths in quick succession: Ùna nic Ailein takes the north-west at Muileann àrsaidh, Coll mac Ailein the hills of the Abhainn fhionn at Ceann àrsaidh, Gormlaith nic Ailein the south-east at Tobar dhearg, and Tadhg mac Ailein the Abhainn ìseal and the Hawk bay at Cnoc bheag.

title: The cord of the heirs lies in nine pieces
body: With the ninth cut made, the cord no longer runs the floor of the gathering-house whole. It lies in nine lengths, one over each lord's arm, with the loose ends of the eleven double knots hanging free between them.

title: The Red Hill declares itself sworn to nobody
body: The holder of the Red Hill, whose line had sworn to Ailean Mòr alone and to no lord of a share, stands up on the night of the handful and says his oath died with the king, and that the Red Hill is that night sworn to nobody at all.

title: Three great shares claim the Red Hill
body: Murchadh Mòr and two other lords of the nine cross the floor at once to claim the ownerless Red Hill. None yields, and none of the three can make the claim stand, that night or in the years that follow.

title: The Hall's ground confirmed in no share
body: Aodh Crom reminds the nine, on the night of the handful, that the hill of the slab and the gathering-house and the valley about it, as walked by the keepers, lie in no share, as sworn at the Binding, and are not to be argued afresh.

title: The lengths of cord carried out of the gathering-house
body: At dawn the nine lords go out through the door of the gathering-house one after another, each with his length of the cord folded or coiled over his arm, and their households follow, so that the valley empties along nine roads at once.

title: The boundary stones cut and set along the Roinn
body: Through the winter after the handful the stewards of the nine lines ride the boundaries with the reciters, agreeing what they can, and masons cut and set the clachan-crìche, each stone bearing the sign of the share it faces. Some are moved in the night and set again by morning.

title: A stone set on each bank at Dùn thais
body: No steward of the north or of the Red Share will yield Dùn thais to the other, so the masons of both lines set a stone on the north bank of the burn below the old fort, cut with Murchadh's sign, and another on the south bank, cut with the sign of the Red Share, and leave the hill itself between the two.

title: Ìomhar Dearg claims the grazing above Dùn thais
body: At his own supper-table Ìomhar Dearg tells his grandson Ruairidh Glas that the grazing on the northern slope above Dùn thais belongs to the Red Share, stone or no stone, and that it is time the cattle grazing there under the northern share's sign were driven off it.

title: First blood among the heirs
body: At Dùn thais, on the line between the great share of the north and the Red Share, the men of Aonghas Bàn mac Mhurchaidh and of Ruairidh Glas of the line of Ìomhar come to blows over which share the fort lies in. Aonghas Bàn is killed. With his death begins Aimhreit nan Oighrean, the strife of the heirs, between the line of Murchadh and the line of Ìomhar and then between many lines.

title: Aonghas Bàn carried home to his brother's hall
body: Ruairidh Glas's men carry Aonghas Bàn mac Mhurchaidh down off the hill of Dùn thais in a cloak between two spear-shafts, in the rain, and word runs ahead of them to his own household, where his brother Eachann Ruadh is already waiting at the gate.

title: Eachann Ruadh's oath over his brother's body
body: Eachann Ruadh mac Mhurchaidh kneels by his brother's body in the yard of their own hall and swears that the blood spilt at Dùn thais will be answered, blood for blood, by his own hand or his sons' after him, without naming the man he means, which by the old custom of the households leaves the quarrel open to a settling short of a second death.

title: Ìomhar Dearg refuses to answer for the killing
body: Ìomhar Dearg tells his grandson Ruairidh Glas that he did no more than a man does when his own are threatened, and that he is not to trouble himself with an oath sworn by a boy over his brother's body. The line of Ìomhar makes no answer to Eachann Ruadh's oath.

title: The shares parted into countries and provinces
body: Under each of the nine great shares the households sworn to it are parted again into countries, and the countries into provinces, as the lines of the king's dead children are fitted in among the living heirs' claims.

title: Provinces parted again into counties and holdings
body: Below the provinces the land is cut finer still, into counties and, under the counties, holdings no larger than a single steading, sworn by whichever household holds them to whatever county's steward stands nearest and troubles to ride out and take the oath.

title: Holdings sworn to two counties and to three
body: A stream that shifts its bed in a wet winter leaves more than one holding claimed by two counties at once, and some households, rather than fight for the difference, swear to both and pay both, and the two counties are slow to compare their rolls.

title: The three lords of the mill on the Abhainn dhomhain
body: Three counties meeting at a bend of the Abhainn dhomhain each claim the eel-catch of an old mill's pond, and the miller, who built the wheel before the Roinn was thought of, takes to paying each lord a third of the autumn catch unasked, and the quarrel goes no further.

title: Shares of shares
body: The great shares are parted again among their holders' children and grandchildren, into countries, provinces, counties and holdings, until the lesser blood of the portion of the dead is fitted in. Many holdings owe oaths to two lords, and some to three. The boundary stones of the Roinn are set up, and moved, and set up again.

title: Aodh Crom's charge to the new Keeper
body: At the choosing on the slope below the slab, Aodh Crom, eldest of the keepers, holds out a lit rush to Beathag Bhàn and charges her to hold it for Brìde and answer to Crom for what is taken from the vein. She says nothing, and the keepers count her silence in her favour.

title: Beathag Bhàn keeps the first flame
body: At Dùn ìseal under the central mountains the keepers of the slab and the households sworn to the Binding choose Beathag Bhàn to hold the first flame for Brìde and to answer to Crom for what is taken from the vein. She is of no heir's blood and holds no share, and the heirs let her be chosen for that. The spoken roll of the Keepers begins with her name. Of her life before it nothing is remembered.

title: The knot-keepers count forty-four countries
body: Riding the boundaries themselves with cords of their own, the knot-keepers of Dùn ìseal come to a count of forty-four countries under the nine great shares, a count that holds for a season before two countries are found to have quietly divided themselves into three apiece.

title: The count of a hundred and thirty-one provinces
body: The knot-keepers count a hundred and thirty-one provinces under the countries, and hold the number the better part of a year, though even as it is counted two provinces of the eastern share split into three over a fishing-weir.

title: The knot-keepers give up the count at the counties
body: Cairistìona, Sìne's eldest daughter, tells Aodh Crom that the counties change their own boundaries faster than any cord can be tied to hold them, and that a knot-keeper who tries to count them all will chase a number that is never the same twice. The count of counties is given up unfinished.

title: A boundary quarrel brought to the Hall's ground
body: Stewards of the Red Share and the great share of the north, come to lay a raid and a cattle-theft before the keepers, nearly bring their quarrel armed onto the ground under the mountain. Aodh Crom stands between them and says again that no spear may come onto that ground in anger.

title: The heirs go home from the valley
body: In the second summer after the stones went up at Dùn thais, the heirs and their households go home from the valley below Dùn ìseal, most of them for the first time in nearly two years without a boundary still openly disputed.

title: The flame kept in a turf hut
body: With no hall yet raised, the households build Beathag Bhàn a one-room hut of turf at the mountain's foot, and she carries the newly given flame into it and sits up with it through the first night, having found no words to answer the keepers with.

title: Beathag Bhàn learns the galleries
body: Aodh Crom leads Beathag Bhàn down into the low galleries under Dùn ìseal and names them for her one by one, though he will not let her cut the coal herself, telling her that the hand which holds the flame does not also cut the vein.

title: The watch set on the cairns above Cnoc ghlas
body: Beitris, an old keeper of the slab, teaches Beathag Bhàn to read the cloud on the high passes from the cairns above Cnoc ghlas, the sign by which the Hall judges when a gallery may safely be opened for the season.

title: The nine districts argue the turn of the hearths
body: Before the first season is set, two of the nine districts about the mountain's foot claim the tending of the flame for themselves alone, on the ground that their people sat nearest the old slab the longest, and are outvoted by the other seven.

title: The nine hearths
body: Nine households about the mountain's foot, one for each district of the old keepers of the slab, take the tending of the flame in turn, each sending a son or daughter to sit with it through a season. The later houses of custody all claim descent from one or another of the nine. Not all the claims can be true.

title: Cailean of the northern hearth sits the first season
body: Cailean, a boy of the northern district, is the first of the nine hearths sent up to sit a season with Beathag Bhàn and the flame, arriving expecting a shrine and finding a cold hut with one keeper barely older than himself.

title: The first cairns raised above Cnoc ghlas
body: Before fixed cairns marked the ridge, watchers of the weather climbed wherever their own eye judged best each morning. An eastern woman, Sorcha, first piles stone at the three places she finds she reads the sky truest, so that watchers after her need not guess afresh each dawn where to stand.

title: Niall Òg offers Beathag Bhàn a silver cup
body: Niall Òg climbs to the Hall's ground alone and offers Beathag Bhàn a cup of worked silver beaten with running deer, so that she might have one thing of her own.

title: Beathag Bhàn refuses the gift
body: Beathag Bhàn gives the silver cup back to Niall Òg, saying that whatever she holds she holds for every hand in the valley, and that taking a gift from one heir would oblige her to answer for refusing every other.

title: Mòrag nan Càrn named watcher of the ridge
body: A child of the fifth hearth who could tell one grey sky from another better than watchers grown old at the work is named, at not yet twenty, to keep the cairns above Cnoc ghlas in her own right, the youngest the mountain has yet trusted with the reading of its weather.

title: The door of Talla na Lasrach set toward the vein
body: Aodh Crom walks the ground of the new hall with Beathag Bhàn before the first stone is laid and marks where its one door must stand, facing the vein and turned from the sea, giving no reason he will afterward repeat the same way twice.

title: Talla na Lasrach raised
body: A long hall of dry stone and turf is raised over the flame at Dùn ìseal, with one door toward the vein and none toward the sea. It is rebuilt many times on the same footings, and the footings are all of it that anyone can now swear to.

title: The nine hearths raise the hall's walls
body: Sons and daughters of the nine households build Talla na Lasrach's walls of dry stone and turf under Beathag Bhàn's eye, each household's work known afterward by the set of its stones, straight where the ninth hearth laid it and less so where the second did.

title: Ruairidh Glas and Eachann Ruadh stand at one fire
body: At Samhain on the Hall's ground, Ruairidh Glas, who killed Aonghas Bàn at Dùn thais, and Eachann Ruadh, the dead man's brother, stand at opposite sides of the same fire the whole night and speak no word to one another, but neither draws.

title: Sìne nan Snaidhm ties a knot for good news
body: Sìne nan Snaidhm comes up to Dùn ìseal for the carrying of the flame into the finished hall and ties a plain unmarked length into her long cord-record, the first knot she has ever tied for good news alone rather than for a claim or a grief.

title: The flame carried into Talla na Lasrach
body: On the shortest day of the year Beathag Bhàn lifts the flame from the hearth-stone of the turf hut that had held it eleven years and carries it into the finished hall, where it burns that evening for the first time under a roof built to hold it.

title: The reverence about the mountain given a name
body: Asked by a walker of the eastern share what the households call the milk left on the sill and the silence kept on the ridge, old Beitris of the Hall answers for them: Seann Spioradan nan Dia-thìreach, the ancestors, the sìth, the vein and the weather held together, owed remembering and courtesy and watching, and needing no priest to speak for any of them.

title: Seann Spioradan nan Dia-thìreach established
body: At the hearths the eldest of the island's folk-ways takes shape: reverence for the ancestors, for the vein, for the weather that rules the mining season, and for the sìth of the hills and mounds. It keeps no priests, and it has never ceased.

title: The weather-cairns of Cnoc ghlas
body: Watchers build cairns on the ridge above Cnoc ghlas and read the cloud on the high passes from them, to tell the Hall when the galleries may be opened for the season. A wrong reading costs the whole mountain its season, and the watchers are chosen with more care than the Keeper.

title: Fearchar Glas reads the cloud wrong
body: A watcher of six years' standing judges a low grey sky wind only and sends the galleries open; the rain that follows floods the low gallery past saving and costs the households the whole autumn's cutting. Fearchar comes down off the ridge unbidden to tell the keepers of the slab what he did.

title: The cairns given a stricter choosing
body: After the season lost to a wrong reading, the keepers of the slab rule that no one may watch the cairns alone who has not first stood a full season under an elder watcher's eye and been judged fit by more than one. Mòrag nan Càrn sits among those who judge the youths who come after.

title: A boy of Doire uaine chooses the cold over the flint
body: In the hardest winter the slopes have seen, a boy sent to bring in a ewe is caught by the wind and found two days later, alive, having refused to strike a fire within sight of the forbidden hills though he carried flint enough. His mother carries him down to the Hall herself rather than risk the road past the standing stones.

title: The ban on fires in sight of Doire uaine
body: In obedience to the old inscriptions the Keepers forbid any fire, of wood or of coal, to be lit in sight of the Doire uaine hills. Herders who winter on those slopes eat cold for the season. The ban is never lifted, and none is known to have owned to breaking it.

title: The Hall's hearth opened to the Doire uaine households
body: Beathag Bhàn sends word that any household of the forbidden slopes may bring a sick child or a frost-bitten hand to the Keeper's own hearth at Dùn ìseal, the ban forbidding only a fire lit within sight of those hills. Few households make the long journey, but the offer is remembered longer than it is used.

title: Beathag Bhàn walks alone to the temple ruin
body: Telling no one where she goes, Beathag Bhàn crosses broken ground to Làrach an Teampaill and finds its altar-slab, worn by hands no one living can name, turned toward her own mountain. She returns and tells the keepers of the slab plainly that she cannot say whose place it is, only that it is neither Brìde's nor Crom's.

title: Làrach an Teampaill left unentered
body: Beathag Bhàn walks to Làrach an Teampaill, finds its altar already turned toward the mountain, and declares the place not the Hall's to keep. The Keepers set no foot in it for the rest of the age. Whose it was they did not say, and it seems they did not know.

title: The keepers swear never to enter the ruin
body: After argument over whether the temple ruin should be cleared and watched like the cairns or left untouched, Beathag Bhàn ends it: no keeper of the slab, and no Keeper of the flame after her, will set foot inside it again, a reverence built on courtesy to what it cannot read being no reverence at all if it tramples the ground.

title: Death of Beathag Bhàn
body: After a winter's slow failing, Beathag Bhàn dies at Dùn ìseal without ever having risen ill from her bed. She is laid on the slope facing the vein with her back to the sea, at Beitris's word, since she never once turned from the mountain living and none will have her do it the one day she cannot choose.

title: Death of Beathag Bhàn
body: Beathag Bhàn dies at Dùn ìseal and is laid on the slope facing the vein, with her back to the sea. The nine hearths choose Muireach Liath, her sister's son, to keep the flame after her.

title: Muireach Liath chosen to hold the flame
body: The nine hearths gather within the week and name Muireach Liath, Beathag Bhàn's sister's son, faster than any choosing the mountain has seen. Old Beitris puts the rush into his hands with words close to Aodh Crom's own, and he carries the flame into the Hall that same evening.

title: The basket argued to one size
body: Muireach Liath asks the nine hearths for a common measure, a lidded basket of plaited heather, one to a household, filled once a season. The households argue the size of it until they have argued themselves into agreeing on one.

title: The weavers of the third hearth take the basket's making
body: The plaiting that holds the measured basket's shape under a full load proves particular enough that the weavers of the third hearth keep the craft for their own. Baskets of that weave outlast a season's use before any other household's do.

title: A second and third sinking answered
body: Two more households of Caol shean come forward with tales like the first woman's, of boats kept whole after a drink of the stream in what each judges the right quarter of the moon. The laughing that met her first telling thins.

title: Coal by the basket
body: Muireach Liath fixes the first common measure for coal carried down from the galleries: a lidded basket of plaited heather, one to a household, filled once a season. Baskets of that weave are made at Dùn ìseal still, for no purpose but the making.

title: Muireach walks up to Muileann ruadh
body: In his fourth year Muireach Liath goes up to the warm springs himself rather than let the households' carrying run past him unquestioned, and finds an old woman keeping her granddaughter's ill-set arm a season longer in the water before anyone speaks of breaking it again.

title: A hearth-elder puts the stream to Muireach
body: One of the hearth-elders who kept the ancestors' watch before Beathag Bhàn's own choosing asks Muireach Liath directly whether a stream running off the vein's own mountain belongs to the Hall's reckoning. His answer, given plainly in a few sentences, is repeated by every Keeper who follows him.

title: Allt an Àigh named
body: A stream is held to bring good fortune to any who drink of it in a certain quarter of the moon. Pilgrims come to it, and have never wholly ceased to come.

title: Gille-Brìde dies in the high valleys
body: Gille-Brìde of Somhairle's line, who carried a coal of the First Flame home from the Binding and asked for nothing since, dies among his own people at two hundred and twenty-four, in an early winter hard on the hill-folk of Coille naomh.

title: Ceallach keeps the coal
body: Ceallach mac Ghille-Bhrìde takes up his father's hearth and the coal of the First Flame kept on it, changing nothing the hill-folk who sit by that fire can name, since he had been feeding it quietly on his father's behalf for years before.

title: Niall Òg sits an evening at Ceallach's hearth
body: Niall Òg goes up alone to the high valleys on hearing of Gille-Brìde's death, and finds, for the first time in sixty years of burying his father's kin, a death that leaves him nothing to feel bitter about.

title: The pilgrims' path from Caol shean
body: A path is worn from the river landing at Caol shean up the valley to Allt an Àigh. It is walked by night, so that pilgrims reach the water in the right quarter of the moon. Fishermen who walk it are said to lose fewer boats; no count was kept either way.

title: The Hall declines the stream
body: Muireach Liath rules that Allt an Àigh belongs to the ancestors and the weather and not to the vein, and that the Hall will not keep it. Here the Keepers' rite and the older folk reverence first plainly part, and each side afterwards cites the ruling as proof that it was right.

title: Murchadh Mòr dies at Baile Mòr mhòr
body: Murchadh Mòr, eldest of Ailean's living sons and the first knotted on Sìne's cord, dies at his own seat close on three thousand years old, having outlived every one of his generation but Eithne and a scattering of the youngest.

title: Eleven knives for the north
body: Murchadh Mòr's eleven sons, none by the same mother, divide the great share of the north among themselves with a knife to each of the north's chief holdings, over eleven nights of arguing which hall goes with which knife.

title: Lachlann Mòr takes Baile Mòr mhòr
body: The eldest of Murchadh Mòr's eleven sons is given his father's own seat and its name with less argument than the rest of the division, none of his brothers wanting the weight of a hall so long held.

title: Donnchadh Iar disputes the western glens
body: The fourth of Murchadh Mòr's sons wins the western glens only after the longest argument of the whole division, and goes on calling the settlement unjust for years after.

title: The north's counties too small for twenty spears
body: What comes out of Baile Mòr mhòr's last division is a floor of small halls, none able to raise so much as twenty spears alone, a smallness the tellers already read as proof the long-lived blood was fading fastest from that line.

title: The sick carried to Muileann ruadh
body: The sick are carried up in litters to the warm springs below Muileann ruadh and bathed at dawn. The Keepers allow it, for the heat of the water comes from the mountain and no one breaks the stone for it.

title: Eachann Ruadh raids the Red Share's cattle
body: Eachann Ruadh rides a dozen men across the boundary stones into the Red Share's northern grazing and drives off near forty head before the alarm is fully raised, the old feud from Dùn thais finding a fresh grievance to spend itself on.

title: Muireach refuses the Hall's ground to the cattle
body: Asked to shelter the Red Share's recovered cattle on the Hall's own ground, Muireach Liath refuses, ruling that the ground was sworn to keep a man safe from a knife and never to make holy ground of every quarrel brought to his door.

title: A grey stone found apart from the vein
body: A shepherd of the ninth hearth, hunting a ewe caught in bracken a few miles north of Dùn ìseal, finds a grey stone with a bright wound where her stick scraped the moss away and carries it down out of curiosity. It sits on a sill at Dùn ìseal a season, turned over by whoever passes, before anyone thinks to put fire to it.

title: Fearchar Airgeadach smelts the first bead
body: Fearchar, a basket-carrier of the ninth hearth who has spent three winters tending the vein's fires, builds his own fire apart from the Hall on the spur where the stone was found and feeds it through a day and half a night. Old Tormod, dozing beside him, wakes to find a bead of soft bright metal in Fearchar's hand that answers to no fire the Hall has ever kept.

title: Muileann chiar named
body: Within a month Fearchar has raised a proper furnace of clay and dry stone on the spur and is hammering beads into rings. The households of the ninth hearth call the place Muileann chiar, the dark mill, after the smoke that hangs over it of a still morning, unmindful of the older place of that name far to the east.

title: Muireach Liath rules the silver shows no blood
body: Asked whether the new metal falls under the flame, Muireach Liath presses a ring's softest edge with his thumbnail, finds no colour beneath the break as a coal always shows, and rules that the Hall has no claim on a thing that shows no colour when it breaks. Fearchar is left free to dig on, and to keep or give what he digs.

title: Muileann chiar founded
body: A seam of silver is found near the great vein but apart from it. It is the first wealth of the island other than the coal.

title: The first ring set out for Goibhniu
body: Fearchar takes up the custom of setting the first ring off every new furnace whole on a flat stone at the mouth of the workings, an offering to Goibhniu, before a second ring is begun. No furnace of his ever fails in its first season, which the smiths of Muileann chiar take as proof the god has taken the offerings kindly.

title: Fearchar Airgeadach works the silver
body: Fearchar Airgeadach, a basket-carrier of the nine hearths, is the first known to smelt the silver of Muileann chiar and hammer it into rings. His furnace burns wood and peat. It is the first fire on the island that answers to no one in the Hall.

title: Silver is not holy
body: Asked whether the new seam falls under the flame, Muireach Liath answers that silver shows no colour when it breaks and so is not the mountain's. Muileann chiar is left free to dig as deep as it likes, and it digs. Every later quarrel over the silver begins from these words.

title: Two cousins of the eastern share claim the silver ground
body: Grandsons of one grandfather through different daughters, whose households have shared an unremarkable boundary along a dry burn since their grandfather's day, each send word to Dùn ìseal within days of the other, swearing the spur of Fearchar's furnaces lies on his own side of the burn. The keepers of the slab find the seam outside their reach to judge and send the cousins back to settle it themselves.

title: Fearchar pays a ring to each cousin
body: Weary of digging under a dispute he did not start, Fearchar offers a ring from the season's working to each of the two cousins, on condition that both let the digging go on undisturbed while their elders argue the boundary. Both take the ring, neither gladly, and the quarrel is settled within the year by a boundary stone the two households cut and raise together at the driest point of the burn.

title: The first ring traded at Ros fhionn
body: A carrier of the ninth hearth strikes the first known trade of a ring against a whole boatload of salted fish and sealskin at the river quays of Ros fhionn. The measure holds for every later bargain on the quay, so that a boatman naming a price says simply "a ring's worth" and is understood without further reckoning.

title: Death of Ceallach mac Ghille-Bhrìde
body: Ceallach, who has kept the coal of the First Flame in the high valleys since his father Gille-Brìde's death, dies in his sleep at the age of a hundred and forty, the last of Somhairle's line in whom the long years still showed. His household carries the coal down to the Hall's own flame; his children leave the high valleys within the year and settle among the lower hearths.

title: Silver for salt at Ros fhionn
body: Carriers take rings of Muileann chiar down to the river quays at Ros fhionn and trade them for salt fish and sealskin, one ring for a boatload. It is the first trade in anything but food, and the first whose price is remembered.

title: Three candidates passed over for the flame
body: On Muireach Liath's death the nine hearths weigh three households' candidates at length: a steady grandson of the sixth hearth, a daughter of the third hearth whose grandmother helped choose Beathag Bhàn, and Muireach's own nephew of the ninth hearth. All three are passed over in favour of Muireach's daughter Gormshuil, chosen on the work alone.

title: Death of Muireach Liath
body: Muireach Liath dies at Dùn ìseal, keeping the flame. The nine hearths pass over three of other lines and choose his daughter Gormshuil nic Mhuirich. After her the Keeper's office stays in the house of Muireach for many generations.

title: Muireach's nephew goes to the furnaces
body: Passed over for the flame on the strength of blood alone, Muireach Liath's nephew of the ninth hearth goes north within the year to take up work at one of Fearchar's furnaces at Muileann chiar, where he is said to prosper a good deal more than he might have as a Keeper chosen by kinship rather than by the households' own will.

title: Sliochd Mhuirich named
body: The kin of Gormshuil nic Mhuirich at Dùn ìseal begin to be called Sliochd Mhuirich, the house of Muireach, the first house of custody known by a name and not by a hearth. No account that survives tells of the other eight hearths objecting.

title: Sìleas counts the coal's colours
body: At the far-eastern Muileann chiar, Sìleas nic Coinnich begins counting which strokes of her own pick break the vein bright with colour and which break it plain dull coal, and notices the bright breaks come to no cutter's hand alone, not even her own, on every shift.

title: Sìleas's mother warns against the asking
body: Sìleas's mother, who cut the same wall before her, tells her that a question put to the vein is better left unput, and that the mountain has fed the house four generations without being asked why. Sìleas holds her tongue, but not her counting.

title: Sìleas moved from wall to wall
body: The overseer of Muileann chiar's galleries, wearying of a cutter who tries the coal's answer against fasting, singing and the hour of the day, moves Sìleas nic Coinnich from wall to wall until no face is left that has not already been asked her questions.

title: Sìleas withdraws to the holy wood
body: Sìleas nic Coinnich goes up into Coille Naomh Muileann chiar meaning only to sit and think, and finds three cutters of her own galleries have followed her there unasked, each carrying the same unspoken question from the face.

title: The first school of the druids founded
body: The first of the Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, the druid schools, gathers about one question: why the vein answers some hands and not others. For the first time within the Old Faith the coal is reasoned about, and not only revered.

title: Forty gather in the clearing
body: Two springs after the first evening in the wood, near forty cutters, basket-carriers and children of the overseer's own house sit in the clearing above Muileann chiar to hear Sìleas nic Coinnich set out her counting, more than the old fallen trunk she taught from can seat.

title: Sìleas nic Coinnich in the wood
body: Sìleas nic Coinnich, a cutter from Muileann chiar in the far east, begins to teach in Coille Naomh Muileann chiar. At the galleries she had seen the coal break bright with its colours under some cutters' picks and dull under others, and she will not let the question be.

title: A hearer walks a fortnight to the wood
body: A woman of the northern shore, having heard a story of a stag grown taller with every telling between her home and the wood, walks a fortnight to sit in Sìleas's clearing, and is told plainly that the counting, not the stag, is the whole of what is taught there.

title: The stag in the grove
body: The hearers of Sìleas nic Coinnich at Muileann chiar name themselves the stag's people, for a stag said to have stood in the grove through a whole lesson. The school's later name, the stag's name Camaran, and the telling that it was the white stag of Flidais, lady of the deer, are found first in writings far younger than these days.

title: Ìomhar Dearg killed at the ford
body: Riding to see a moved boundary stone on the Red Share's northern march, Ìomhar Dearg is speared through the throat at the ford of the Abhainn dhomhain by Eachann Ruadh mac Mhurchaidh, in payment for Aonghas Bàn's death at Dùn thais sixty years before. His riders bring him from the water dead.

title: The Red Share held whole under Dùghall Dearg
body: Dùghall Dearg mac Ìomhair takes up the Red Share entire the week his father is buried, and tells the four lines who come to Dùn dhearg with old claims that the share was won with a sword and will be kept with one. None presses a claim against his household.

title: Eachann Ruadh flees to the Hall's ground
body: Eachann Ruadh mac Mhurchaidh rides through the night from the ford to the ground before the Hall of the Flame, throws down his second spear, and sits within sight of Brìde's fire until the Keeper's cutters come out to him, asking the ground and nothing of the flame itself.

title: Gormshuil rules the Hall's ground holds even a killer
body: Gormshuil nic Mhuirich rules that no spear may follow Eachann Ruadh mac Mhurchaidh past the Hall's boundary stone, though what waits for him beyond it is not hers to answer for, and lets him raise a hut at the ground's edge to cut turf for the Hall's own fires.

title: A loaned cutter's report reaches Gormshuil
body: A cutter of Dùn ìseal's own galleries, home from a season's loan to Muileann chiar, tells the Hall in passing that the eastern cutters count their strokes and ask why the coal answers one hand and not another. Gormshuil sends her own cutter east to see the wood for herself.

title: Sìleas summoned to Dùn ìseal
body: Gormshuil nic Mhuirich summons Sìleas nic Coinnich to Dùn ìseal, and the two speak alone in the keepers' hut by the flame Beathag Bhàn once held. Neither afterwards gives a full account of what passed between them; only the ruling that follows is known.

title: The Hall shuts the galleries to the stag's people
body: Gormshuil nic Mhuirich forbids the hearers of Sìleas to cut in the galleries of Dùn ìseal, holding that a question asked of the vein is a demand made of it. The stag's people keep their school in the east and send no cutters to the mountain for a long while after.

title: The eastern cutters walk further into the hills
body: After the galleries of Dùn ìseal are shut to them, a dozen of Sìleas nic Coinnich's oldest hearers walk east out of Muileann chiar to raise a house of their own further from the mountain's shadow, following the wood where it thickens and the seam where it runs deeper.

title: Gormshuil nic Mhuirich dies at Dùn ìseal
body: Gormshuil, Keeper after Muireach Liath for thirty-eight years, dies in the small room off the Hall at the age of eighty-seven, her cutter's daughter and Fionnlagh Dall at her bedside. Her last words are a complaint about the cold of the room rather than any ruling, and the household keeps the telling of it fondly afterward.

title: Fionnlagh Dall chosen Keeper
body: The nine hearths choose Fionnlagh, blind since a childhood fever and a sitter with the flame for thirty years, over a cutter of the fourth hearth and Gormshuil's own niece, on the argument of the niece's household that his hands judge a measure more truly than a sighted man's. He is thirty-eight years old, the first blind Keeper the island has known.

title: Calum Beag begins leading the blind Keeper
body: A boy of ten who has followed Fionnlagh about the Hall since he could walk is brought to him by his own mother and asked to guide him through the galleries, on the one condition that he keep a Keeper's silence about what he sees there. He agrees at once, and the two go about Dùn ìseal together from that day.

title: A household at Cnoc dhubh burns by the basketful
body: In a bitter winter a household of the high ground above Cnoc dhubh, its measured handful not enough to warm three children and an old woman through the worst nights, burns the coal by the basketful instead, a measure no household has burned before. The smoke lies down in the still valley air and will not lift.

title: The smoke at Cnoc dhubh
body: In a hard winter a household at Cnoc dhubh burns its coal by the basketful and not by the handful. The smoke settles in the valley, and three of the household and two neighbours die of it. The Keepers are sent for, and the case is argued at Dùn ìseal for the rest of the season.

title: Five die of the smoke at Cnoc dhubh
body: Three of the burning household, a grandmother of the house beside it, and a neighbour's infant carried past the settling smoke are dead within three nights. Calum Beag carries the word to Fionnlagh, who goes up to the valley himself before any council is called.

title: The season of argument at Dùn ìseal
body: The dead household's kin argue that a law which lets a house freeze rather than burn what the mountain holds in plenty is no law worth keeping; the other eight hearths, frightened by what one family's basketful did to two houses that burned nothing at all, argue the measure must hold unargued or hold not at all. Fionnlagh gives no ruling for the better part of two months.

title: Calum Beag finds the grey stone
body: Sent into the hills above Dùn ìseal to find stone hard, fine-grained and free of any crack, Calum Beag returns three days later with a cutter of the fourth hearth and a slab slung between two poles. Fionnlagh spends the better part of a month testing it by hand before he lets the chisel near it.

title: The stone cup cut to two palms
body: Fionnlagh has the new cup cut hollow to the exact measure of his own two hands cupped together, palm to palm, trusting his own hands to be the one instrument that never changes. He tests the fill again and again by touch alone until he can judge a hair's difference against the stone's cold lip.

title: Fionnlagh Dall and the stone cup
body: Fionnlagh Dall, Keeper after Gormshuil, has the old keepers' stone cup cut anew in grey stone to hold just what a cupped pair of hands will hold, and sets it for the measure on the threshold of Talla na Lasrach at Dùn ìseal. He is blind, and fills it by touch before the council, and none can say afterwards that he favoured anyone's hands.

title: The cup set on the threshold
body: Rather than keep the new cup within the Hall where a favoured keeper's hand might reach it first, Fionnlagh sets it on the worn threshold stone of Talla na Lasrach, in the open, where any household or its neighbour can see the measure given. He finds the threshold's true centre by walking it barefoot.

title: An old woman of the fourth hearth trusts the measure
body: The first household to bring its claim to the new cup is a poor one, its elder's hands shaking with palsy. Fionnlagh fills the cup by touch, says "Enough" when the measure is met, and closes his hand over its lip. She weeps at a fairness she says she has not trusted from a sighted keeper in three years.

title: The lords swear the Small-Burning Law
body: At the Samhain gathering the lords of every share, grumbling but pressed by the memory of Cnoc dhubh and the weeping woman of the fourth hearth, swear the measured handful into a law binding on every share alike, each laying a hand on the stone cup itself. It is the first law the island has ever kept the same in every share.

title: The Small-Burning Law
body: The custom of the handful is made law: no household may burn more than a measured handful of the coal in a season. It becomes the holy law of the Keepers of Brìde's flame and Crom's stone, and it holds for centuries.

title: The first sentence under the Law
body: A household of Seann Tarr burns twice its measure in a season and loses its right to the coal for the season after, the first sentence given under the Small-Burning Law. Its name is set on the roll with the offence beside it, and for many centuries its descendants petition to have the offence struck out.

title: Seann Tarr sentenced under the new law
body: A fishing household of Seann Tarr, its catch ruined by wet weather, burns twice its measure to save its dried fish and is the first sentenced under the Small-Burning Law: it loses its right to the coal for the season following, its name and offence set on the roll. Fionnlagh gives the ruling with real reluctance.

title: The question of the beacon at Tobar dhearg
body: A fisherman of the southern coast asks the council whether a beacon lit to warn strangers off the rocks, and no household's own hearth, should be counted against a household's handful at all. Fionnlagh takes the better part of a day alone with the stone cup before he answers.

title: No coal on the beacons
body: The Keepers rule that no coal may feed a beacon, since a beacon burns for strangers. The fire on the headland at Tobar dhearg is kept with driftwood and seal fat, and so are all the sea-lights of the island after it.

title: Driftwood and seal fat light the sea-lights
body: Fionnlagh rules that no coal may feed a beacon meant for strangers, since the vein answers to the island's own and to no boat that might never touch its shore. The beacon at Tobar dhearg is kept after with driftwood and rendered seal fat, and every sea-light raised on the island after it is kept the same way.

title: Ailean Clachair takes on the steps to Ceann chaol
body: The council at Dùn ìseal asks the nine hearths' cutters whether any will cut a proper path down the steep mile above the harbour of Ceann chaol, where carriers going down sideways on bare rock have turned more ankles than the Hall has troubled to count. Ailean Clachair, a cutter of the fourth hearth four and twenty years old, steps forward first.

title: The carriers' path to Ceann chaol
body: A carriers' path is cut from the mountain down to the harbour of Ceann chaol, with steps hewn at the steep places. The Hall's baskets go down it to the southern households, and the dried fish of the south comes up.

title: The steps to Ceann chaol are finished
body: After two years of work by Ailean Clachair and six others of the fourth hearth, the stepped path down to the harbour of Ceann chaol is finished, cut stone where the rock allows a step and fitted stone where it does not. A carrier with a full basket can go down to the harbour on a wet morning without setting a hand to the rock.

title: Eleven carriers drown at the ford of the Abhainn dhomhain
body: A party of eleven carriers bound south with the Hall's baskets crosses the ford of the Abhainn dhomhain on a night of hard rain, led by Beathag nan Cliabh on her own word that the rising water looks no worse than a flood she remembers from her youth. The river rises over a tall man's head before the last of them is across; only the one carrier who turned back at the water's edge survives to carry word of it.

title: The carriers drowned on the Abhainn dhomhain
body: The Abhainn dhomhain rises in the night and takes eleven carriers and their baskets at a ford. The Hall mourns the coal with the carriers, and Fionnlagh Dall asks the council for a way across that the river cannot take.

title: The Hall sets the names of the drowned upon its roll
body: Fionnlagh Dall has the eleven names read to him twice before he will let the roll be closed, among them Beathag nan Cliabh, Griogair mac Ailig, Sìneag nighean Dhonnchaidh, and a boy the roll gives only as young Tormod of the salt shore, who went on the crossing in place of an uncle whose knee had gone bad in the wet.

title: The carriers' joke of the mourned coal
body: The carriers who come after the drowning make a joke of their own grief, saying the Hall mourns its coal along with its dead, since eleven baskets went into the river with the eleven who carried them. Fionnlagh, hearing it repeated to him, does not rebuke it, and says a mountain that measures its coal so carefully may be allowed to grieve a basketful lost the same way its people grieve a life.

title: Fionnlagh asks the council for a crossing the river cannot take
body: Fionnlagh brings the drowning before the council within the fortnight and asks for a crossing the Abhainn dhomhain cannot take in any weather. An elder of the southern hearths argues the river's risk is no worse than any ordinary misfortune; Fionnlagh answers that he asked only whether the risk could be made smaller, and asks who can name him a mason proved against water and weight.

title: Ailean Clachair is charged with the crossing at Ros fhionn
body: The council calls Ailean Clachair, whose steps above Ceann chaol a wet winter has not yet broken, and charges him with a single stone span above Ros fhionn, where the river runs narrower and its banks stand higher and firmer than anywhere else along its reach. Ailean answers that he does not know whether such a span can be built at all, but will try rather than tell a Keeper who has just buried eleven carriers that it cannot.

title: Ailean gathers the forty of the nine hearths
body: Over a winter Ailean draws forty cutters and masons from the nine hearths, none of whom has ever cut anything meant to hold a river's weight rather than a roof's. They quarry grey stone near Ros fhionn and spend a season learning how stone cut to a wedge's shape leans upon its neighbours and holds itself up by leaning.

title: The first bridges
body: Stone crossings begin to join the mining paths of the interior to the coast. From them in time come Drochaid Cathair dhearg and Drochaid Ros fhionn.

title: Aonghas Beag falls on the centring
body: In the sixth week of the building, a mason of the ninth hearth named Aonghas Beag puts a foot wrong on wet timber and is caught at the edge of the fall by two others. Ailean keeps him off the scaffold for two days, saying a mason frightened in his own body cuts stone worse than one who has never learned fear.

title: Ailean Clachair's crossing at Ros fhionn
body: Ailean Clachair and forty masons of the nine hearths bridge the river above Ros fhionn with a single span of fitted stone, from which Drochaid Ros fhionn descends. Ailean sets a hearth-sign in the keystone. Every bridge the masons build after bears one, and a bridge without it is not trusted.

title: The single span above Ros fhionn is closed
body: The keystone is raised on ropes and levers and set into the arch above Ros fhionn, Ailean himself guiding it the last hand's-width into place while the forty stand silent on both banks. The scaffold comes down within the week and the span stands alone over the water on its own weight and shape.

title: Ailean cuts the first hearth-sign in a keystone
body: Before the scaffold comes down, Ailean cuts the fourth hearth's own mark into the keystone's face, unasked, so that any eye that looks for it may know the stone was raised by hands that answer for their own work. The mark spreads to every span the forty raise after, and within a handful of years a crossing without it is said, not always fairly, to be a crossing built by hands that had not troubled to answer for themselves.

title: The masons swear the oath of the stone cup
body: Gathered at Dùn ìseal to be paid for the season's labour, the forty ask Fionnlagh whether they may swear a fellowship of their own. Each lays a hand on the stone cup at the threshold of Talla na Lasrach and swears that no span will ever be closed to a traveller in the dark, and none ever paid for in coal.

title: The masons' custom
body: The bridge-masons form a fellowship bound by an oath sworn on the stone cup at Dùn ìseal: no span to be closed in the dark, and none to be paid for in coal. Their lodge is kept near the western crossing, in the country of Ros dhomhain.

title: The masons' lodge is raised at the western crossing
body: Having kept together under Ailean's leading and raised three crossings more, the forty build a plain stone lodge beside the widest of the three, above a badly-used ford in the country of Ros dhomhain, where a mason called from any share may find a roof, a fire, and a fellow of the trade.

title: A carrier refuses an unsigned bridge
body: A cart-builder of Ros dhomhain throws an unmarked crossing of his own upriver of the western span. A carrier of the Hall's baskets, reaching it after dark, will not cross it, saying he knows whose oath a bridge without the fourth hearth's sign was not built under, and sleeps cold on the near bank rather than trust it.

title: Mòr nic Dhùghaill feeds three carriers in the rain
body: A widow of Doire shean with more buffalo than grass boils a haunch for three carriers caught by a mud-slicked path, and asks no coin for it. Word of the free bowl travels the mountain road faster than any basket on it, and within a year she has built a second room to feed the men it sends her.

title: The tavern roads begin
body: The first waypoint houses are raised along the mining roads. From them come in time Am Buabhall Fortanach, An Taigh-òsta Grianach and the others of the circuit.

title: The turf longhouse raised at the crossing
body: Three families of the fourth hearth build a long turf house where the mountain road meets the road to the western harbours, a hearth burning at either end for carriers going up and carriers coming down. Its long central table becomes the place where news of the whole road first gathers as one telling.

title: Mòr nic Dhùghaill's house
body: Mòr nic Dhùghaill, a widow of Doire shean, keeps the first waypoint house on the site of Am Buabhall Fortanach. She serves the carriers jugged buffalo from her own herd, and the house has served it ever since.

title: Seann Mhorn resettled and its name kept
body: Fishers of the nine hearths find old house-footings above a good landing on the western shore of Loch chrom, and a name already fixed to the place that is not of their own tongue. They keep the name rather than giving it a new one, judging that a name found standing has more right to stay than one a stranger could invent.

title: The house at the middle of the road
body: A second waypoint house is built where the carriers' road from the mountain meets the road to the western harbours, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr. It is a turf longhouse with a hearth at either end, one for carriers going up and one for carriers coming down.

title: Seann Warr resettled beside it
body: Families walking the same road find a second harbour a short way along the shore, house-footings there as well, and build on them without asking whose. Seann Warr and Seann Mhorn grow together within the century, sharing a landing, a market day and a single waypoint house where the mountain road meets the sea.

title: A chase stopped at Mòr's door
body: A man fleeing his cousin's kin over an old knife-wound takes shelter at Mòr nic Dhùghaill's table, and his three pursuers, knives at their belts, find her standing between them and the fire. She swears there will be no blade drawn under her roof for any grievance, old or new, and feeds all four from the one pot until the debt walks back out onto the open road unsettled between them.

title: The road-peace
body: The keepers of the waypoint houses agree that no feud may be pursued under an inn roof or within a spear's throw of its door. The custom is first set down at the house on the site of An Sligeanach Fad' às. It is the oldest law on the island that neither Keeper nor lord made.

title: The road-peace kept as custom
body: Word of the chase stopped at Mòr's door runs the mountain road faster than any basket that season, and other waypoint houses along the circuit take up the same custom unasked: no feud pursued and no blade drawn under a road-house roof or within a spear's throw of its door.

title: Niall Òg sits at Mòr's table
body: The old heir Niall Òg walks the mountain road to see for himself the house where a widow's word held two feuding kin to one table, and is given the same bowl and the same seat as any other traveller. He leaves a ring behind that Mòr will not keep, saying a man who has outlived his own quarrels can afford, once in a while, to pay for a peace he did not make.

title: Seann Mhorn resettled
body: Fishers of the nine hearths settle the harbour at Seann Mhorn and keep the name they find there, which is not of their own tongue; the old name came with the stones, they say. It is the first such name known to be taken over and not replaced.

title: Seann Warr resettled
body: Families walking the new road from the mountain settle the harbour of Seann Warr on the western shore of Loch chrom in like manner. They find house-footings there already, and build on them, as the carriers' song has it, without asking whose.

title: Death of Fionnlagh Dall
body: Fionnlagh Dall dies at Dùn ìseal. At his own asking he is not laid on the slope with the Keepers before him, but carried south to the old graves near Cnoc dhìreach, which no living people had yet claimed.

title: Fionnlagh Dall carried to the old graves
body: The bearers are eleven days on the road with the body of Fionnlagh Dall, and lay it at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach among graves older than any name. The Keepers after him cannot agree why he asked it; two answers are given, and neither is chosen.

title: Fionnlagh Dall asks to be carried south
body: Dying at four-and-ninety after fifty-six years keeping the flame, Fionnlagh Dall tells Calum Beag he wishes to be laid not on the Keepers' own slope but in the unclaimed old graves near Cnoc dhìreach, ground no household's cord has ever divided. He dies within the month, his last words a question about whether the flame had been fed.

title: The eleven days' bearing
body: Bearers carry Fionnlagh Dall's body the twenty miles to Cnoc dhìreach in eleven days rather than three, as every hearth on the road asks to carry him some part of the way. Calum Beag walks the whole distance at the litter's head, the only bearer who never once hands off his own share of the weight.

title: Tuam Cnoc dhìreach hallowed
body: Fionnlagh Dall is laid in the ancient, unclaimed burying-ground near Cnoc dhìreach, the first burial there any living hand has set down by name. The Keepers hallow the ground that same season, and it passes from belonging to no one to belonging, by the Hall's own reckoning, to everyone.

title: The grave-keepers of Cnoc dhìreach paid in coal
body: A handful of families settle by Tuam Cnoc dhìreach to tend the grave, and the Hall pays them one measured handful of coal each a season, the only service the Small-Burning Law is ever known to reward in coal rather than coin or kind.

title: Mòr nic Dhùghaill dies at her own hearth
body: Found sitting upright in her fireside chair one morning by her own daughter, Mòr nic Dhùghaill dies at sixty-two, two years after Fionnlagh Dall. Her daughter and a niece take up the pot the same week, and the house does not miss a single night's fire.

title: The mausoleum consecrated
body: Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, already ancient, is hallowed by the Keepers over the grave of Fionnlagh Dall, the first burial there that is set down by name. The burial-ground that no one claimed is claimed.

title: Calum Beag sets a marker at the grave
body: Calum Beag, now an old man, carries a plain stone the whole way to Cnoc dhìreach on his own back and sets it at Fionnlagh Dall's grave-head with his own hands, cut with nothing but the shape of the stone cup and no name, judging the shape said enough on its own.

title: The grave-keepers of Cnoc dhìreach
body: A few families settle at Cnoc dhìreach to tend Tuam Cnoc dhìreach after the Keeper's burial. The Hall pays them in coal, a handful each a season, the only payment in coal the Law ever allows.

title: The wedding insult at Ros dhomhain
body: At a mason's wedding on the western share, Griogair mac Lachlainn of Sliochd Fhionnghail strikes Tormod mac Ruairidh of Sliochd Artair across the face with a drinking-horn after a slight against Fionnghal nic Ailein's memory. Both men are dragged from the hall still nursing the insult, and the two lines that had traded fish for grain for three generations begin refusing each other's carriers at their waypoint houses.

title: The first raid of the wedding quarrel
body: A dozen head of cattle are lifted from a salt-shore pasture by men who call it payment owed for the insult at Ros dhomhain. A barn burns on the western share's ground within the season in answer, and within five years neither line can say with certainty who struck first.

title: Eimhir nic Mhuirich chosen to keep the flame
body: The nine hearths choose Eimhir nic Mhuirich, of the hearth-line and past sixty already, to keep the flame at Dùn ìseal. She holds the Hall to its measure through the widening quarrel of the king's blood, judging no man's raids and taking no side between Sliochd Fhionnghail and Sliochd Artair.

title: Tormod mac Ruairidh asks the Hall's blessing on a raid
body: Tormod mac Ruairidh comes to Dùn ìseal asking Eimhir nic Mhuirich to bless a raid he calls justice rather than vengeance. She hears him out and refuses, telling him the Hall keeps coal and not grudges, and that the flame she keeps was lit before his own great-grandfather was born.

title: Fionnghal nic Ailein dies
body: Fionnghal nic Ailein, daughter of Ailean Mòr and holder of the western share since the age's early years, dies at Ros dhomhain some two thousand eight hundred and forty-four years old. Her funeral is the last occasion on which Sliochd Fhionnghail and Sliochd Artair stand under one roof without a blow struck.

title: Eimhir nic Mhuirich dies
body: Eimhir nic Mhuirich dies at Dùn ìseal some eighty years old, having kept the flame through fifty-four years of the widening strife of the heirs more steadily than the quarrel's own principals kept their tempers. The nine hearths choose a younger Keeper who holds much the same course.

title: Artair mac Ailein dies
body: Artair mac Ailein, son of Ailean Mòr and holder of the salt shore at Baile ghorm, dies at his own hall some two thousand six hundred years old, the widening feud between his own descendants and Fionnghal's a weight he carried into his last years and could not set down.

title: Cormac mac Ailein dies
body: Cormac mac Ailein, son of Ailean Mòr and holder of the eastern share at Caol shean, dies some two thousand four hundred and fifty-three years old, the last of Ailean's own children still living at the strife's true middle. His last wish, that his household keep clear of the western quarrel, is honoured for less than a generation.

title: Niall Òg calls a peace at the crossing of Ros fhionn
body: Niall Òg sets a long table on neutral ground at the crossing of Ros fhionn and brings the heads of Sliochd Fhionnghail and Sliochd Artair to it unarmed, hoping to loosen a quarrel now two generations old. Each recites a longer account of wrongs than he came with, neither offers an apology, and both walk home by the same road they came by.

title: The raids resume after the failed peace
body: Within the season of Niall Òg's failed peace at Ros fhionn, raids between Sliochd Fhionnghail and Sliochd Artair begin again, if indeed they had ever truly stopped for the meeting.

title: The tally-stick of Cnoc leathan
body: A household of the fourth hearth at Cnoc leathan, sworn to neither quarrelling line, keeps a tally-stick notched for whichever share's steward calls first each season. By the century's turn it carries better than a hundred and fifty notches on each face, a plainer record than either quarrelling line keeps of its own raids.

title: Eachann Ruadh mac Mhurchaidh dies in his bed
body: Eachann Ruadh mac Mhurchaidh, who killed Ìomhar Dearg at a ford four generations before in vengeance for his brother, dies quietly in his bed at seven hundred and twenty-nine years old, the last of his generation of the king's kin. His own line, long at peace with the Red Share, takes no fresh quarrel from his death.

title: The hearth-elders sound out Eilidh nic Ìomhair
body: Two elders of the nine hearths walk from Dùn ìseal to Dùn dhearg to ask Eilidh nic Ìomhair, a granddaughter's granddaughter of Ìomhar Dearg who keeps the Red Share's granary rolls, whether she would be persuaded to sit a season with the coal. She names the difficulty herself before they can raise it: her own blood.

title: Eilidh tells the elders to choose another
body: Eilidh nic Ìomhair tells the two hearth-elders plainly to choose one of the other names put forward, having no wish to force the question of her own blood against the Binding's old rule.

title: Eilidh nic Ìomhair keeps the flame
body: The nine hearths choose a Keeper from outside the house of Muireach for the first time: Eilidh nic Ìomhair, of Dùn dhearg, of the line of Ìomhar Dearg and so of the king's blood. Sliochd Mhuirich, holding to the Binding, refuses for a season, then yields at Dùn ìseal, on the condition that the stone cup never leaves Talla na Lasrach.

title: The Keeper before Eilidh dies at the cup
body: The Keeper who held the flame after Eimhir nic Mhuirich dies sitting on the low stool beside the stone cup at Talla na Lasrach, her hands folded in her lap. The small lamp beside her burns out unfed in the night, the first time in living memory that any lamp in the Hall has been let go dark.

title: The cup left unfilled a season
body: For the better part of a year after the nine hearths choose Eilidh, Sliochd Mhuirich refuses to yield the flame, and the stone cup at Talla na Lasrach sits under the care of the hearth-line's own eldest, unfilled by any new hand, while every market and threshing floor on the mountain airs an opinion on the matter.

title: The argument of the diluted blood
body: Eilidh's own kin argue to her, and to anyone who will listen, that half the households in the hills carry some thread of the king's blood by now, so that the Binding's old rule has become a rule against nearly everybody or nobody. Eilidh answers that the argument settles nothing Sliochd Mhuirich has actually asked.

title: The hearth-line eldest offers the cup's condition
body: The eldest of Sliochd Mhuirich comes to the Hall's threshold and offers a single condition for yielding the flame to Eilidh nic Ìomhair: that the stone cup Fionnlagh Dall cut to the measure of two palms shall never, for any cause, be carried out through the door of Talla na Lasrach.

title: Eilidh swears to the cup's condition
body: Eilidh nic Ìomhair swears before the nine hearths that the stone cup will never leave Talla na Lasrach, her hand flat on its rim, and takes the coal that same afternoon, the measure poured level to her palm exactly as for every Keeper before her.

title: Sliochd Thormoid names Tormod Liath
