body: At a gathering of the nine hearths, the eldest of Sliochd Thormoid names for the first time an ancestor called Tormod Liath, said to have held the hill itself under the old king, as the ground of the house's claim to a voice in the Keeper's office.

title: Sliochd Raghnaill names Raghnall Ceannfhionn
body: Sliochd Raghnaill answers Sliochd Thormoid's claim with its own, naming an ancestor Raghnall Ceannfhionn, though the house rests its true weight less on any hill than on the plain fact that its boats carry more coal down the coast in a bad season than any other house's carts carry inland.

title: Eilidh binds the office to four houses
body: Eilidh nic Ìomhair puts to the nine hearths that the Keeper's office be bound from that season to four houses of custody alone, Sliochd Mhuirich, Sliochd Ìomhair, Sliochd Thormoid and Sliochd Raghnaill, and that the other hearths keep their council seats but surrender any further claim on the flame.

title: The Four Houses sworn
body: Under Eilidh nic Ìomhair the office of Keeper is bound to four houses of custody: Sliochd Mhuirich of Dùn ìseal, Sliochd Ìomhair of Dùn dhearg, Sliochd Thormoid of Seann Dunn and Sliochd Raghnaill of Seann Tarr. The other hearths keep their seats on the council, but lose their claim to the flame. Most of the later nobility of the island descends from one of the four, or says it does.

title: The grumble over Seann Dunn's fullest lamp
body: The other three houses grumble that Sliochd Thormoid's coal-lamp at Seann Dunn always burns fuller than the Law's measure allows, though no cutter sent to check it ever finds a grain over the handful. Eilidh judges the grievance one best left to wear out on its own.

title: The house of Tormod at Seann Dunn
body: Sliochd Thormoid raises a hall and a shrine at Seann Dunn, facing the mountain across the river. A lamp of coal burns in the shrine at the Law's measure. The other houses complain that the measure of Seann Dunn is always the fullest.

title: Sliochd Raghnaill grows rich on the fishing
body: The house that took its seat at Seann Tarr, the very town first sentenced under the Small-Burning Law, keeps no galleries and cuts no coal, choosing boats instead, and grows rich enough within two generations that its neighbours stop mentioning the old offence.

title: The house of Raghnall at Seann Tarr
body: Sliochd Raghnaill takes for its seat Seann Tarr on the north-eastern coast, the town whose household was first sentenced under the Law. The house keeps boats and not galleries, and grows rich on the fishing.

title: The wager at Seann Tarr's quay
body: Tormod Ruadh, a steersman of Sliochd Raghnaill, insists through a winter of evenings at Seann Tarr's quay that a boat could as easily be sailed round the black island Eilean dhubh as fished within sight of it, and finds himself, come spring, with a crew of four and a wager too large to back out of.

title: Round Eilean dhubh
body: Boats of Sliochd Raghnaill sail round Eilean dhubh and come home, the first voyage made to see a coast and not to fish it. The house's songs name the steersman Tormod Ruadh. He brings back word of rock and birds, and of having gone, and of nothing else.

title: The strand mistakes Tormod Ruadh's boat for a stranger's
body: A strand that has never before had reason to look for a boat of Seann Tarr's from that quarter of the sea sights Tormod Ruadh's boat rounding Eilean dhubh's far side and takes alarm at it, word of the strange sighting reaching Dùn ìseal well ahead of the boat's own return.

title: Murchadh Ruadh's household loses its right
body: The household of Murchadh Ruadh of Baile chrom is stripped of its right under the Law for a third offence, and goes down to the strand with what it can carry rather than beg cold porridge from kin. No hearth on the coast will give it coal after, or discuss why.

title: The outlaws of the north-west waters
body: Households stripped of their right under the Law for a third offence take to boats, live off the north-western waters, and raid the fishing strands. They are called spùinneadairean, plunderers, and the name stays with those waters after them.

title: A strand south of Baile chrom burned in the dark
body: Boats out of no household raid a fishing strand half a day south of Baile chrom in the small hours of a moonless night, burning two houses to their footings and stripping the drying-racks bare. A woman of the strand says she knew two of the raiders by their voices, and will not name them.

title: The boat lost off the north-west
body: A fishing boat out of Baile chrom is lost in calm water off the north-western coast. The two men who swim home say that something rose under it. Each year thereafter the boat's village keeps a wake for it. Of the thing they saw no more is told.

title: The wake first kept for the five
body: A year to the day after Cailean Buidhe's boat is lost in the calm off Baile chrom, the strand sets out a bowl for the five who went out on her and speaks the boat's name once over it. Anndra Cìobair, one of the two who swam home, pours the first cup, and goes on pouring it every year after.

title: The fire at Baile chrom relit
body: After the loss the fishers of Baile chrom light the old beacon on the point again, fed with driftwood as the Law requires. From it comes Taigh-solais Baile chrom.

title: The keeping of the beacon falls to the households in turn
body: Once the old beacon on the Baile chrom headland is relit, the carrying of driftwood to feed it becomes a charge the coast's households take up one season at a time, the way other coasts keep a granary door or a toll-stick.

title: Seann Bhrenn resettled
body: Fishers from the north side of the mountain settle the harbour of Seann Bhrenn on the northern coast and keep its old name, as the western settlers kept Seann Warr's. They find a stone quay under the silt and use it.

title: Word of the stone quay travels the coast
body: News of the worked stone quay found under the silt at Seann Bhrenn reaches Baile chrom by trader's boat, grown in the telling to a buried town in one mouth and shrunk to a single stone in another, neither telling closer to the truth than the other.

title: The ancestor-cairn at Cathair naomh
body: The people of Cathair naomh in the north raise a cairn for their dead on the hill above the town, and bring it a stone at every burial. It is the greatest ancestor-cairn in the north, and it grows still.

title: Word of the cairn at Cathair naomh travels the coast
body: Word reaches Baile chrom of the growing ancestor-cairn on the hill above Cathair naomh, carried a stone at a time at every burial, and travellers who see it years apart swear the hill itself looks changed.

title: The panthers let pass
body: The crossing of the great cats is found to run straight over the carriers' southern road. Eilidh nic Ìomhair rules that no panther may be killed on the road in its season, and the carriers wait in the waypoint houses until the crossing is done. The rule is kept, for it costs the carriers only time.

title: The carriers of the southern road grumble at the panthers' ruling
body: Told as far as Baile chrom, the tale of Eilidh nic Ìomhair's ruling on the great cats' crossing carries with it the carriers' first grumbling at the delay, and her answer that a Law which measures every handful can measure a few days' patience too.

title: The granaries of Dùn dhearg opened to households not its own
body: Sliochd Ìomhair opens the new granaries at Dùn dhearg to any household of the lowland plain caught short by the storm season, not only its own. Coinneach Mòr, still a young man of Seann Dunn, watches the queue at the gate and hears his father call it a debt of bread that few who take it yet feel as a debt.

title: The granaries of Dùn dhearg
body: Sliochd Ìomhair builds stone granaries at Dùn dhearg and fills them from the lowland fields of its share, holding grain against the storm season as the old custom of sharing asks. So the house gains what the Hall never had: people who owe it their bread.

title: Anndra Cìobair dies at Baile chrom
body: Anndra Cìobair, who swam home from Cailean Buidhe's boat and kept the wake's first cup for near forty years, dies in his own bed above the strand he never left, and is buried within sight of the headland he tended.

title: The resting-place at the foot of the pass becomes Baile Mòr dhomhain
body: The carriers' resting-place at the last flat ground before the high pass grows byres, a smithy and an inn that is never empty in the season the pass is open, and takes the name Baile Mòr dhomhain, though it stands on no deep water and lives by the pass and little else.

title: Baile Mòr dhomhain at the foot of the pass
body: Carriers who take the Hall's baskets north over the high pass settle at its southern foot, where Baile Mòr dhomhain now stands, to rest their beasts before the climb. The town lives by the pass, and by little else.

title: The reverent centuries
body: Generation after generation mines the same small measure and burns the same small measure, and the people neither grow nor dwindle, whichever lord's share they live in. The rolls call them the reverent centuries.

title: Coinneach Mòr chosen Keeper of Sliochd Thormoid
body: In the month of Giblean, the four houses choose Coinneach Mòr mac Tormoid, five-and-twenty, first Keeper of his house, for his patience rather than any gift of speech, judging a Keeper who keeps a flame steadily worth more than one who keeps it brilliantly for a short while.

title: Coinneach Mòr mac Tormoid keeps the flame
body: Coinneach Mòr mac Tormoid of Seann Dunn becomes the first Keeper of Sliochd Thormoid. He keeps the flame longer than any Keeper before him, and changes nothing while he keeps it.

title: Griogair Ruadh asks a seat for Achadh chaol and is refused
body: The headman of the shepherds at Achadh chaol asks the council at Dùn ìseal for a seat among the houses that govern the plain, and is refused for want of hearth-right cut in stone at the Roinn. He sits one courtesy season and goes home with the dues still owed and no seat won.

title: The shepherds of Achadh chaol
body: Shepherds settle the upland fields at Achadh chaol in the north-east and send their wool down to the harbours. Their headman sits one season on the council at Dùn ìseal, is found to hold no hearth-right, and goes home.

title: Coinneach's walkers set out to list the ruins
body: Coinneach Mòr sends six walkers the length of the plain to list every ruin standing on ground the four houses claim, ruling before they leave that the list shall say only who does not own each place, and never guess who built it.

title: The walkers return with the list of the old people's ruins
body: The walkers come home after two years with Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, Làrach an Dùin, Làrach an Teampaill and the plain's scattered standing stones set down on one list, each entry naming who does not hold the ground and none guessing at the builders, who are called after only the old people.

title: The first ring of stakes raised round Carragh Cnoc bheag
body: Once the walkers' list names the standing stone above Cnoc bheag, the household nearest it fences the rise to keep cattle from rubbing the cut letters smooth. Each generation after renews the stakes, and the stone itself is never moved.

title: The Keepers' count of the old places
body: Coinneach Mòr sends walkers to list the ruins of the old people. They bring back Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, Làrach an Dùin, Làrach an Teampaill and the standing stones. The list says who does not own each place, and not who built it; the Keepers rule that it shall not guess.

title: The bath-house roofed over the springs of Muileann ruadh
body: After a cousin of his own house is carried to the warm springs half dead of a wasting cough and comes home breathing, Coinneach Mòr orders a bath-house raised over the largest pool, with sleeping-places for the sick and benches for those who wait out the cure beside them.

title: A keeper of the springs named in Dian Cècht's name
body: Coinneach Mòr names a widow who nursed her own husband through a wasting fever as keeper of the springs at Muileann ruadh, the office set in the healer Dian Cècht's name and answering to no measure of coal, the first such office the flame at Seann Dunn has made.

title: The silversmiths of Muileann chiar cast their weights
body: Weary of disputes at their own market, the silversmiths of Muileann chiar cast a set of weights from a barley-corn to a newborn lamb, checked one against another and set out for any trader to use. Within years a thing weighed there is called, the length of the carriers' roads, weighed fairly.

title: Torcall Donn weds Muireall nic Ìomhair
body: Torcall Donn, great-grandson of Eithne nic Ailein and five-and-eighty, weds Muireall nic Ìomhair, not yet four-and-twenty, at Dùn dhearg, a match both houses call costless and both houses are pleased with, her marriage-portion drawn to satisfy both grants at once.

title: Muireall nic Ìomhair dies in her first winter
body: Muireall nic Ìomhair dies of a nine-day fever in her first winter as a wife, leaving no child and no settled answer to which grant, the house of Ìomhar's or the line of Eithne's, should hold her lands should she die too soon, since no one had thought she would.

title: The fence round Carragh Cnoc bheag
body: The people of Cnoc bheag set a ring of stakes round the old standing stone above their town, that the cattle may not rub against it. Every generation after renews the ring. The stone is never moved.

title: Both houses claim Muireall's lands
body: The house of Ìomhar claims Muireall's marriage-lands as returning to the kin that granted them; the line of Eithne claims the same ground as passing to the husband's holding. Both claims are argued with equal heat by men who never asked, while she lived, which grant should prevail.

title: The first double-sworn field burned
body: A holding sworn to both Dùn dhearg and Cathair mhòr since Muireall's marriage-portion touched it is burned in a single night by its own near neighbours, byre first and standing barley after. The household goes to kin elsewhere, and the ground lies unsown, claimed loudly and worked by neither house.

title: The bath-house at Muileann ruadh
body: A roofed bath-house is built over the warm springs below Muileann ruadh, with sleeping-places for the sick and their bearers. The Hall appoints a keeper of the springs, who tends them in the name of Dian Cècht, the healer. It is the first office the Hall makes that has nothing to do with the coal.

title: Coinneach Mòr dies at Seann Dunn
body: Coinneach Mòr mac Tormoid dies at Seann Dunn in his eighty-seventh year, two-and-sixty years into his keeping, asking after the walkers' list and the burned marriage-lands in his last days, and leaving the flame to a nephew chosen in his stead with the smoke of the burnings still on the southern horizon.

title: The silver weights of Muileann chiar
body: The silversmiths of Muileann chiar cast a set of weights, the least the weight of a barley-corn and the greatest that of a newborn lamb. Every trader on the carriers' roads comes to use them, and for the rest of the age a thing weighed at Muileann chiar is said to be weighed fairly.

title: Fearghas sends the last untroubled tithe
body: Fearghas Dà-Mhionn weighs out his sheaves for Dùn dhearg and for Cathair mhòr at Muileann chiar as he has every harvest of his long life, a little short to each, not yet knowing it is the last year either hall will let the joke stand.

title: The black-eaved holding east of Achadh mhòr
body: A double-sworn household two valleys east chooses the Red Share and is burned to its field-walls by Cathair mhòr's men before the next harvest, its cattle driven off and its house left standing empty as a warning to the next household asked to choose.

title: A holding that chose neither is burned by both
body: A double-sworn holding south of Achadh mhòr refuses to choose between its lords and is burned within the year by both hosts in turn, the Red Share's riders taking the barn first and a company of Cathair mhòr's finishing it, each telling its own men it punished only what the other began.

title: Fearghas rides to see a burned holding
body: Fearghas rides to the black-eaved holding east of his own fields to see with his own eyes what a double-sworn household looks like once burned, and finds only standing walls, fallen roofs and a dog that will not leave the ruin, and speaks of the war differently after.

title: A burned widow's household shelters at Achadh mhòr
body: A widow and her three sons, burned out in the southern raids, shelter three nights at Fearghas's hall on their way to kin beyond Ceann leathan, and Fearghas feeds them without asking any oath of them, telling his steward a household already burned has paid enough.

title: Torcall Donn killed on the road below Dùn thais
body: Torcall Donn, great-grandson of Eithne and husband of the dead Muireall nic Ìomhair, is killed at a hundred and eighteen years old when his company meets a company of the Red Share's riders on a narrow road and the pushing between them turns to blows.

title: Fearghas sends barley to be burned at Torcall Donn's grave
body: Fearghas sends a measure of his own barley to be burned at Torcall Donn's graveside at Cathair mhòr, the old rite for a man dead before his harvest is in, asking that no word go with it saying who sent it; the giver is known within the season regardless.

title: The Red Share presses its claim after the widower's death
body: With Torcall Donn dead, the Red Share presses its claim on Muireall's three granges harder rather than less, judging Cathair mhòr's grip on lands held only through a dead man's marriage weaker than before, and the war burns on past the quarrel that began it.

title: Ciorstaidh's stone set in Fearghas's hall
body: Fearghas has a stone cut for his grandmother Ciorstaidh and set into his own hall wall, her name and the sign of the cut knot beside it, wanting it known in stone that the house he holds was held first by one of the eleven who answered for their double oath all their lives.

title: The mason of Muileann chiar carries the tale
body: The stone-cutter who set Ciorstaidh's memorial breaks his promise of silence at the first market he reaches, and the setting of the stone becomes, within a season, one more thing told of Fearghas Dà-Mhionn on both sides of the war, read two different ways by two different hearths.

title: The burning of Achadh mhòr
body: Cogadh an Dà Mhionn, the War of the Two Oaths, ends where it began. Fearghas Dà-Mhionn, lord of the granary fields of Achadh mhòr, sworn both to the line of Ìomhar and to the lords of Cathair mhòr, is called to arms by each against the other, and both come to take his fields. The fields are burned to the stubble, and Fearghas dies in his hall.

title: Sìth an Stairsnich
body: The lords of the shares swear the Peace of the Threshold, Sìth an Stairsnich, on the threshold of Talla na Lasrach, beside the stone cup, with the Keeper as witness. No share may be parted again at a death: a holding passes whole to one heir. No man may swear to two lords. The boundary stones are set where they stand that day. So ends Aimhreit nan Oighrean.

title: The market under the Hall
body: A market is held under the walls of the Hall at Dùn ìseal on the four quarter days, Samhain, Là Fhèill Brìde, Bealltainn and Lùnastal, when the households of the eastern hills come up with their dues. Hides, venison, charcoal, honey and the silver of Muileann chiar change hands there on the new weights. The Keepers allow no coal to be sold on their ground, and none is.

title: Both hosts called out for Achadh mhòr
body: In the heat of Lùnastal the Red Share's council and Cathair mhòr's both resolve within the same week to take Achadh mhòr's granary whole, and two riders reach Fearghas within an hour of each other, each astonished that his own lord's host was not first to move.

title: The last sheaf of Achadh mhòr carried clear of the fire
body: The reapers finish the western cutting and carry the last sheaf, bound and cut high as the custom asks, clear of the burning fields before the wind turns, and it is this sheaf, not the granary, that the households round about keep afterward at every harvest's end.

title: The waypoint house at Muileann chiar begins tallying grain
body: In the season after Achadh mhòr's burning, the keeper of the waypoint house on the road below Muileann chiar chalks a slate with every granary along the carriers' road still holding grain, and rubs it out and chalks it again as the hungry winter empties one store after another. Carriers come to ask him for news of bread before they ask for news of the war.

title: A household of the middle plain sends its youngest son begging seed corn
body: A family two days' walk from Achadh mhòr's blackened fields sends its youngest son round every kinsman it has, sworn or unsworn to either share, asking only for seed corn against the spring sowing and not for grain to eat that winter. He comes home with less than he asked for, gathered a handful at a time from households as pinched as his own.

title: Ruairidh Glas writes to Eithne nic Ailein
body: Ruairidh Glas, holder of the Red Share at Dùn dhearg, sends word to Eithne nic Ailein of Cathair mhòr's plain that a war fought over a granary which no longer stands profits neither of their hungry households, and asks her to name ground where neither hall need be ashamed to meet.

title: Eithne nic Ailein names the threshold of Talla na Lasrach
body: Eithne nic Ailein answers Ruairidh Glas that she will set foot in no hall of the Red Share's, as he will set foot in none of hers, and names instead the threshold of Talla na Lasrach at Dùn ìseal, where the stone cup stands on ground that belongs to no share and never has.

title: A reluctant lord is shamed into the swearing
body: The steward of a lesser holding north of Achadh mhòr answers Eithne's summons that his lord sees no profit in standing bareheaded before an old woman to be told what he knows already. Eithne sends back that he may explain to his own hungry households why the peace that feeds everyone else's has passed his door by, and he comes a season late to swear it.

title: Eithne nic Ailein is carried up to Dùn ìseal
body: Eithne nic Ailein, whose legs have long since stopped carrying her, is borne up the old carriers' road to Dùn ìseal in a chair, one pole carried by Niall Òg, who has outlived nearly every other soul that remembers the valley of the Roinn, and who tells her, on the road, that she is the last one left who remembers what he remembers.

title: The Keeper drafts and reads the terms of the Threshold
body: At the asking of both halls, neither of which trusts the other's clerks to write the terms fairly, the Keeper of the flame drafts the peace herself and reads it aloud to the gathered stones before any lord is asked to swear, so that the households standing beyond the lords may carry the whole of it home in their own words.

title: Ruairidh Glas speaks of the first blood at Dùn thais
body: Swearing the Peace of the Threshold with his hand still on the stone cup, Ruairidh Glas says before the gathered lords that he shed the first blood of the strife at Dùn thais over cattle on a wet slope, when he was young enough to think a stone worth a life, and that he would not buy it again for twice the grazing on the island.

title: A double-sworn household on the old boundary gives up one oath
body: A household sworn to two lords since a marriage two generations back keeps the oath that has cost it least and lets the other lapse before the spring sowing, its eldest son reasoning aloud that neither hall's carrier had once knocked on their door in the whole of the hungry winter past.

title: The first Threshold market stands thin and unparted
body: The first quarter-day market held below Talla na Lasrach after the Peace draws little to sell, the hungry winter having left small surplus, and many households come only to watch whether a trader of the Red Share can stand at a stall beside one of Cathair mhòr's plain without a steward of either hall coming to part them. None comes.

title: The boundary lines of the middle plain settle by the sowing
body: By the time of the spring sowing after the Peace, the boundary lines that had shifted and blurred through forty years of burning have settled again into a shape that will hold for longer than any lord who swore to it that Samhain will live to see, with only small mendings asked at Dùn ìseal in the years after.

title: The stag's people at Cnoc bhàn
body: A house of the stag's people is founded at Cnoc bhàn, north of the mountain, and after the long exclusion takes cutters again. Its teachers keep the question of Sìleas nic Coinnich as she left it: why does the coal show its colours for one hand and not another?

title: The nine hearths raise Seonaid Chiar to the flame
body: The nine hearths of Dùn ìseal raise Seonaid Chiar of the house of Muireach to the flame at six-and-twenty years old, the youngest Keeper chosen since Muireach Liath's own day. Her grandmother, a cutter of the galleries all her working life, warns her that a young Keeper who bends once in her first year is asked to bend again for the rest of her keeping.

title: Three teachers of Cnoc bhàn set an unlit lamp before the Hall's door
body: Three old teachers of the stag's school at Cnoc bhàn climb the mountain road on foot and set an unlit lamp on the stones before Talla na Lasrach, asking only to be let back among the cutters already working the galleries, and swearing to ask nothing of the vein aloud if the Hall will stop asking whether they have any right to stand near it.

title: Seonaid Chiar reopens the galleries to the stag's people
body: Seonaid Chiar, Keeper of the house of Muireach, lets cutters trained by the stag's people back into the galleries at Dùn ìseal, sworn to ask nothing of the vein aloud. The Hall's roll calls it a reconciling. The school remembers it as a truce.

title: Cathair mhòr walled
body: The people of Cathair mhòr on the southern coast build a wall of fitted stone about their headland town, the first town wall on the island. What they feared no one has told.

title: Ceann leathan's fish-market
body: Ceann leathan becomes the market of the southern fishing and sends dried fish inland along the carriers' paths. Its harbour-master keeps tallies on notched sticks. Several are kept at Muileann chaol, the oldest counted things in its keeping.

title: Seonaid Chiar's guild judgment at Cnoc leathan
body: Hearing two carriers of Cnoc leathan's guild each accuse the other of taking a fee out of turn, Seonaid Chiar asks only which of them had first offered to give the disputed load back, and, hearing neither had, tells them the Hall's grant is a right to carry and not a right to quarrel. The two settle the matter themselves before they have gone a mile down the mountain road.

title: The shrine at Inis thais
body: A shrine to the ancestors lost at sea is raised at Inis thais on the western coast. Its keepers burn their season's handful on the shore and not indoors, so that the drowned, gone west over the sea, may see it.

title: Cuan shean's salt-pans
body: The people of Cuan shean on the western coast dig salt-pans on the flats below the town and boil sea-water over peat. Their salt goes inland along the western road and keeps the fish of half the island.

title: Salt-carriers on the heath above Baile fhiadhaich
body: Salt-carriers from Cuan shean settle on the western heath above Baile fhiadhaich, by a stream that runs all summer. The heath about it is not worth the plough, and its people keep goats.

title: The sunny house
body: A waypoint house is built on the eastern road where the carriers from Cnoc leathan meet the southern coast path, on the site of An Taigh-òsta Grianach. It faces south, and from the first is known for its warmth, which is all its name has ever meant.

title: Cnoc leathan's market
body: Cnoc leathan, at the eastern end of the road past the sunny house, becomes the market town of the south-eastern hills. Its carriers' guild holds the right to carry for the Hall on the stretch down to the coast.

title: Ruairidh Glas stands once more before the stone cup
body: In his nine hundred and ninth year, Ruairidh Glas, holder of the Red Share, asks unasked leave to climb Dùn ìseal on foot and stand again before the stone cup, though no lord of a share is required to outside the quarter days. He says nothing aloud that any living ear catches, and goes back down the same evening to Dùn dhearg.

title: Ruairidh Glas dies at Dùn dhearg
body: Ruairidh Glas dies in his own bed at Dùn dhearg, having lived nine hundred and ten years and never once returned to Dùn thais since the morning he shed the first blood of the strife of the heirs there. He outlives every soul who stood beside him at the ford where his grandfather's line first took the Red Hill.

title: The Red Share passes without a summons to the Hall
body: Ruairidh Glas's son takes up the Red Share at Dùn dhearg without any summons to the Hall, as the Peace of the Threshold requires none where an heir is named and undisputed. The season's rolls, careful to name every lesser lord, stay strangely thin about naming this one, a silence the Hall's clerk lays to the household's own quiet rather than to any failure of the pen.

title: The fall in the high gallery
body: A roof falls in the highest gallery at Dùn ìseal and kills four cutters. The gallery is walled up and left. Seonaid Chiar orders props of oak set in every gallery after, and for the first time the Hall spends timber on the mountain.

title: The four dead of the high gallery are buried on the Hall's own ground
body: The four cutters killed when the roof of the highest gallery falls at Dùn ìseal are carried up and buried on the Hall's own ground, the one ground on the island no feud has ever been let to follow a man. Seonaid Chiar sets the last stone over the last of them with her own hands, which no Keeper before her is remembered to have done.

title: The first oak props are cut for the galleries
body: After a season's argument over how a gallery roof should ever be held against another such fall, Seonaid Chiar orders timber props of oak set in every gallery the Hall works, the first timber the Hall has ever spent on the mountain itself. The first oak is felled and cut within the season, so that no gallery stands unpropped by the following year's cutting.

title: Seonaid Chiar dies above the galleries she kept
body: Seonaid Chiar dies in her own quarters above the galleries at Dùn ìseal, eighty-five years old, having held the flame the better part of six decades. The nine hearths that raised her young choose another after her without any dispute the rolls think worth setting down.

title: The school at Cnoc bhàn returns its unlit lamp
body: On word of Seonaid Chiar's death, the school at Cnoc bhàn sends no delegation and no message of grief, only the same unlit lamp its three old teachers once set before her door, carried back up by cutters young enough to have known no other Keeper, and left again on the same stones, still unlit.

title: Cathair dhomhain founded
body: Carriers settled at the mouth of the western road raise a town on the rise above the harbour and name it Cathair dhomhain. Its shrine keeps the Law's measure strictly, and its people are proud of it.

title: Cathair dhomhain's shrine holds the Law to the grain
body: The new shrine at Cathair dhomhain keeps the Small-Burning Law to the very grain from its founding day, a strictness the town becomes known for beyond any other pride it holds. Lowland households speak of it for a lifetime, though the town itself remains a place carriers pass through on the way to somewhere else.

title: A fishing town at Cathair dhearg
body: The old settlement of the Red Hill, shrunk to a small fishing town, grows again at the western bridge-foot on the Abhainn dhomhain, a little above its meeting with the Abhainn gheal below Loch chrom. The ground is afterwards called Cathair dhearg, for its red stone. As yet it is a place carriers pass through on the way to somewhere else.

title: The death of Cailean
body: Cailean, a cousin of Goraidh mac Ìomhair through their grandmothers, dies under a wall he is mending at his own hall in a night of high wind. He leaves no child of his body, and his county of the east goes unclaimed.

title: The death of Donnchadh
body: Donnchadh, Cailean's younger brother, dies of a cough the hearth-women cannot cut, with his sister's hand in his. He too leaves no child, and the second of the three old counties east of Dùn dhearg is left without an heir named.

title: Goraidh's marriage to Muirne nic Dhonnchaidh
body: Goraidh mac Ìomhair rides to Muirne nic Dhonnchaidh, a widowed kinswoman of four hundred years who holds the third of the old eastern counties alone, and marries her in the spring. Her county comes whole into the marriage, as the Peace of the Threshold allows, and Goraidh takes on her dead husbands' debts to the county's smiths.

title: Goraidh rides the three counties
body: Through the first year of the marriage Goraidh mac Ìomhair walks the boundaries of all three gathered counties with Muirne beside him, eating at the hearths and not the halls, learning which streams have moved and which grazings are old enough to fight over.

title: The hungry harvests
body: Two summers running the rains come at the wrong end of the season and the barley rots standing in the low ground east of Dùn dhearg. Goraidh mac Ìomhair opens all four of his granaries and gives grain outright to nine households that cannot pay even the lowered price.

title: Goraidh gathers the shares of the east
body: By two cousins dead without heirs and a marriage to a third, Goraidh mac Ìomhair holds in one hand three of the old counties of the east round Dùn dhearg, parted since the Roinn. He is the first of the kin to gather again what the Roinn had divided, and the Peace of the Threshold lets him keep it whole.

title: Goraidh mac Ìomhair called rìgh
body: At Dùn dhearg the lowland households who eat from the granaries of Sliochd Ìomhair begin to call its head, Goraidh mac Ìomhair, their rìgh, their king. No one had been so called since Ailean Mòr, for at the Roinn the heirs swore that none of them would take the word. Goraidh claims nothing over the vein, and is careful to tell the Hall so.

title: Death of Muirne nic Dhonnchaidh
body: Muirne nic Dhonnchaidh dies in her sleep in the ninth year of her marriage to Goraidh mac Ìomhair, with her own county's reciter in the room. He buries her among her own dead, as she asked him.

title: The timber hall of Dùn dhearg raised with a granary at each corner
body: Goraidh mac Ìomhair raises a long hall of squared oak on his father's rise at Dùn dhearg, with a granary at each of its four corners. The carpenters of the Red Share and of the three gathered counties raise it side by side, and the granaries are filled from all four counties in one season.

title: Goraidh leaves his spear at the last house
body: Come to answer the council's word, Goraidh mac Ìomhair leaves his spear with his men at the last waypoint house on the mountain road and climbs to Dùn ìseal on foot and unarmed.

title: The division of keeping
body: The council at Dùn ìseal and Goraidh mac Ìomhair agree on a division. The Keeper keeps the flame and the galleries; the rìgh keeps the roads, the granaries and the peace of the lowlands. The rìgh may not enter the galleries, and the Keeper may not raise spears. On this division the island is governed for the rest of the age.

title: The waypoint-keepers gather the road toll for a share
body: Goraidh does not gather the toll of one fish in twenty himself. He gives it to the keepers of the waypoint houses along each road, who have kept a bed and a fire for carriers since before his grandfather's day, and lets each keep a share of what they take.

title: A waypoint-keeper's short tally forgiven
body: At a waypoint house on the northern road a keeper's first season's toll comes in a tenth short, for want of anyone at the door by night. Goraidh mac Ìomhair laughs at the reckoning and lets the shortfall stand.

title: Goraidh Mòr's hall
body: Goraidh mac Ìomhair, called Goraidh Mòr, builds a timber hall on the hill at Dùn dhearg, with a granary at each corner. Its post-holes could still be seen when the surveyors of the Library walked the hill, and they measured and drew them.

title: The first road-toll
body: Goraidh Mòr sets a toll on the carriers' roads, one fish in twenty or its worth, to pay the road-guards and keep up the bridges. The keepers of the waypoint houses gather it, and keep a share of it, and the rolls say so.

title: Mòrag takes up the walking of the roads
body: Goraidh's daughter Mòrag, who could never sit still in a hall, takes over the walking of the island's roads from her ageing father long before he will call it a handing-over. He lets her.

title: Dòmhnall's fall from the cart
body: Dòmhnall, riding the back board of a laden cart above the ford, is thrown under its wheel where it strikes a stone left standing proud of the road-bed. His leg is set and set again and never knits true; he walks with a stick the rest of his life.

title: Death of Goraidh Mòr
body: Goraidh mac Ìomhair dies in his own hall at Dùn dhearg in his two hundred and thirteenth year, in the granary month, asking after the notching of the western road's toll-sticks. His daughter Mòrag and two waypoint-keepers rendering their tallies are with him.

title: The toll-stick notched at Mòr nic Dhùghaill's old house
body: Days after Goraidh Mòr's death, the keeper of the old waypoint house that was Mòr nic Dhùghaill's notches a fresh toll-stick for a carrier's fish and a carrier's wool, as she has every week before and will every week after, whoever holds the hall at Dùn dhearg.

title: Mòrag of the Roads
body: Mòrag nic Ghoraidh takes the hall at Dùn dhearg after her father Goraidh Mòr. She is called Mòrag nan Rathad, Mòrag of the Roads, for in her first years she walks every carriers' road on the island and orders the bad stretches made anew.

title: The toll-chest counted at a keeper's own door
body: Mòrag nan Rathad finds the toll-house two days east of the ford unanswered longest of all its keepers' letters. She has her road-guards open the keeper's own chest and counts the silver on a cloth before him, takes half for the mending, and leaves half for his household.

title: Mòrag meets Niall Òg on the northern road
body: On a wet stretch of the northern road, Mòrag nan Rathad shelters from rain beside an old man on a milestone: Niall Òg, grandson of Ailean Mòr, now past his sixteen hundredth year. He tells her his name and sits with her a while before going on afoot.

title: Niall Òg tells Mòrag of the cord
body: Niall Òg tells Mòrag nan Rathad of the cord of seven hundred and twelve knots laid on the floor at Dùn ìseal, and says she is the first of the line he has met who looks at the cord itself and not at her own knot in it.

title: The golden house opened free of toll
body: Mòrag nan Rathad opens the new waypoint house on the eastern road north of Seann Dunn with a night's feast for every carrier who can be reached in time, none of them charged the toll. Carriers call the new timber the golden house before it has weathered, and the name holds.

title: The golden house
body: Mòrag nan Rathad has a waypoint house built on the road north of Seann Dunn, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Òir, to shorten the carriers' stage from the coast to the mountain. It is the first waypoint house raised by a ruler and not by a family.

title: The bridge-foot rebuilt
body: At the bidding of Mòrag nan Rathad the western crossing of the Abhainn dhomhain is rebuilt in wider stone, so that two laden carriers can pass on it. The hearth-sign of Ailean Clachair is cut again in its keystone. From this time the town at the bridge-foot begins to grow.

title: The bridge-foot town begins to grow
body: After the western crossing of the Abhainn dhomhain is widened for two laden carts abreast, the small fishing town at the bridge-foot below Dùn ìseal begins to grow in earnest, outgrowing three neighbouring towns within Mòrag nan Rathad's own lifetime.

title: Mòrag names Dòmhnall her heir
body: Mòrag nan Rathad has her lame son Dòmhnall carried the length of three road-stretches in a covered chair, then names him before the household at Dùn dhearg as her heir, past her hundred and sixtieth year herself.

title: Mòrag's last circuit of the roads
body: Against the advice of her household, Mòrag nan Rathad rides the whole western circuit in her hundred and eighty-ninth year, finding less to mend than in any year of her reign, and tells the waypoint-keepers so at every house she stops in.

title: Mòrag nan Rathad dies at Dùn dhearg
body: Mòrag nan Rathad dies at Dùn dhearg in the winter, a hundred and ninety-four years old, with her son beside her. Carriers from three days' distance come to stand outside the hall, and Dòmhnall feeds them from the golden house's own stores.

title: Dòmhnall Crùbach
body: Dòmhnall Crùbach, Dòmhnall the Lame, follows his mother Mòrag at Dùn dhearg. He cannot walk the roads as she did, and rules through the keepers of the waypoint houses, who grow mighty in his reign.

title: Niall Òg speaks over Mòrag's grave
body: At Mòrag nan Rathad's grave, Niall Òg says that of the seven hundred and twelve heirs he once watched knotted on the cord, she alone spent her life looking at the cord itself, and that her roads are the nearest thing since to that cord laid honestly on the ground.

title: Sìleas Dhonn finds the Ceann mhin rolls do not add
body: Dòmhnall Crùbach's young niece Sìleas Dhonn, asked to check the waypoint-keepers' tallies, finds three years in which the Ceann mhin keepers' own count does not match what passed through their gates, though never provably by theft. She keeps her own copy of the figures and says nothing of it while her uncle lives.

title: The scorpion's sting sworn on at a trade
body: At Baile àrsaidh a woman stung on the hand during a trade of cattle for salt fish finishes the bargain with her fingers still swelling, saying a hurt taken in the open is worth more than a promise given behind a closed door. Others take up her way of it, keeping a dried sting in a box to swear by.

title: The waypoint-keepers of Ceann mhin
body: In the reign of Dòmhnall Crùbach the keepers of the waypoint houses about the harbour town of Ceann mhin take the gathering of the road-toll into their own hands and pay the rìgh what they judge fair. Their judgement is generous to themselves, and the rolls keep the sums.

title: Baile àrsaidh on the western heath
body: Settlers from Cathair dhomhain take the wet heath of the west coast and found Baile àrsaidh, where the soil is thin and the yellow scorpions thick. They swear their oaths on a scorpion's sting kept in a box, and their neighbours think it a strange custom.

title: The storm at Seann Chwen
body: A storm drives the sea over the harbour at Seann Chwen and takes the boats and a third of the houses. The Keeper sends the Hall's grain from Dùn ìseal, and Dòmhnall Crùbach sends his from Dùn dhearg. The survivors remember that the Hall's came first.

title: The Hall's grain-carts reach Seann Chwen first
body: After the storm at Seann Chwen, the Keeper's grain-carts reach the ruined harbour a full day ahead of Dòmhnall Crùbach's, running the whole way on the road above the ford that Mòrag nan Rathad raised out of the mud in the first summer of her reign.

title: The sting first sworn on at a wider trade
body: The scorpion's-sting oath of Baile àrsaidh is sworn for the first time at a trade with an outside harbour town, at Ros bheag, carrying the custom beyond the settlement that began it.

title: Rònat sent to the stag's school
body: A boy of ten with a talent for losing count past thirty is sent from his father's holding to the stag's school in the holy wood east of Muileann chiar. Aonghas Cam, the old cutter, scores his first tally-stick through the middle and sets him cutting sticks two years before he is trusted near a beast to be counted.

title: Aonghas Cam's failing thread
body: A fever settles in the old cutter's crooked leg and will not draw out. Through that winter Rònat watches him grope after names and lines of the long teaching-thread and not always find them, and it is by that fireside, and not by any beast to be counted, that the shape of the sound-marks first comes to him.

title: The first name cut in strokes
body: Rònat cuts his own name onto a length of ash by a scheme of small strokes, one to a sound, and reads it back cold three days after. He sets the same trick to Aonghas Cam's own name and lays the stick in the old man's hand, who reads his name off it and calls it a count of sounds where he had always cut a count of fish.

title: The death of Aonghas Cam
body: The old cutter of Muileann chiar's stag school dies in his sleep, having asked that his own years be counted the old way at the last, one stroke to a year, having spent his life trusting a count over a name. Rònat cuts the tally himself.

title: The western teachers come east
body: Two teachers of the western druid school travel to the far-eastern Muileann chiar to learn Rònat's sound-marks, and stay a season under a man twenty years their junior. Among them is Sìleas nic Ruairidh, eldest of the two, who carries the scheme home and turns it over in her own mind.

title: The letters set against the obelisk
body: Rònat and two others walk five days east to the grey stone at Cnoc bheag and set the sound-marks stroke for stroke against the old marks cut there. Nothing answers: no vowel, no grouping, no order in the stone's marks matches theirs.

title: The first thing written of the old marks
body: Before the road home, Rònat cuts onto ash the finding at Cnoc bheag: that the makers of the old stone did not teach the makers of the stag's marks and are not known to them. It is the first thought, rather than a name or a count, that the new marks are made to carry.

title: Niall Òg at the stag's school
body: The ancient heir passes through the far east on foot and sits two evenings by the school's fire, telling pupils tales of the night of the handful. He asks, at the second evening's end, after the trick of marks he has heard tell of on the road.

title: Niall Òg reads his own name
body: Rònat cuts Niall Òg's name in the sound-marks and sets the stick in his hand. The old heir, who has been called by his name more times than there are fish in the western sea, reads it back within the hour and laughs until he coughs, saying he has found, at last, a name that stays after the mouth that gave it has gone home.

title: The stag-letters
body: At Muileann chiar in the far east the teachers of the stag's people make the cutters' tally-notches into signs for sounds, so that a teaching may be kept without a teacher. These are the first letters the Dia-thìrich use: the ogham, which the druids call the gift of Ogma.

title: The letters set against the obelisk
body: Scholars of the stag carry their new letters to Carragh Cnoc bheag and set them beside the marks on the obelisk. They match nothing. The scholars write that the stone's makers were not their teachers, and that is the first thing the Dia-thìrich ever write of the old people.

title: The chest of mismatched tallies opened
body: Sìleas Dhonn, new in the chair at Dùn dhearg after Dòmhnall Crùbach's death, has brought out and opened before the household the chest she has kept locked for years: her own fair copy of three seasons' Ceann mhin tallies that never matched the toll counted at the gate.

title: Sìleas Dhonn
body: Sìleas Dhonn, niece of Dòmhnall Crùbach, holds Dùn dhearg after him. In her reign the keepers of the waypoint houses are bidden to render account of the tolls at her hall once a year, and several of them do.

title: Beathan mac Dhonnchaidh's memory found wanting
body: The old keeper of Muileann shean recites his tally to Sìleas Dhonn from memory, the old way, name for name; she asks him plainly how she is to know it is the same tally he gave the road-guard three seasons past. He has no answer beyond his own honesty, and she sends east for a teacher of the sound-marks.

title: Rònat teaches Sìleas Dhonn's clerks
body: Rònat walks the last long road of his active years to Dùn dhearg and teaches the ruler's clerks the sound-marks over a winter, finding grown clerks trained to a column of figures quicker with the knife than any pupil he taught in the holy wood.

title: Ailig mac Ruairidh caught by his own gate
body: The keeper of Ceann mhin's toll, first summoned to render account cut in the new marks and checked against the road-guard's own cutting at his gate, is found short by a sum no honest forgetting explains. It is the first time a keeper's own tally, and not his word, answers for him before the hall.

title: The first whole sentence
body: Cutting the record of Ailig mac Ruairidh's shortfall for the hall's keeping, Rònat sets down the first whole sentence any hand has yet cut in the sound-marks: that the toll of Ceann mhin was counted short and the keeper answered for it. It stands after him in the hall, saying the same thing to every thumb that reads it.

title: The lords of Caol leathan
body: The harbour town of Caol leathan in the south-west grows rich on the western fishing and the southern end of the carriers' road. Its leading family, under Lachlann Ciar, takes the road-toll for itself and sends none of it to Dùn dhearg.

title: Sìleas Dhonn dies at her ledger
body: Sìleas Dhonn dies in the chair at Dùn dhearg with a keeper's tally open on her knee, in her hundred and ninety-fourth year. She has asked that the chair stand its customary night and day and no longer, having had forty years at her uncle's side to learn the feel of it.

title: Iain Garbh
body: Iain Garbh, Iain the Rough, son of Sìleas Dhonn, takes the hall at Dùn dhearg and demands the western tolls of Caol leathan. Lachlann Ciar sends back a basket of fish-bones.

title: Iain Garbh's demand sent south
body: On his first morning in the chair Iain Garbh reads Caol leathan's thin account and sends a rider south with a plain demand in his own hand: the toll owed in full, counted before Dùn dhearg's own man at the harbour, or an answer for why it should not be paid.

title: The basket set on the hall floor
body: Iain Garbh's rider returns from Caol leathan white about the mouth, carrying a covered basket he will not open himself. Iain lifts the lid to find it packed in rows with fish-bones, picked clean, and no letter with it.

title: Iain Garbh calls the levy
body: Iain Garbh laughs once over the basket of fish-bones, then calls the road-guards from every waypoint within three days' ride and tells the lowland households their levy stands, raising his voice at no one the whole of that week.

title: The War of the Roads begins at Muileann òg
body: Iain Garbh marches west with the road-guards and the lowland levies, and burns the toll-house at Muileann òg that the men of Lachlann Ciar had taken. It is the first war of Dia-thìreach against Dia-thìreach since the Peace of the Threshold, and the first fought over a road; every war before it was fought over a share. The Hall will bless neither side.

title: Uisdean mac Ruairidh's refusal
body: The Keeper Uisdean mac Ruairidh refuses the messengers of Iain Garbh at Dùn ìseal the Hall's handful for the warband's hearths, saying that the flame does not warm men who go out to kill. The warband winters on peat. Iain Garbh never forgives the Hall, and never enters it.

title: Iain Garbh folds the Keeper's answer
body: Iain Garbh's messengers return from Dùn ìseal empty-handed, made to repeat Uisdean mac Ruairidh's refusal word for word. Iain folds the written answer once and puts it inside his coat, and never again sets foot on the Hall's ground.

title: The fight at Àth fhiadhaich
body: The men of Caol leathan meet the levies of Iain Garbh at the ford of Àth fhiadhaich and hold it for a day before they give way. Forty lie dead of both sides. Long afterwards the carriers call it the ford of the forty.

title: The coughing winter at Muileann òg
body: The warband winters on peat smoke at the burned toll-house of Muileann òg. Men who marched south whole come home in spring with a cough some of them carry the rest of their days, so that the older road-guards are known ever after by the sound of a hard winter's night.

title: Baile ghlas burned
body: The men of Lachlann Ciar, falling back on Caol leathan, burn Baile ghlas, that the levies of Iain Garbh may find no grain. Its people walk to Cathair dhomhain, and many never return.

title: The unnamed man of the ford
body: At the ford of Àth fhiadhaich a man of Caol leathan holds a split shield upright well past any sense left in the holding, until a spear from behind Iain Garbh's own rank finds him. No name is ever kept for him.

title: Baile chiar holds
body: Baile chiar, south of the western bridge-foot, shuts its gate on both hosts in the War of the Roads and feeds the burned-out folk of Baile ghlas through the winter. Neither side forgives it, and neither attacks it.

title: Beathag of Baile chiar turns back a spear
body: Riding to Baile chiar for a night's lodging, Iain Garbh is met on the wall by the town's reeve, Beathag, who will open the gate to the hungry and to no one carrying a spear. He leaves the spear on the road and sleeps that night among the burned-out of Baile ghlas.

title: The siege of Caol leathan
body: Iain Garbh shuts Caol leathan in from the land for a season, but its boats bring in fish from the sea, and the harbour he cannot close. His levies begin to go home for the harvest, and the siege ends without an assault.

title: The peace at Mòr nic Dhùghaill's house
body: Iain Garbh and Lachlann Ciar meet under the roof of the waypoint house that is afterwards Am Buabhall Fortanach, where by the road-peace neither may draw. Caol leathan keeps half its tolls and sends half to Dùn dhearg, and Lachlann Ciar swears to the Law before the Keeper's witness. So the War of the Roads ends in a house built to feed carriers.

title: Lachlann Ciar's confession at the peace-board
body: At the waypoint house on the road-peace, Lachlann Ciar tells Iain Garbh that the basket of fish-bones was his son's notion, sent out under his own name because a father does not answer for a son's foolishness by naming him. The two talk the evening out.

title: The wolf-sworn of Caol leathan
body: Men who fought for Caol leathan become its road-guards and swear their watch on a white stone carved as a wolf, kept at the town gate. They call themselves the wolf-sworn.

title: Iain Garbh witnesses the wolf-sworn
body: At Lachlann Ciar's own asking, Iain Garbh rides south to stand at the gate of Caol leathan while the men of its siege swear their new watch on a white stone cut as a wolf, and are called from that day the wolf-sworn.

title: News of the fish-bone war reaches Cathair mhòr
body: A wool-merchant brings Eithne nic Ailein, last living of the nine who cut the cord at the Roinn, the tale of Iain Garbh's war on Caol leathan. She does not ride to it and does not send to it, judging it another share's quarrel to end.

title: Word of the harbour wall at Caol fhiadhaich
body: The wool-merchant's next journey brings word to Cathair mhòr of how Caol fhiadhaich fed besieged Caol leathan by night and was given a share of the western tolls, with which it raised the first stone wall that coast has had. Eithne asks after the wall every year after.

title: Lachlann Ciar dies within sight of the harbour
body: Lachlann Ciar dies in his ninetieth year, worn down by slow degrees by the cough he carried from the coughing winter. His household buries him within sight of the harbour he grew fat and then thin defending, his son standing at the peace-board in his place.

title: Caol fhiadhaich rebuilt
body: Caol fhiadhaich on the south-western shore had sent its boats to feed Caol leathan through the siege. In thanks Lachlann Ciar gives it a share of the western tolls, and with it the town builds a harbour wall.

title: Iain Garbh never climbs to the cup
body: Iain Garbh rules forty years past the end of the War of the Roads and never once goes up the mountain road to stand before the cup, unlike every rìgh before or after him. He dies unreconciled to the flame that had refused his warband its blessing.

title: Death of Iain Garbh
body: Iain Garbh dies at Dùn dhearg. His daughter Catrìona buries him in the floor of the hall and not on the slope at Dùn ìseal, and the Hall does not ask for him.

title: Catrìona Ghlic crowned at Dùn dhearg
body: Catrìona, daughter of Iain Garbh, is crowned at Dùn dhearg on her father's death and takes within ten years the name Catrìona Ghlic, Catrìona the Wise, for undoing the coldness he had left between the rìgh's hall and the Hall of the Flame.

title: Catrìona Ghlic
body: Catrìona Ghlic, Catrìona the Wise, rules from Dùn dhearg. She sends her own son to sit a season with the flame, the first child of the royal house to do so since the division of keeping. By the end of her reign the Hall and the hall are on speaking terms again.

title: The rìgh's tithe sent again to the Hall
body: Eithne nic Ailein, hearing that Catrìona Ghlic's son has sat a season with the flame unasked, orders that Cathair mhòr's own hall send its tithe to the Hall's handful again, unwaited-for, as it had not done since her own father's day.

title: The Keeper keeps a place for the rìgh's son
body: After his first season carrying the baskets at Dùn ìseal, Catrìona Ghlic's son returns each year at the turn of the season, and the Keeper comes to keep a place for him at the long table without being asked, a small thing the island reads as the breach mended.

title: Inis mhòr asks the crown for its own guard
body: The wool port of Inis mhòr, grown past every other town in the north on the trade the two new waypoint houses carry, asks Catrìona Ghlic's crown for a road-guard of its own, and is given one without argument.

title: The house on the northern road
body: Catrìona Ghlic has a waypoint house built on the northern road above Inis mhòr, on the site of An Leòmhann Buidhe. It serves the carriers who take the Hall's baskets to the northern households and bring back wool.

title: The house on the cold road
body: A stone house is built on the open moor, on the road between Baile Mòr dhomhain and the northern coast, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, for carriers caught by snow. The Hall pays its keepers in grain and the crown in cloth, and they complain of both.

title: Inis mhòr grows
body: The river port of Inis mhòr in the north becomes the gathering-place of the northern wool trade and outgrows every other northern town. Its people ask Catrìona Ghlic for a road-guard of their own, and are given one.

title: Niall Òg walks his last road
body: Niall Òg comes on foot and unannounced to Eithne nic Ailein's hall at Cathair mhòr, the last road he means to walk, so that the night of the handful should be told once more, to the only other living witness of it, before he dies.

title: Death of Niall Òg
body: Niall Òg dies in his sleep by Eithne nic Ailein's own fire at Cathair mhòr, some two thousand years old, three days after telling her the night of the handful for what proves the last time. She sends his body up the mountain at her own cost.

title: Niall Òg laid near the first heirs
body: Eithne has Niall Òg laid near the old graves on the slope below Dùn ìseal, among the first heirs of the Roinn, though he was of no kin to her own share, judging that a man who spent four hundred years walking every road on the island had earned the ground.

title: Eithne asks the count of her own years
body: In her last year Eithne nic Ailein asks her steward more than once to reckon the exact tale of her days, wanting the number fixed precisely at the end, though her mind has not begun to fail her.

title: Death of Eithne nic Ailein, last of the nine
body: Eithne nic Ailein, daughter of Ailean Mòr and youngest of the nine who took the great shares at the Roinn, dies in her hall at Cathair mhòr. And all the days of Eithne were three thousand and twenty-one years, and she died. After her none of the nine is living, and the great shares are names on the boundary stones.

title: The market at the fords of Baile Mòr dhomhain
body: The lords of the deep river set a market at Baile Mòr dhomhain, where the carriers' road from the south meets the paths down from the hill pastures. Cattle, sheep, horses, hides and the white stone of the hills are sold at the fords on the day after each new moon, and the lords take one fleece in forty from the sellers.

title: Eithne's hall at Cathair mhòr falls silent
body: With Eithne nic Ailein's death her hall at Cathair mhòr is left to her stewards and her reciters, who keep the rolls but crown no one there, the lowland share having long since ceased to answer to any single hand of her line.

title: The mill at Muileann shean
body: A mill is raised on the northern road at Muileann shean to grind grain for the carriers crossing the pass; the miller pays the Hall in grain and the rìgh's toll in flour, and a town grows round the mill within two generations.

title: Catrìona Ghlic dies at a hundred and twenty-two
body: Catrìona Ghlic, who mended the breach her father Iain Garbh's war had opened, dies at Dùn dhearg. Her son takes the hall at ninety-two, the first of eleven rulers the later king-list will give only by name and order.

title: The Hall's own roll for the same years
body: For the span the king-list gives eleven rulers, the Hall's spoken roll gives only five Keepers, a mountain's years running longer than a lowland's, as every teller of the Fire already knows.

title: Muileann shean on the northern road
body: A mill is built at Muileann shean on the northern road, to grind the grain the carriers bring over the pass, and a town grows round it. The Hall pays the miller in grain, and he pays the rìgh's toll in flour.

title: The last of the long years in the ruling line
body: The last ruler of the house of Ìomhar and Goraidh to carry any of the long years in his blood dies at a hundred years old, an age that was a boy's age in his grandmother's grandmother's day. After him the line ages and dies at the pace of any household on the island.

title: The unremembered rulers
body: Eleven rulers hold Dùn dhearg between Catrìona Ghlic and Ealasaid Chiar. The later king-list gives their names and their order, and nothing more. For the same years the Keepers' roll gives five Keepers, and of them too only the names.

title: Tormod mac Iain born to the house of Tormod
body: Tormod is born at Dùn dhearg, a younger son of a house that has held no great office in the hall for three generations. His father Iain keeps a stretch of the crown granaries, and the boy grows up among grain-tallies.

title: Tormod sent east to Muileann chiar
body: A passing stag-teacher's tale of letters that can hold a teaching without a teacher fixes itself in the fifteen-year-old Tormod's mind. His father, a younger son's post being cheaper found elsewhere than at home, sends him east to Muileann chiar to learn the stag-letters.

title: Tormod Scrìobhaiche learns the letters
body: Tormod mac Iain, a younger son of the house of Tormod, is sent east to Muileann chiar to learn the stag-letters. He is the first of the royal kin to read, and for the rest of his life he is called Tormod Scrìobhaiche, Tormod the Writer.

title: Tormod's first written leaf
body: In his second summer at Muileann chiar, Tormod writes his first whole leaf, a grain-debt tally copied twice over from an old woman's spoken account. He keeps it inside his shirt a full year, the oldest surviving thing in his own hand.

title: Tormod returns to the granaries
body: After four years at Muileann chiar, Tormod comes home to Dùn dhearg and his father's trade of the granaries, carrying unspoken a want to write down a thing that would outlast every mouth that had ever spoken it.

title: Ealasaid Chiar
body: Ealasaid Chiar takes the hall at Dùn dhearg and brings Tormod Scrìobhaiche there as her clerk. She bids him set down in order the name of every ruler of the hall that the reciters can give him.

title: The first written king-list
body: Rulers are first set down by name, and no longer only remembered in tales. The rolls of succession in every later age are kept after this pattern.

title: Ealasaid Chiar takes the hall
body: Ealasaid Chiar, granddaughter of the ninth of the eleven, takes the hall at Dùn dhearg at twenty-nine, out of patience with hearing her own house's roll given a different order at every telling.

title: Ealasaid Chiar sets Tormod to the writing
body: Ealasaid Chiar hears of a granary clerk who can set a thing down in marks and have it read back the same way twice, and sets Tormod Scrìobhaiche, now fifty-nine, to write down every ruler the reciters can name, in order, freed of all other duty.

title: The contents of Tormod's roll
body: Tormod Scrìobhaiche's roll, kept in the hall at Dùn dhearg, runs from Goraidh Mòr to Ealasaid Chiar. The earlier names he has from the reciters and the later from living memory, and he marks which are which. In three places it differs from the Keepers' spoken roll; Tormod writes down both readings and does not choose.

title: The reciters disagree
body: Questioning the hall's reciters in turn, Tormod finds them certain and contradictory: a mother's name given two ways, a reign given nine years by one mouth and eleven by another, three rulers set in different orders by a southern reciter than by the hall's own.

title: Ealasaid Chiar bids the doubt be written too
body: Told of the disagreements, Ealasaid Chiar orders Tormod to set down the sure thing where he has it and the doubt where he has that, rather than hide the roll's own uncertainty from those who could not otherwise judge it.

title: Tormod's roll finished
body: After six years' careful writing, reading each page back to whoever gave it before counting it done, Tormod brings Ealasaid Chiar the finished roll from Goraidh Mòr to herself, with three disputed places marked and left unresolved.

title: Death of Tormod Scrìobhaiche
body: Tormod Scrìobhaiche dies at seventy in the clerk's room off the hall at Dùn dhearg, a half-begun copy of the disputed reign still under his hand. Ealasaid Chiar names the room, ever after, Tormod's room.

title: The Hall shamed into writing its own roll
body: Word of the written king-list reaches the blind Keeper on the mountain, who sits three days in silence and then tells the Hall's own reciters that a Hall out-remembered by a rìgh's clerk has no one to blame but itself.

title: The Keepers' roll written down
body: Shamed, in the Hall's own words, by the rìgh's clerk, the Keepers have their spoken roll written in stag-letters at Dùn ìseal. It begins with Beathag Bhàn, and it is longer than Tormod's by several centuries.

title: Cairistìona reads the cord for the scribes
body: Cairistìona nan Snaidhm, last of Sìne's line who can read a knot without letters, comes to the Hall and unties the cord of the heirs knot by knot over two days, naming each heir aloud so a young scribe can set the roll down in the new marks.

title: The cord coiled in its chest
body: The last of the cord's seven hundred and twelve knots comes free, and Cairistìona coils it in the old way and lays it in the chest the Hall has made for it, telling the scribe that after her no hand living will be able to make it speak.

title: The death of Ealasaid Chiar
body: Ealasaid Chiar dies at sixty, having reigned thirty-one years and had the first king-list written, and is carried up the mountain road to lie among the house of Ìomhar. Her son takes the hall after her.

title: The roll falls silent
body: After Ealasaid Chiar's son and granddaughter, the king-list Tormod began keeps no ruler's name for a span the reciters cannot close. The Keepers' roll at Dùn ìseal keeps its own count through the same years, naming its Keepers where the hall names none.

title: The Hall's clerks learn the stag-letters
body: Shamed that it cannot read its own roll without borrowing another order's letters, the Hall at Dùn ìseal sets two of its own clerks to learn the stag-letters, taught by a stag-teacher paid in coal for the winter. From that year the Hall keeps its roll in its own hand.

title: A Keeper named in the silent years
body: A Keeper is named at Dùn ìseal of whom the roll keeps only the years of her reign, twenty-two, and the year of her death; of the rest of it nothing is told, the households burning their handful and the carriers walking their roads as their grandparents had.

title: The birth of Conall Dubh
body: A household above Cnoc bheag, keeping sheep in sight of the wood the island has never cleared, has its fourth child, a son they name Conall and call Dubh for the black hair he is born with.

title: Conall Dubh sees the black horned beast
body: At twenty years old, going up before first light to bring down strayed ewes, Conall Dubh meets a black horned beast at the edge of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, standing and watching him before it turns back into the trees. His mother believes him.

title: The watch grows to nine
body: Conall Dubh's sister and two cousins join his watch at the wood's edge, and within five years of his own first sighting nine keep it by turns, waiting on a beast none of them can explain to a stranger's satisfaction.

title: The watchers of the dark wood
body: A small company settles at the edge of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the wood never cleared, and keeps watch for a black horned beast that they say walks in it. The people of Cathair dhearg call them the wood-watchers. None of their own accounts is older than Òrd Mhacha, the order of Macha, which afterwards claims them and takes the beast for a sign of Dubh Sainglenn, the black horse.

title: The wood called sacred
body: The watchers, near thirty now and housed in a turf hut at the wood's edge, are named the wood-watchers by the people of Cathair dhearg, and a Hall clerk counting the season's coal is the first outsider to write Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag sacred in his own report.

title: The wood-watchers in the stag's grove
body: Wood-watchers come east and cut a black-barked tree in Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, saying that the beast had shown it to them. The stag's people call it theft from a place of teaching. Both sides send to Dùn dhearg and to Dùn ìseal.

title: The death of a teaching elder
body: In the second winter of the two orders' silence over the cut tree, the teacher who first spoke for the stag's people dies of an ordinary winter cough. Conall Dubh crosses to the teaching-circle unbidden to say he is sorry for their loss, the first word either side has spoken to the other.

title: The stag's people claim the dark wood
body: In answer the stag's people send teachers west to hold their lessons in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, saying that the first stag came from there. Now each side claims both woods, and in either wood the two companies meet and do not speak.

title: The holy-wood dispute
body: Rival rites contend for Coille Naomh Muileann chiar and Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the first such strife that is remembered. It is settled by dividing the keeping of the woods, and no side is judged the victor.

title: Fearchar Òg brought to the hall
body: A boy of seven, a great-grandson of the house that once held Dùn dhearg, is brought to Dùn ìseal by his mother's hand and acknowledged heir by the Keeper of that year, the first claim in longer than the roll can say with certainty found worth the Hall's confidence.

title: Calum Liath takes the flame
body: Calum Liath is made Keeper at forty-five, in Fearchar Òg's ninth year, and judges at once that the wood-watchers and the stag's people will share their silence forever unless someone outside both orders sets a boundary between them.

title: The boundary stones of the woods
body: The woods are divided at Dùn dhearg before Fearchar Òg, a rìgh of Ealasaid Chiar's line who had come to the hall as a boy, and the Keeper Calum Liath. The stag's people keep the eastern wood and the wood-watchers the western, and each may walk in the other's wood unarmed and without cutting. Boundary stones are set at the edges of both woods with the terms cut on them in stag-letters. Two of the eastern stones remain.

title: Conall Dubh walks the eastern wood
body: The day after the last boundary stone is set, Conall Dubh walks unarmed into Coille Naomh Muileann chiar for the first time in his life, a guest under the terms he helped make, and stands a while at the border stand before turning home.

title: The households of the northern road go short
body: With cutters set to counting rather than cutting, the waypoint-keepers send less than the Law's full measure to households a day's carry and more from the mountain, marking each short delivery against a day it might be made good.

title: Calum Liath's surveyors
body: The Keeper Calum Liath sends cutters with knotted cords and lamps into every gallery at Dùn ìseal, to follow the vein as far as it can be followed and mark where it thickens and thins. The work keeps the cutters from the coal for three seasons, and the households go short to pay for it.

title: Calum Liath sends cutters to measure the vein
body: The Keeper Calum Liath gives every cutter of Dùn ìseal a knotted cord and a lamp of the Hall's own oil, and sends them into the galleries to walk the vein from end to end and mark on slates where it runs thick and where it runs to blind rock.

title: A steward of the northern road questions the Keeper
body: Three households short of their measure send the steward Uisdean to Dùn ìseal to ask whether the counting will end before their own stores do. Calum Liath answers only that he cannot yet say, and the steward walks home with the truth and nothing else.

title: Two cutters lost a day in an old working
body: Sent to measure a gallery cut and abandoned in Fionnlagh Dall's time, two young cutters lose a full day in the dark and come out half starved, saying only that they heard something moving beyond their lamp's reach.

title: The measuring of the vein
body: For the first time men try to reckon how much coal the mountain holds. Their reckoning proves far too hopeful.

title: The clerk Mòr nic Aonghais cuts the reckoning
body: A clerk of the Hall who learned her letters from a wanderer of the stag's school sets the sum of the cords into a slab of grey stone, reckoning the mountain's coal against the grains in the granaries of Dùn dhearg, the largest measure a household could hold in its own hand and believe.

title: The reckoning of the cords
body: The reckoning of Calum Liath is cut on a slab in the Hall at Dùn ìseal: the mountain can give every household its handful for more generations than there are grains in the granaries of Dùn dhearg. It is read out at the council and heard in silence, and the Hall takes the silence for assent.

title: The reckoning read and met with silence
body: Calum Liath reads the slab's sum to the assembled stewards and hearths at Dùn ìseal. No one speaks against it and no one praises it; the northern stewards, who paid for the counting in short seasons, say nothing at all, and the Hall takes the silence for assent.

title: Ealasaid Rìoghach asks the council what is owed
body: Griogair's mother stands before the council at Dùn ìseal and asks what the Hall owes her son, sent into a gallery already marked dangerous by a slate no cutter had carried down in memory. The council has no answer ready.

title: The deaths in the lower gallery
body: Two youths of the nine hearths, sent into the lower gallery at Dùn ìseal without a Keeper's cutter to guide them, break the wrong face and are crushed. They had been less than a season in the galleries. Their families ask the council what the Hall owes them, and the council has no answer.

title: Griogair mac Dhonnchaidh and Sìne Bheag crushed in the lower gallery
body: Sent without a Keeper's cutter to bring up a left basket, two youths of one season in the galleries break a face already marked unsound on Aonghas's own slates two years before. Griogair dies at once; Sìne Bheag does not outlive the digging.

title: The council sits three days and turns from fault to custom
body: The stewards of the great shares spend a first day laying blame before Ealasaid Rìoghach's second asking turns the council from fault to remedy: a binding of seven years before any young Dia-thìrich may touch the vein alone.

title: The apprentice-binding custom is agreed
body: The council of Dùn ìseal sets down that no young Dia-thìrich will go into any gallery of the vein's custody until bound seven years to a master cutter of proven years, to learn the mountain's marks and unsound faces before working it alone.

title: The apprentice-binding custom
body: Young Dia-thìrich are first bound for seven years to a master of the vein's custody before they may go near the coal themselves. Every later guild of the mines is shaped on this binding.

title: Calum Liath dies at the Hall's door
body: The Keeper Calum Liath dies by the doorway where he had the reckoning-slab set, in the ninth year after it was cut, and is carried up to lie among the Keepers' own dead near the two youths he had buried before him.

title: Oighrig Bhàn chosen Keeper
body: The nine hearths choose Oighrig Bhàn, a woman of the northern road who had sat with Calum Liath through his last winter, to hold the flame after him.

title: Oighrig Bhàn asks why the binding stands unkept
body: Within her first year Oighrig Bhàn asks why the apprentice-binding, agreed by the council after Griogair and Sìne Bheag's deaths, still stands only as a thing sworn and not a thing done, and finds no better answer than that grief cools faster than custom is kept.

title: Oighrig Bhàn's first bound
body: Oighrig Bhàn, Keeper after Calum Liath, binds the first twelve apprentices under the new custom at Dùn ìseal, each to a master cutter by name. They swear on the stone cup to serve seven years before they touch the vein. Four of the twelve are afterwards Keepers, which is the best that can be said for the custom.

title: Oighrig Bhàn binds the first twelve apprentices
body: In the Hall's own doorway Oighrig Bhàn binds twelve apprentices by name to twelve master cutters, each swearing on the stone cup to serve seven years before touching the vein alone. She stands through every oath and does not sit until the last is sworn.

title: Four of the twelve later hold the flame
body: Of the twelve first bound under Oighrig Bhàn, four in later years are themselves chosen Keeper, which the reciters of Dùn ìseal count the custom's best proof, though none of it answers in full the question Ealasaid Rìoghach asked.

title: Rìoghnach writes the first strike-book entry
body: A novice of the first bound company at Cnoc bhàn, Rìoghnach, sets down the school's first written account by lamp-light in a hand still stiff from her letters: three words, I struck a stroke, and the day beneath them.

title: The birth of Mòrag Dhubh
body: Aonghas Ruadh and Sìne of Cnoc mhòr have a daughter, black-haired against the fairness of both their houses, and name her Mòrag. She is raised at a hearth already full of staves and toll-talk, in the first winters of the hall's new silver.

title: The stag's people take apprentices
