body: The house of the stag's people at Cnoc bhàn takes the seven years for its own cutters and adds a rule: an apprentice keeps a written account of every stroke, and the account is read. These strike-books are the school's chief record for the rest of the age.

title: Cnoc bhàn takes up the seven-year binding
body: Hearing of the binding at Dùn ìseal, the stag's teachers of Cnoc bhàn take up the seven years for their own cutters, binding each apprentice to a master of the school as the Hall bound its own.

title: Cnoc bhàn adds the written account of every stroke
body: The teachers of Cnoc bhàn set a rule the Hall never made: that every bound apprentice keep, once the stag-letters are learned, a written account of every stroke cut in a season, so a master may read back exactly where the hand went wrong.

title: Aonghas Ruadh is paid in the first silver rings
body: Among the guards of the southern ford paid that winter in Fearchar Òg's new stamped rings is Aonghas Ruadh of Cnoc mhòr, who carries his home turning it over in his hand, unsure at first that so small a weight can be a whole season's wage. His wife Sìne trades it for cloth within the week and proves him wrong.

title: The long reign of Fearchar Òg
body: Fearchar Òg, who divided the woods, rules long at Dùn dhearg and is remembered chiefly for dying old. He was named Òg, the young, for coming to the hall as a boy, and the name stuck.

title: Dòmhnall Beag sent to keep the toll at Àth ghlas
body: Fearchar Òg's clerks send a hall-trained man, Dòmhnall Beag, to weigh the new silver toll at the ford of Àth ghlas, where the Griogaraich have kept the crossing's toll by their own standing for longer than anyone can say. It is the first toll-house on any road kept by a man not chosen at the place.

title: The Griogaraich come round to Dòmhnall Beag's scale
body: A year into his keeping of the toll-house, Dòmhnall Beag is still unhelped by the ford's own family, until the winter's firewood and the spring floods force first one and then most of the Griogaraich to take his silver for their labour, never all admitting it to one another.

title: The silver tokens
body: The clerks of Fearchar Òg begin to pay the road-guards in small silver rings of the Muileann chiar weight, stamped with the hall's mark. It is the first payment in metal by any ruler on Dia-thìr. The rings travel further than the guards do.

title: Mòrag Dhubh cuts her own staff
body: Having outgrown every staff her father owns, Mòrag Dhubh cuts one of her own from a young ash at the wood's edge, straight-grained and a hand's breadth taller than she is, and carries it everywhere a girl of the southern road may carry a staff without remark.

title: Mòrag Dhubh's first bout at Ceann leathan
body: Against her father's own doubts, Mòrag Dhubh enters the guards' yearly meeting at Ceann leathan, the first woman to do so, and loses in the second round to a guard twice her age and size, who tells her afterward she had the surest staff of anyone he fought that day.

title: The toll-house at Àth ghlas
body: A toll-house is built on the ford at Àth ghlas, where the southern road crosses the river toward Ceann leathan, and the road-guards are paid there in the new silver rings. Its keeper is the first sent from the rìgh's hall, and not chosen in the place.

title: The road-guards' games at Ceann leathan
body: The road-guards of the south begin to meet each year at Ceann leathan and fight with blunted staves for a silver ring. The meeting outlives its purpose, and on its field Còmhrag Ceann leathan is afterwards fought. The first winner whose name is kept is a woman, Mòrag Dhubh of Cnoc mhòr.

title: The fair at Muileann òg
body: Muileann òg, burned in the War of the Roads, is rebuilt as a market town. A fair is held there each harvest at Lùnastal for the trade of the western and southern roads, and from it Fèill Muileann òg descends.

title: The landing on the Abhainn uaine
body: A landing for river-boats is built on the Abhainn uaine at the place since called Cidhe Beag, so that the grain of the lowlands may go upriver by boat and not on carriers' backs. The carriers of the eastern road protest to Fearchar Òg, and lose.

title: Mòrag Dhubh wins the meeting at Ceann leathan
body: In her fifth year entering, Mòrag Dhubh of Cnoc mhòr beats Ruairidh Fada of Muileann chrom, twice the meeting's winner before her, in the last bout by torchlight, and is given the finest ring struck that season. She is the first winner of the meeting whose name the reciters keep.

title: Ceann leathan's own mark is asked of the hall's smiths
body: With the guards' meeting grown into a day the whole market profits by, Ceann leathan's traders ask Fearchar Òg's smiths for a ring carrying the ford's own mark beside the hall's hearth-sign, so that the finest ring struck each season may be known at a glance as the meeting's own.

title: Muileann òg's households ask a charter for the harvest meeting
body: Seeing what silver a season's traders leave behind them, the households resettled at Muileann òg's ford ask Fearchar Òg's clerks for a charter of the trading already grown up there at Lùnastal, and are granted it, the hall having learned a fed market pays more toll than a starved one.

title: The landing built at Cidhe Beag
body: The hall's clerks raise timbered piers at the old scramble of stones called Cidhe Beag on the Abhainn uaine, judging a river running near empty beside a road worn to ruts a waste the granaries can no longer afford, and put out word for boats to be built to work it.

title: Ciorstaidh leads the carriers' protest to Dùn dhearg
body: Ciorstaidh, who has carried grain on the eastern road sixty years, walks with two other elders the whole distance to Dùn dhearg to tell Fearchar Òg that a river-boat will starve half their households of the wages that have fed them since before the hall was built. He does not turn the landing back.

title: Mòrag Dhubh trades wool at the Lùnastal fair
body: Some years after her win, Mòrag Dhubh walks a season's wool to Muileann òg's fair to trade for cloth her own household cannot weave as fine, and is asked there by an eastern trader whether the tale of the ring she wears is true.

title: The boatmen of Muileann chrom swear the paddle-oath
body: The young crews of Muileann chrom who take up the new river trade settle among themselves, without any hall's asking, that no man may call himself one of their fellowship until he has sworn on his own paddle to answer another boatman's need on the water before his own household's.

title: Dòmhnall of Cnoc mhòr swears his paddle
body: Mòrag Dhubh's younger brother Dòmhnall, who never took to the staff as she did, swears his paddle-oath among the second crews of Muileann chrom the same year her own daughter is born, so that one household comes to hold a ring won on land and an oath sworn on water.

title: Fearchar Òg dies at Dùn dhearg
body: Fearchar Òg dies at ninety-four in the hall his clerks first struck the silver rings in, found gone in his own chair by his steward's grandson. He is buried among the house of Ìomhar after a reign of eighty-seven years, the longest the roll can name, remembered chiefly for its length.

title: Word of the king's death reaches Cnoc mhòr
body: Carried down the southern road by guards paid most of their working lives in Fearchar Òg's silver, word of his death reaches Cnoc mhòr and an aging Mòrag Dhubh, who turns her own worn ring in her fingers at the hearth and says the king made one thing that did not need his hand to keep travelling.

title: The river-boats
body: Flat river-boats of hide over withy begin to carry grain and salt fish up the Abhainn uaine from the landing at Cidhe Beag. The boatmen form a fellowship of their own, sworn on a paddle, and vie with the carriers for the Hall's baskets.

title: The boatmen of Muileann chrom
body: Muileann chrom, up the valley from the landing at Cidhe Beag, becomes the home of the river-boatmen and their fellowship. Its yards build the flat hide boats for every river of the island.

title: Beathag Mhòr
body: Beathag Mhòr, great-granddaughter of Fearchar Òg, takes the hall at Dùn dhearg. The list calls her ban-rìgh, queen, the first so called, and not rìgh with a woman's name after it; the change of word is the list's own.

title: Beathag Mhòr crowned at Dùn dhearg
body: Beathag Mhòr, great-granddaughter of Fearchar Òg, is crowned at twenty in the granary hall at Dùn dhearg. An elder of her own line stands unasked and names her too young to hold ground her house has kept unbroken since the ford. Beathag Mhòr answers with silence and a long look, and the crown is set.

title: Beathag Mhòr rides the northern road
body: Returning from the fleece-market at Baile Mòr fhionn, the young queen rides home by the northern road to see a waypoint-keeper's hearth she has never troubled with her custom. She finds the house at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr thin-fed and sends it grain from Dùn dhearg unmarked, telling its keeper nothing of the gift's source.

title: Sìleas nan Clach paid before the hall's finishing
body: The mason Sìleas nan Clach of Cathair dhomhain raises the red hall at the bridge-foot through two wet winters and a dry summer. Beathag Mhòr pays her in full before the last course is laid, against the custom of paying only on a building's finishing, and Sìleas cuts the hearth-sign into the lintel last of all.

title: Iseabail nic Fhearchair answers for Cathair dhomhain
body: The harbour-master Iseabail nic Fhearchair comes to the new hall herself rather than send a steward, and tells the queen to her face that Cathair dhomhain has weighed its own fish and buried its own drowned since before the Red Share held a single stone. Beathag Mhòr hears her through and grants the harbour its own charter of tolls.

title: The grain-ship saved off Cathair dhomhain
body: A grain-ship out of the western islands loses its mast off Cathair dhomhain's harbour mouth in a winter storm, and the harbour's own boats reach it first and tow it in ahead of the new town's crews. The rescue is told afterward on both quays, and both towns refit boats against the day the sea might drift the other way.

title: The fleece-measure of Baile Mòr fhionn
body: The lords of the western plain hold a market at Baile Mòr fhionn and make the fleece of a grown ewe its measure. Grain, wine, cattle and the horses of the plain are all priced in fleeces. The silver rings of Muileann chiar are taken there too, but reckoned in wool.

title: The hall moves to Cathair dhearg
body: Beathag Mhòr moves her hall from Dùn dhearg to the town at the western bridge-foot, Cathair dhearg, to sit where the roads, the river and the western harbours meet. Dùn dhearg keeps the old granaries and the graves of the house of Ìomhar. From this reign Cathair dhearg is the seat of rule on Dia-thìr, whatever else changes.

title: Dùn dhearg after the move
body: Dùn dhearg, left behind, keeps its granaries and its pride. Its people go on calling it the rìgh's hill, and for many generations its reeves will send their accounts to Cathair dhearg in no hand but their own.

title: The red hall
body: Beathag Mhòr's hall at Cathair dhearg is built on the rise above the harbour, of the red stone that names the town. Its foundations lie under the later citadel. The masons cut the hearth-sign in its lintel as though it were a bridge.

title: Cathair dhomhain against Cathair dhearg
body: The harbour of Cathair dhomhain, older and larger, grudges the new seat on its doorstep and refuses the queen's toll on its boats. Beathag Mhòr grants it a charter of its own tolls. The two towns, a few miles apart, are rivals for the rest of the age.

title: Disputed hands
body: The council at Dùn ìseal is asked to judge more quarrels over the right to the handful than over anything else: new households, divided households, households that claim descent from one of the nine hearths without proof. Dùghall mac Raghnaill, Keeper after Oighrig Bhàn, asks the queen for a counting.

title: Dùghall mac Raghnaill takes the flame
body: The nine hearths choose Dùghall mac Raghnaill of Sliochd Raghnaill to hold the flame, a man of twenty-nine who left his own house's hall as a boy to learn the vein's reckoning. His first sitting at the cup finds the council floor so crowded with disputed claims to the handful that he cannot cross it unhindered.

title: Beitris nic Ailein shames the Keeper into asking
body: An old widow of the eastern road, Beitris nic Ailein, asks Dùghall mac Raghnaill at the crowded council how he means to judge claims to the handful for the rest of his life without ever knowing which he has judged rightly. He has no answer, and rides to Cathair dhearg within the month to ask the queen for a count.

title: The queen and the Keeper agree the count
body: Beathag Mhòr agrees to Dùghall mac Raghnaill's asking before he has finished it, and the two settle on the waypoint houses as the counting's ground, since every household on the island lies within a day of one. The queen pledges to feed the counters at her own cost out of each house's own stores.

title: Ruairidh born to the queen
body: Beathag Mhòr's son Ruairidh is born at the new hall, grey-headed almost from his cradle. Her household takes the colour for an ill sign; the queen, who has buried enough of her own line's short-lived cousins to know better, takes it for nothing more than a child's colouring.

title: Sorcha nic Ruairidh proves a grandmother's claim
body: At the waypoint house An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, the counter Sorcha nic Ruairidh sits six months over one old woman's claim to the handful, hearing it back four generations by name and by story until it stands proved beyond the council's doubt. She writes the four names down in a hand the old woman cannot read.

title: Ruairidh Cam of Seann Tarr refused
body: The counters find no coal-right in living memory at the fisher-household of Ruairidh Cam of Seann Tarr, and refuse his claim. Asked whether his house means to appeal, he answers that they burned peat before the Small-Burning Law was thought of and will burn it after, and that peat, besides, is the warmer fire.

title: Sliochd Raghnaill's plea for Seann Tarr
body: Dùghall mac Raghnaill's own house takes up the refused fisher-families' cause at the council, arguing that a right so long unclaimed ought to be granted rather than denied. The council rules against it: the Small-Burning Law protects a right already held, not one never claimed. The Keeper speaks neither for the argument nor against it.

title: Ruairidh Cam's grandson keeps the light
body: The rebuilt sea-light on the eastern cape is kept by Ruairidh Cam's own grandson, a duty owed to no coal-right but to his family's long knowledge of the cape's rocks in the dark. Asked whether he still holds to his grandfather's saying about peat, he answers that he does, and the saying travels further than the census roll ever did.

title: The refused roll kept in its own chest
body: The roll of the households refused the handful is consulted so often by families proving an old claim through a cousin's cousin that the clerks at Cathair dhearg give it a chest of its own. It is worn soft at the corners within a generation of its writing, more read than the larger roll beside it.

title: Beathag Mhòr orders the count
body: Beathag Mhòr and Dùghall mac Raghnaill agree that every household on the island claiming the handful shall be counted, its right proved or refused, and its name written. The clerks at Cathair dhearg are to write, and the Keepers to judge.

title: The waypoint houses as counting-houses
body: The counters make their stations at the waypoint houses, for every household on the island lies within a day of one. The keepers of the houses feed the counters at the queen's cost, and in the houses the count is afterwards remembered as a good year.

title: The census of hands
body: The households that hold the old right to burn the coal are counted across the whole island for the first time. So it is shown that the burning of the coal was already rationed by rule.

title: The count of hands
body: The rolls of the count, kept at Cathair dhearg, give eleven thousand four hundred households holding the right, and some two thousand whose claims were refused. The refused are written on a roll of their own, and from then on it is that roll families search when they would prove an ancestor's standing.

title: The refused of Seann Tarr
body: Most of the refused households of the north-eastern coast are fisher-families about Seann Tarr who had never burned coal at all, and now find they have no right to begin. Sliochd Raghnaill takes up their cause at the council and loses. The fisher-families burn peat and say it is warmer.

title: The light at Baile ìseal
body: The old beacon on the eastern point at Baile ìseal is rebuilt, kept with driftwood and seal fat as the Law requires, to bring the fishing boats of the eastern coast home in the dark. From it comes Taigh-solais Baile ìseal.

title: The light at Muileann bheag
body: The old beacon on the northern headland at Muileann bheag is rebuilt; from it comes Taigh-solais Muileann bheag. Its keepers are fisher-families of the north-west, who pay no toll to Cathair dhearg in return for keeping it.

title: The light at Àth dhearg
body: Sliochd Raghnaill rebuilds the old beacon on the north-eastern cape at Àth dhearg, to mark the way in toward Seann Tarr. From it comes Taigh-solais Àth dhearg.

title: Death of Beathag Mhòr
body: Beathag Mhòr dies at Cathair dhearg and by her own command is carried back to Dùn dhearg to lie among the house of Ìomhar. No royal journey before it was so long.

title: The refused roll read at Dùn dhearg
body: After Beathag Mhòr is carried the length of the island to lie among the house of Ìomhar, the roll of the refused is brought up from Cathair dhearg in its worn chest and read aloud once before the household of Dùn dhearg, so that the hill that gave up its hall might hear what the giving had bought.

title: Ruairidh Liath
body: Ruairidh Liath, son of Beathag Mhòr, rules from Cathair dhearg. He is grey already when he takes the hall, and his byname is the list's one jest.

title: Ruairidh Liath crowned at Cathair dhearg
body: Ruairidh Liath, grey since his cradle, takes the red hall in his thirty-sixth year, five days after his mother Beathag Mhòr is carried to Dùn dhearg. The crowning is held quietly, in the household's year of mourning, and he keeps her clerks, stewards and reeve in their places.

title: The eastern guard doubled
body: Ruairidh Liath doubles the guard on the eastern road against toll-cheats grown bold in the census years, when every clerk on the island was walking house to house rather than watching the roads. The guard's pay, more than anything else in his reign, brings him at last to ask something of the silver.

title: The Silver Feud begins
body: Ruairidh Liath demands one ring in five of the silver taken at Muileann chiar, saying the tokens that pay his guards should cost him nothing. Sliochd Fhearchair, the silversmiths' house, answers with Muireach Liath's ruling: silver is not holy, and so not the crown's either. They close the workings sooner than pay.

title: Màiri nic Fhearchair refuses the steward
body: A steward rides three days from Dùn dhearg to demand one ring in five of Sliochd Fhearchair's silver. Màiri nic Fhearchair, who speaks for the house, answers with Muireach Liath's own ruling that silver is not the mountain's, and sends him home with no other word.

title: The guards leave Àth ghlas
body: Two of the four road-guards at the toll-house of Àth ghlas leave their posts unpaid, the wages standing on a silver toll no one has yet agreed to gather. The keeper Oighrig nic Ailein stands the house through the winter with the two who remain, turning back no traveller and collecting no toll.

title: The closing of the silver
body: For three seasons no silver leaves Muileann chiar. The road-guards go unpaid, the fair at Muileann òg trades in grain again, and the tolls of the eastern road go ungathered. It is called the Silver Feud, though no one is killed in it.

title: Grain sent unnamed to Àth ghlas
body: Ruairidh Liath sends grain to the toll-house at Àth ghlas without naming himself the sender, as his mother once sent grain to a hungry waypoint house. Oighrig nic Ailein guesses whose it is and never tells a traveller the story of it.

title: Two apprentices go hungry at Muileann chiar
body: In the third winter of the shutting, two of Màiri nic Fhearchair's youngest apprentices go thinner than any she has trained in forty years at the fire. She feeds them from her own table and judges that a right is not worth keeping at the cost of the hands that would keep it after her.

title: The Keeper's judgment on the silver
body: At the asking of both sides the Keeper Dùghall mac Raghnaill rules at Dùn ìseal that the words of Muireach Liath stand, and silver is not the mountain's; but also that the crown keeps the roads the silver travels. Ruairidh Liath takes one ring in ten, Sliochd Fhearchair opens the workings again, and each calls it a victory.

title: Màiri nic Fhearchair's journey to Dùn ìseal
body: Màiri nic Fhearchair rides to Dùn ìseal in four days' unbroken rain with her grandnephew Tormod and a strongbox of rings struck in Fearchar Òg's reign, to ask the Keeper's judgment on a right her house has never before brought before the Hall.

title: The rain-shut hearing at Dùn ìseal
body: Dùghall mac Raghnaill hears Ruairidh Liath and Màiri nic Fhearchair argue the silver a full day in a hall the rain has shut. He has Màiri say Muireach Liath's sentence twice, then rules each of them right and each mistaken, setting the toll at one ring in ten on the roads, not the ore.

title: The Muileann chiar weight made law
body: In the settlement the silver weights of Muileann chiar are declared the only lawful weights on the roads of the island. Copies in bronze are sent to every waypoint house, and the house of Fearchar is paid for each.

title: Sliochd Fhearchair paid for its own weights
body: The crown's clerks pay Màiri nic Fhearchair for every bronze copy cast from Sliochd Fhearchair's own weights, the first silver the house has ever taken from Cathair dhearg rather than given it. She calls it no poor victory to settle for.

title: Beitris nic Aonghais casts the first weight
body: At Muileann dhearg, Beitris nic Aonghais casts the first bronze copy of the Muileann chiar weight, cracked along its rim from cooling too fast. She keeps the poor casting the rest of her life, showing it to every apprentice before letting them near the good bronze.

title: The hearth-sign struck on every weight
body: Beitris nic Aonghais asks leave to cut Sliochd Fhearchair's hearth-sign into the underside of every weight-copy, that a keeper might know the true measure at a glance. Màiri nic Fhearchair grants it gladly, and the two houses trade weights, bells and lamp-bowls for years after.

title: Màiri nic Fhearchair dies
body: Màiri nic Fhearchair dies in her eightieth year, eleven years after the settlement at Dùn ìseal. At her own long-standing word she is buried with the strongbox that carried her rings to the hearing, rather than the ring she wore at her throat.

title: Dùghall mac Raghnaill dies
body: Dùghall mac Raghnaill dies in his ninetieth year, having held the flame longer than any Keeper before him. The reciters of Dùn ìseal remember him less for the census than for the rain-shut hearing where he told two sides they were each right and each wrong.

title: Ruairidh Liath dies
body: Ruairidh Liath dies in the red hall at Cathair dhearg in his eightieth year, in the chamber where his mother died before him. His household remembers him as a rìgh who waited where waiting served and moved where nothing else would.

title: The bronze-casters of Muileann dhearg
body: The bronze copies of the Muileann chiar weights are cast at Muileann dhearg, where a family of casters learned the craft from the silversmiths. They go on to cast bells, pins and lamp-bowls, and their lamp-bowls hold the Law's measure exactly.

title: Seonag Chrom
body: Seonag Chrom, granddaughter of Ruairidh Liath, rules at Cathair dhearg. She gives the clerks a room of their own in the red hall and a wage in silver, and from her reign the king-list is kept year by year and not reign by reign.

title: Seonag Chrom crowned and the clerks given a room
body: Seonag Chrom, granddaughter of Ruairidh Liath, takes the hall at Cathair dhearg in her twenty-first year. Having read the worn, damp-eaten roll of her grandfather's silver settlement, she gives the Hall's clerks their own room and a wage in silver, and the king-list begins to be kept year by year.

title: A teacher of the stag's people comes to Inis bheag
body: A teacher of the stag's people, once a cutter's son, settles at Inis bheag on the northern coast and begins teaching the fisher-marks to children who will never cut coal. The Hall's roll notes the teaching and calls it, in passing, no great matter, since fish have no need of reading.

title: Inis bheag's school of letters
body: At Inis bheag on the Abhainn bheag in the north a teacher of the stag's people begins to teach letters to fishers' children who will never cut coal. It is the first teaching of letters for their own sake. The Hall's roll notes it, and adds that fish do not need reading.

title: The teacher of Inis bheag is buried in his own marks
body: The teacher who first brought letters to Inis bheag dies an old man, having taught three generations of the same dozen families. A pupil cuts his grave-marker in the fisher-marks rather than in the Hall's own hand, the first stone on the island so cut.

title: A stable-boy's tally teaches a clerk's daughter her letters
body: At Cathair dhearg a boy of Inis bheag, sent inland to serve in the red hall's stables, scratches a fisher's tally on a granary door. A clerk's daughter, Peigi nic Tormoid, asks what the marks mean and will not be told they are nothing, and so learns the fisher-marks before she learns the Hall's own hand.

title: Peigi nic Tormoid, clerk of the hall
body: Peigi nic Tormoid, of the line of Tormod Scrìobhaiche, is clerk of the hall at Cathair dhearg, the first whose own hand can be told from the others in the copies that survive. Her entries are short, and she never gives a reason where a fact will serve. Much of what is known of the middle of the age is in her hand, or copied from it.

title: Peigi nic Tormoid takes the clerk's stool
body: Peigi nic Tormoid is given the clerk's stool at Cathair dhearg in her twenty-sixth year, after the death of an elder cousin from fever and for want of anyone else willing to take the work. She keeps the roll of the red hall for four-and-forty years after.

title: Peigi's ruling on the boundary of two descriptions
body: A lord of the plain presses Peigi nic Tormoid to set a boundary dispute down in his own favour. She refuses to keep opinions in the roll and writes instead both sides' own words and the last day they had agreed on anything, a plain record a Keeper's clerk consults to settle a far larger dispute two centuries later.

title: Death of Peigi nic Tormoid
body: Peigi nic Tormoid dies in her own bed at seventy, having kept the roll of the red hall through a reign and the half of another. The clerks who follow her learn to date a leaf by whether her hand lies on it, a truer clock, some say, than the reign it was written under.

title: The fowler households of Seann Skell feed the hawk first
body: At Seann Skell on the northern coast the fowler families begin feeding their hawks before the household eats, on the reasoning that a hunger fed first turns less readily on the house that keeps it waiting. The custom spreads from household to household along the one street.

title: The hawk-keepers of Seann Skell
body: At Seann Skell on the northern coast the fowler families keep a hawk in every household and feed it before the household eats. They burn their season's handful at dawn with the hawk on the wrist, for the flame, they say, is a hunger and should be fed as a hunger is fed. They call the hawk Mòd, the Hawk of Acaill, the grey hawk of time, as old as Fionntan mac Bòchra, eldest of men, who lived down the ages as a salmon, an eagle and a hawk; between them the two remember all things. From them Òrd an t-Seabhaig counts its beginning.

title: Raghnaid nic Chaluim burns her handful with the hawk unhooded
body: Raghnaid nic Chaluim of Seann Skell burns her household's dawn handful with her hawk Mòd unhooded on her wrist, its eye on the flame the whole time it burns. Her own household says of her afterward that she carried the custom the whole distance it would go.

title: A clerk questions Raghnaid on the hawk's watching
body: A clerk sent from Cathair dhearg to set the dawn-hawk custom in the Hall's roll asks Raghnaid nic Chaluim why the bird must watch the burning. She answers that the flame is a hunger too and should be fed in the sight of the thing that hungers, and the clerk writes her words down unaltered.

title: The dawn-hawk kept at Cnoc bheag
body: Households at Cnoc bheag, none of them fowlers by trade, buy hawks at cost from Skell traders and take up the dawn burning with the bird on the wrist. Their neighbours, keeping no hawk, remark that the birds are fed better than the households' own children.

title: The Keeper sends a clerk to see the dawn kept
body: Pressed by an uneasy household of the lowland plain, the Keeper of that season sends a clerk north to Cnoc bheag to see the dawn-hawk rite kept before ruling on it. The clerk reports the hawk-households burn no more of their measure than any other hearth, only in a bird's sight rather than none.

title: The Hall answers that the rite is no concern of its own
body: The Keeper writes to the lowland household, and to every household after it that raises the question, that the dawn-hawk rite keeps the measure exactly and is no concern of the Hall's. It is the last time in the age the Hall answers any rite so simply.

title: The hawk-rite spreads up the Abhainn ìseal
body: The dawn burning with the hawk spreads from Seann Skell on the northern shore up the Abhainn ìseal to Inis ìseal and Cnoc bheag. The Keeper at Dùn ìseal writes that the rite keeps the measure exactly and is therefore no concern of the Hall. Never again does the Hall say so of any rite.

title: Aonghas Ruadh brings the sting-oath north to Ros bheag
body: Aonghas Ruadh, a merchant of Ros bheag trading salt fish for the dry country's dyed wool, returns from Baile àrsaidh with a boxed scorpion and swears his next bargain on its sting before the harbour court has seen the custom done. The court takes to the swearing within the year.

title: A trader of the plain is refused for want of the sting-oath
body: A trader of the plain who will not swear his debt on Ros bheag's sting, calling a boxed scorpion no fit thing to bind a man, is sold no fish by the harbour court, which holds that a man unwilling to swear as every other trader swears is telling the court something his own name does not.

title: The sting-oath at Ros bheag
body: The swearing on a scorpion's sting spreads from Baile àrsaidh up the western coast to Ros bheag, and the harbour court there takes it for every oath of trade. For the rest of the age a merchant who will not swear on the sting is not trusted in the western harbours.

title: Death of Aonghas Ruadh
body: Aonghas Ruadh dies an old man at Ros bheag, still keeper of his own scorpion in its box behind the harbour-master's door. By then no merchant travels the western coast without learning the sting-oath before the prices, from Ros bheag to Baile àrsaidh alike.

title: The shrine-keepers of Inis thais ask for a second stone
body: The shrine-keepers of Inis thais, hearing of the wolf-sworn road-guards' oath-stone at Caol leathan, ask the guild whether a second might stand at their own shrine beside the drowned, where a guard's oath, they judge, would sit well beside an older prayer. The guards, flattered more than they admit, agree to drag one themselves rather than trust any mason unsworn to their own oath.

title: The dragging of the second wolf-stone
body: The road-guards of Caol leathan drag a block of white quartz from the mountain to Inis thais at the cost of more oxen than the guild can easily spare, the sledge breaking twice on the lower slopes and one ox dying under the second breaking.

title: Calum Mòr declines to swear twice at Inis thais
body: Asked by the eldest shrine-keeper whether he wishes to pray before the new stone, the road-guards' captain Calum Mòr answers that he swore on it once at his founding and sees no cause to swear twice, though his guards may pray there as the drowned welcome any stranger's prayer.

title: The Hall's roll outgrows the clerks' room
body: The roll kept at Cathair dhearg since Seonag Chrom first gave the clerks a room runs by now to more chests than the room can hold. A later generation of clerks works from summaries of summaries, the original hands known to them by name and reputation and not by sight.

title: The wolf-stone at Inis thais
body: The wolf-sworn road-guards of Caol leathan set a second wolf-stone at the shrine of Inis thais, and the keepers of the shrine begin to pray before it as well as to the drowned. The stone is white quartz, dragged from the mountain on a sledge at a cost greater than the shrine's.

title: Four keepings named in one breath at Cathair dhearg
body: A trader passing through Cathair dhearg names the hawk fed at Seann Skell, the sting sworn at Ros bheag, the wolf-stone prayed to at Inis thais and the fisher-marks taught at Inis bheag all together, as though of one custom, though none were ever planned as such.

title: Donnchadh mac Iain is born at Cnoc bhàn
body: A cutter's widow of Cnoc bhàn brings her second son to the stag's teachers rather than send him to the vein at ten years old, judging one son owed to the coal enough for her house. He grows up among the school's chests of strike-books before he grows up among the seams.

title: The strike-books compared
body: Donnchadh mac Iain, a teacher of the stag's people at Cnoc bhàn, reads through the strike-books of many generations of apprentices. He finds that the coal breaks brighter in its colours for cutters in their later years than in their first, whatever their house, and argues that the vein answers practice. The elders answer that it answers what a cutter was born with, and that practice only shows it.

title: Donnchadh mac Iain is set to the old leaves
body: In a thin winter Cnoc bhàn's masters set the young teacher Donnchadh mac Iain to clearing dead apprentices' leaves from the school's chests, a task given him more as punishment than trust. He begins, instead, a private tally of when in a cutter's years the coal comes brightest.

title: Aonghas Cam answers the tally
body: The eldest teacher of Cnoc bhàn, Aonghas Cam, hears Donnchadh mac Iain's tally at the midwinter gathering and answers, as the house had always answered, that the vein knows a cutter's blood and the years only show what was already there. The two teachings begin to divide the room.

title: The house at Cnoc bhàn sits in two halves
body: By the eighth year of Donnchadh mac Iain's yearly tally, those who hear him to the end of it and those who answer him before he finishes have come, without any master's ordering, to sit on opposite sides of the long room at every midwinter gathering.

title: Donnchadh mac Iain leaves Cnoc bhàn
body: Donnchadh mac Iain and twenty-two of his hearers leave the house at Cnoc bhàn and settle at Muileann chaol, taking copies of the strike-books with them. The elders of Cnoc bhàn call it theft of the books. Donnchadh calls it copying, which it is.

title: The twenty-two leave Cnoc bhàn
body: Donnchadh mac Iain and twenty-two hearers load copies of the strike-books they judge their own onto two borrowed carts and walk south to Muileann chaol. The elders of Cnoc bhàn call it theft; Donnchadh calls it copying, since every leaf they made a copy of stands where it always stood.

title: Muileann chaol's reeve houses the school
body: The reeve of Muileann chaol lets Donnchadh mac Iain's twenty-two hearers a millwright's storehouse for a rent none of them can pay in coin, taken instead that first winter in mended roofs and re-hung doors for half the town.

title: Muileann chaol's books are ruled to keep no parentage
body: Donnchadh mac Iain sets the rule for the new school's strike-books: no cutter's father, mother or house is written on a leaf, only the name, the day and the stroke. More than one of the twenty-two finds the old habit slower to unlearn than the rule was to set down.

title: The founding of the rival druid school
body: A school of druids breaks away, holding that the vein answers labour and not birth.

title: The school at Muileann chaol
body: The school of Donnchadh mac Iain at Muileann chaol keeps strike-books of its own under a rule the elder school never had: a cutter's parentage is not written in the book at all. The two schools of the stag dispute by letter for the rest of the age, and both keep the letters.

title: Donnchadh mac Iain writes north
body: Seventy years old and less able to travel, Donnchadh mac Iain sends the first letter to Cnoc bhàn, addressed to the house rather than to any one master, asking whether its own century-and-a-half of leaves shows the same rise with a cutter's years that his own count once showed.

title: Donnchadh mac Iain dies at Muileann chaol
body: Donnchadh mac Iain dies at eighty in the storehouse-schoolhouse his twenty-two hearers first took shelter in forty years before, having taught six generations whose leaves carry no father's or mother's name. He is buried under a leaf of oiled hide cut with one word: one who writes.

title: Raonaid Dhubh is born at Dùn ìseal
body: A clerk's daughter is born at Dùn ìseal in the same year Donnchadh mac Iain dies, given the name Raonaid Dhubh for the black hair she keeps unusually from her first day.

title: Raonaid Dhubh takes the Keeper's stool
body: Raonaid Dhubh comes to the Keeper's own chest of clerks at twenty, an elder cousin's death leaving the stool empty at a season when no one else in the room wants the sitting of it, and reads there, among other papers, the growing archive of letters between Cnoc bhàn and Muileann chaol.

title: The Hall hears the two schools
body: The Keeper Raonaid Dhubh hears both schools of the stag at Dùn ìseal and gives no ruling, saying that the vein has not asked the Hall to decide. The Hall's roll sets down the hearing and the refusal. No refusal of the Hall is more often cited.

title: Both schools ask the new Keeper for a ruling
body: Within her first year holding the cup, Raonaid Dhubh receives word from both Cnoc bhàn and Muileann chaol asking her to say, once and plainly, which school's reading of the vein is the truer, as every Keeper before her has been asked and never once has answered.

title: What the people of Cnoc ghorm say of their stone
body: Scholars of the stag from Muileann chaol come to Calbh Cnoc ghorm and cannot read it. The people of Cnoc ghorm tell them the stone says: we did not come; we were here. The scholars write that the people say so. No later hand explains either the stone or the saying.

title: The scholars of Muileann chaol cannot read Cnoc ghorm's stone
body: Scholars of the second school travel east to Cnoc ghorm to read the standing stone at the town's centre, and spend the better part of a day turning its worn face to the light without making out a single letter of its cutting.

title: The digging at Làrach an Dùin
body: Men of Baile ghorm dig under the fallen walls of Làrach an Dùin for the riches the ruin was said to hold, and find ash and nothing else. The Keeper has them sentenced as if they had broken the Law, though no law covered it, and the sentence stands as the rule for all the old places after.

title: Baile ghorm's diggers find only ash
body: A company from Baile ghorm breaks into the fallen walls of Làrach an Dùin by night on the strength of an old tale of riches, and finds at dawn nothing beneath the stone but cold, undisturbed ash that no fire any of them can name had left.

title: Baile ghorm's penance
body: The families of the diggers at Baile ghorm do penance by keeping in repair the road from their town to Tuam Cnoc dhìreach. In the southern hills it is called the diggers' road still.

title: The diggers' road earns its name
body: The road the families of Baile ghorm keep in repair as their penance, from their own town south to Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, is by this year known in the southern hills by no other name than the diggers' road, kept long past any term the Keeper's sentence set.

title: The hungry season at the halting-house below the pass
body: Calum Ruadh of Àth dhìreach and the other carriers of the mountain road read, on the tally board of a small halting-house, the shape of a poor year no custom yet mends: coal going down the road and next to no grain coming up. The house's keeper, an old woman named Mòr, tells them she has buried a husband to just such a winter before.

title: Lachlann Bàn
body: Lachlann Bàn takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. He builds granaries in every province seat that will have one, and makes a law about them, and for these he is remembered.

title: Lachlann Bàn's vow at his crowning
body: Lachlann Bàn, come to the red hall in his twenty-sixth year, finds granaries that fill and empty by no rule but a steward's whim, and resolves to build a common granary in every province seat that will keep one, to the same plan, so that no district need go hungry beside another's plenty.

title: The reeve of Cnoc mhòr's silver ring
body: Cnoc mhòr raises its common granary before any other province seat and sends word of it to Cathair dhearg the same season. Lachlann Bàn sends the reeve a silver ring for his own hand, and within two years no province seat on the plain is willing to be named last where Cnoc mhòr was named first.

title: Lachlann Bàn's journey to Dùn ìseal
body: Lachlann Bàn climbs to Dùn ìseal to ask the Keeper Raonaid Dhubh to set the island's old neighbour-custom of shared grain under his new granaries as law. She asks whether he means his own hall's granary bound by the same terms as any household's; he swears it will be, and she puts her hand to the writing.

title: The shared-meal law written
body: Lachlann Bàn and the Keeper Raonaid Dhubh make the old unwritten custom law at Cathair dhearg: a household with grain above its winter's need gives the surplus to the common granary of its district before the storm season, and the granary feeds any household of the district that runs short. The successors of Peigi nic Tormoid write it into the rolls in full. It is the first law made by rìgh and Keeper together.

title: Lachlann Bàn and Raonaid Dhubh swear the shared-meal law
body: The rìgh at Cathair dhearg and the Keeper at Dùn ìseal set their names together to the law of the common granary: that no district's store be kept from a neighbour's hunger, and that what is lent in a hard year be repaid harvest by harvest.

title: A reeve of the plain protests the mountain's granaries
body: A reeve of the lowland plain writes to Cathair dhearg that his district is asked to fill granaries for mountain households that grow no grain of their own. Lachlann Bàn answers that a household which carries the plain's coal all winter has already paid, in the coin of its own back, for whatever grain comes up in return.

title: Cathair mhòr's fisher-towns pay their share in fish
body: The granary raised within Cathair mhòr's old wall, the first anywhere behind a town wall, draws its share from the southern fishing strands in dried fish rather than grain, packed in baskets as the old toll fish once were packed for the Hall at Dùn ìseal.

title: Death of Raonaid Dhubh
body: Raonaid Dhubh, Keeper of the flame at Dùn ìseal for the better part of forty years and the woman who set the shared-meal law beside Lachlann Bàn, dies in her own eightieth year, having seen the law hold unbroken through two poor seasons.

title: Ruairidh mac Nèill burns the raiders' boats at Seann Tarr
body: Ruairidh mac Nèill of Sliochd Raghnaill catches the eastern raiders at their own anchorage with the tide against them and burns two of their low black boats. Asked why he let the rest escape, he says a boat burned at its own anchorage teaches the strand's watch more than a raider hanged at Seann Tarr.

title: The granary of Cnoc mhòr
body: Cnoc mhòr builds its common granary under the new law before any other district, and sends word of it to Cathair dhearg. Lachlann Bàn sends back a silver ring for the reeve.

title: The common granaries of the mountain
body: Common granaries are raised under the new law in the mountain districts round Muileann chiar, where the households live by cutting and carrying and grow little of their own. The lowland districts grumble at filling them.

title: The Four Houses begin their quiet counting
body: With Oighrig nic Lachlainn newly widowed and childless, Sliochd Ìomhair, Sliochd Thormoid and Sliochd Raghnaill each begin, without speaking of it before her, to reckon what it might claim of the red hall should she die without an heir; Sliochd Mhuirich, holding the Keeper's own office, makes no claim at all.

title: The granary at Cathair mhòr
body: A common granary is built within the old wall at Cathair mhòr, the first behind a town wall. The southern fishing towns, having no grain, send dried fish to it for their share.

title: Raiders in the eastern waters
body: Outlaws in boats raid the eastern fishing strands from the islets offshore, taking dried fish and nets. Sliochd Raghnaill arms its boats at Seann Tarr and burns two of the raiders' boats. The rest escape.

title: Oighrig nic Lachlainn
body: Oighrig nic Lachlainn, daughter of Lachlann Bàn, takes the hall at Cathair dhearg. She has no children, and before her reign is half done the houses begin to count their claims.

title: Death of Lachlann Bàn
body: Lachlann Bàn dies in his own bed at one-and-eighty, five-and-fifty years after his crowning, mourned chiefly by the reeves whose granaries he built and the carriers of the mountain roads, who never once in his reign went a whole winter without knowing where the next grain was coming from.

title: Oighrig nic Lachlainn takes the hall at one-and-twenty
body: On her father's death Oighrig nic Lachlainn takes the red hall in her one-and-twentieth year. She will hold it the better part of fifty years and bear no child.

title: Calum Ruadh tells his son of the old want
body: With the passes above Cnoc ghlas still white with late snow and the mountain households eating their seed, Calum Ruadh tells his son Iain Caol, a boy of fifteen, of the very want he carried through as a young man, and doubts aloud whether the new law will hold where the old custom never had to be tried.

title: Calum Ruadh and Iain Caol carry grain to Àth dhìreach
body: Calum Ruadh, past his own heaviest carrying, walks down for the grain Dùn dhearg has sent unasked, and his son Iain Caol, too young by the town's reckoning to carry a full load, carries half of one beside him, the boy's first sight of what the shared-meal law meant in a true want.

title: Àth dhìreach grants the carriers the right to rest
body: The reeve of Àth dhìreach calls the town together and grants every carrier who walked the famine road that winter the right to rest, for life, in any house of the town without payment; the households swear to keep it as their own word rather than write it into any roll at Cathair dhearg.

title: Gilleasbuig born to a copying clerk of Seann Dunn
body: Gilleasbuig is born at Seann Dunn to Tormod Beag, a copying clerk of Sliochd Thormoid who puts down on scraped hide, in the house's small square hand, whatever the red hall sends him to copy. The boy grows up under his father's bench.

title: The late snow on the high passes
body: The weather-watchers on the cairns above Cnoc ghlas see snow lying on the high passes long past the opening of the galleries. The Hall keeps the galleries shut for the cutters' safety, and the mountain households wait.

title: The poor season in the mountain
body: The galleries open late and close early, and the coal carried down is a third of a common season's. The mountain households of Muileann gheal, Doire uaine and Àth dhìreach, who trade their carrying for grain, have nothing to trade, and by the season's end they are eating their seed.

title: The first recorded famine averted
body: A poor mining season brings three settlements near to starving. The shared-meal law, made in the reign before, holds and saves them. It is the first true trial of the custom.

title: The granaries opened
body: Under the shared-meal law the common granaries of the mountain districts are opened at Muileann gheal. When they run low the granaries of Dùn dhearg and the southern coast send grain up the carriers' roads without being asked twice, and the carriers bear it for no fee. None in the three settlements is known to die of hunger that winter.

title: Iain Caol's first load up
body: Iain Caol, grown to a man's height, takes up his first load as a carrier proper, walking the same track his father Calum Ruadh had walked before him, with a company of four other young men of Àth dhìreach carrying their first working loads that same season.

title: Àth dhìreach after the poor season
body: At Àth dhìreach, one of the three settlements the granaries fed, the carriers who brought up the grain are given the right to rest in any house of the town without payment for as long as they live. The last of them dies old, and the right with him.

title: The reeves of Dùn dhearg send the grain
body: The reeves of Dùn dhearg, who had withheld their accounts from Cathair dhearg for generations, open the old granaries of the house of Ìomhar to the mountain without waiting for an order. Oighrig nic Lachlainn writes that she would have given the order had they waited. The successor of Peigi nic Tormoid notes that they did not.

title: Why the king-list is kept in six copies
body: Asked by his small son why the king-list needs six copies where a tithe needs one, Tormod Beag answers that a tithe is true for a year and a king-list must be true for longer than any man who writes it, so that if fire takes one house the rest will still agree.

title: A tithe-roll scraped clean for one wrong stroke
body: Tormod Beag, a copying clerk of Sliochd Thormoid at Seann Dunn, scrapes clean a province's tithe-roll his young son Gilleasbuig has copied with a single stroke too many in it, and makes the boy write the whole roll again from the beginning rather than mend the one line, so that he learns early a mistake quietly mended teaches a clerk less than a roll done wholly over.

title: Gilleasbuig rides alone to Cathair dhearg with the rolls
body: At fourteen Gilleasbuig first rides the day and a half from Seann Dunn to the red hall alone, the rolls in a satchel on his back and a hearth-sign token that lets him sleep free at any waypoint house. He learns every waypoint keeper's name before he knows half the great families.

title: Oighrig nic Lachlainn's word to a clerk's son
body: A young Gilleasbuig, carrying his father's rolls to Cathair dhearg at sixteen, is asked by Oighrig nic Lachlainn whose son he is; told his father's name, she says only that the hand is known to her, the one exchange of the whole reign between the woman who holds the red hall and the clerk who will one day fill it.

title: Death of Oighrig nic Lachlainn
body: Oighrig nic Lachlainn dies at Cathair dhearg with no heir of her body, and with her ends the line of Goraidh Mòr, as the list reckons it. The red hall is shut, and its clerks keep it.

title: The clerks keep the shut hall's tallies
body: Gilleasbuig Mòr, sent down from Seann Dunn the winter after Oighrig nic Lachlainn's death, spends a season sealing rolls and answering reeves at the shut red hall who no longer know whose name to render account to, keeping every tally true on the plain reasoning that whoever fills the hall next will want them so.

title: The four houses meet
body: The Four Houses of custody meet at Dùn ìseal to choose a ruler, for no custom covers a hall without an heir. Sliochd Ìomhair claims it by blood, Sliochd Thormoid by the clerks, Sliochd Raghnaill by its boats. Sliochd Mhuirich, holding the Keeper's office, makes no claim.

title: Sliochd Mhuirich makes no claim to the empty hall
body: At the Four Houses' meeting at Dùn ìseal, Sliochd Ìomhair claims the red hall by blood, Sliochd Thormoid by the unbroken rolls, Sliochd Raghnaill by its boats and silver. Sliochd Mhuirich, which holds the Keeper's office, makes no claim and says the vein has not asked it to judge.

title: Gilleasbuig watches the Four Houses argue
body: Called down from Cathair dhearg twice a year to lay the shut hall's own rolls before whichever house asks to see them, Gilleasbuig Mòr sits at the edge of the Four Houses' long sitting at Dùn ìseal, and hears blood, boats and silence argued past each other for three years without once being asked his own mind on the matter.

title: Sliochd Ìomhair's condition of the graves
body: Sliochd Ìomhair consents to the clerk's choosing on one condition: that whoever takes the red hall, the graves at Dùn dhearg remain the kings' burying-place. Gilleasbuig answers that he never expected to be buried anywhere else, and the condition is sworn on the spot.

title: The election of Gilleasbuig Mòr
body: The houses choose Gilleasbuig Mòr mac Tormoid of Seann Dunn, a grandson of the clerks' line, to hold the red hall. The Keeper sets the stone cup in his hands before the council, and so for the first time a ruler is made at Dùn ìseal. Sliochd Ìomhair consents, on condition that its graves at Dùn dhearg remain the burying-place of the kings.

title: Sliochd Raghnaill first names the clerk of the shut hall
body: Sliochd Raghnaill is the first of the Four Houses to put Gilleasbuig Mòr's own name forward for the red hall, on the reasoning that a clerk who kept the shut hall's rolls straight three years running, favouring no house's claim over the work, has already shown the hand a red hall wants at its head.

title: Tormod mac Gilleasbuig sits at the rolls
body: Gilleasbuig Mòr sends for his son Tormod, already taught the clerks' bench at Seann Dunn at sixteen, to sit beside him at Cathair dhearg and learn the red hall's own rolls before he is taught anything else of ruling, the same order his own father once taught him a road in.

title: Gilleasbuig Mòr at Cathair dhearg
body: Gilleasbuig Mòr takes the red hall. He keeps the clerks' office in the hands of his own house and has the king-list copied again from the beginning, with a line drawn beneath Oighrig nic Lachlainn. The line is in every later copy.

title: The line drawn beneath a queen's name
body: In the year after the cup is set in his hands, Gilleasbuig Mòr has the king-list copied again from its beginning in his own house's hand, with a single line drawn beneath the name of Oighrig nic Lachlainn to mark the ending of Goraidh Mòr's whole line, so that no clerk after him need hunt a kinship no longer there.

title: Gilleasbuig sleeps in the clerks' room of the red hall
body: Coming to Cathair dhearg by the lowland road, the new rìgh sleeps his first night in the small room off the rolls-chamber where the clerks keep their beds, the queen's chambers having stood empty five years and no one having thought to air them. He keeps that room to his death.

title: The meadow of Muileann àrsaidh and Ceann àrsaidh
body: Gilleasbuig Mòr judges the one dispute of his reign the rolls set down whole, a water-meadow claimed whole by two households on notched sticks that agree for forty years and then part company; he sends a clerk to copy both sticks stroke for stroke and gives the meadow to both households at once, with a boundary stone cut down its centre for the first time in living memory.

title: The shrine at Seann Dunn enlarged
body: Gilleasbuig Mòr enlarges his house's shrine at Seann Dunn into a temple with a court for pilgrims. The other houses say still that its coal-lamp burns fuller than the measure, and every season a Keeper's cutter is sent to try it.

title: The Keeper's cutter tries Seann Dunn's lamp
body: The other three houses say the enlarged temple at Seann Dunn burns fuller than the Law allows. A Keeper's cutter is sent every season to try its measure by the island's common weights, and every season finds the measure kept, which changes nobody's mind.

title: Death of Iain Caol, the last of the grain-carriers
body: Iain Caol dies at Àth dhìreach in his ninetieth year, the last living of any who could say he had carried the road when the famine and the right to rest were both still new. The right the town kept for its carriers dies with him, though the town still sets out, at the turn of every year, the one bowl he had kept for whichever carrier walked the road that night.

title: Death of Gilleasbuig Mòr
body: Gilleasbuig Mòr dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried among the house of Ìomhar at Dùn dhearg, as was agreed. His son Tormod Òg follows him without a meeting of the houses, and none asks for one.

title: Gilleasbuig Mòr carried five days to Dùn dhearg
body: Gilleasbuig Mòr's bier is carried the five days' road from Cathair dhearg to Dùn dhearg, stopping each night at a waypoint house whose keeper had known him first as a boy with a satchel of rolls, to be buried among the house of Ìomhar as Sliochd Ìomhair had sworn at his choosing.

title: Tormod Òg follows his father without a meeting of the houses
body: Gilleasbuig's son Tormod takes the red hall in his one-and-fortieth year without any meeting of the Four Houses, and none asks for one; a son following a father now seems to every house the plainer course.

title: The gap in the list
body: Nine rulers of the house of Tormod reign between Tormod Òg and Anna Ruadh, and the king-list at Cathair dhearg gives their names and years and little else. The successors of Peigi nic Tormoid were diligent and brief; for these reigns the rolls tell mostly of harvests, tolls and the mending of bridges.

title: The bridge at Cathair dhearg is widened a third time
body: The masons' fellowship widens the old bridge at Cathair dhearg a third time on Mòrag nan Rathad's own piers, broad enough now for two carts to pass abreast. The old keystone, carrying the fourth hearth's sign, is set into the new parapet rather than broken for rubble.

title: The road-guards first ride the lowland roads
body: The road-guards of Dùn dhearg take to the small tough horses of the southern grass country rather than walking their circuits, and can reach a waypoint house before a night's quarrel has cooled into a grievance. Theirs are the first riders' names the road-guard's own roll keeps.

title: The road-guards' roll first names its riders
body: The first mounted company of the road-guards of Dùn dhearg, riding the small tough horses of the southern grass country, are the earliest guards whose names the road-guards' own roll troubles to keep.

title: The flood takes the eastern approach at Ros fhionn
body: A wet spring swells the river at Ros fhionn past every bank built to hold it, carrying off the eastern approach of Ailean Clachair's span and three households built too near the water. The span itself, and Ailean's own hearth-sign in its keystone, stand untouched.

title: The fellowship mends Ros fhionn on deeper footings
body: Masons called down from Cathair dhearg lay a new causeway on stone footings deep enough to outlast the flood that took the old one, and leave Ailean Clachair's hearth-sign untouched, cutting their own new work a course below it rather than over it.

title: The masons leave Ailean's sign standing at Ros fhionn
body: Clearing the old approach at Ros fhionn, the masons find the keystone Ailean Clachair cut with the fourth hearth's sign and leave it as it is, cutting their own work a course below. The fellowship keeps the custom after: old signs are left standing wherever the stone beneath them stands.

title: The bridge at Cathair dhearg widened
body: The bridge at Cathair dhearg is rebuilt a third time, wide enough now for a cart, for carts have come onto the lowland roads. The hearth-sign is cut again in the keystone. The span stands on the piers of Mòrag nan Rathad.

title: The bridge at Dùn chrom is built at half toll
body: The fellowship bridges the river below Dùn chrom, joining the southern road to the western without the long way round by Cathair dhearg, and sets its own toll at half the capital's. Cathair dhearg's reeves complain in letters the rolls still keep; none takes up the fellowship's offer to hand the crossing to the crown.

title: Cathair dhearg's reeves complain of the half-toll at Dùn chrom
body: The reeves of Cathair dhearg protest that a toll set by anyone but the crown will in time be set anywhere by anyone. The fellowship offers to hand the crossing to the crown, tolls and upkeep together. No reeve takes up the offer, and the half-toll stands.

title: Riders on the lowland roads
body: The road-guards of Dùn dhearg begin to ride the lowland roads on the small horses of the southern grass country, and a guard can now reach a waypoint house before a quarrel there has cooled. They are the first riders whose names are kept, and for long the only ones.

title: The fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill bridge Ceann àrsaidh
body: Forty of the fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill, taught the mason's craft in an idle season after the burning at Seann Tarr, build the fourth stone bridge of the lowlands at the river town of Ceann àrsaidh. The fellowship's roll names all forty, a courtesy not always given to borrowed hands.

title: The forty fisher-masons named on the fellowship's roll
body: The masons' roll at Cathair dhearg names all forty fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill who built the bridge at Ceann àrsaidh, on the reasoning that people who learned a new trade rather than sit idle deserve to be named among the masons.

title: The crossing at Ros fhionn repaired
body: A flood takes the eastern approach of Ailean Clachair's span above Ros fhionn, and it is mended. The masons find their founder's hearth-sign still sharp in the keystone, and leave it untouched.

title: Caol mhòr gathers under its own headman
body: The fisher-families of Caol mhòr on the north-western coast gather under a headman of their own choosing and send tolls to Cathair dhearg only in the years a road-guard comes so far to collect them. A reeve of Ros dhomhain writes that the coast might as well keep its own law for all the crown's writ reaches it.

title: A reeve of Ros dhomhain writes of Caol mhòr
body: A reeve of Ros dhomhain writes more than once to the red hall that Caol mhòr pays what it pleases and answers to whom it pleases. The red hall mostly sends no answer; the north-west's tolls are not worth a road-guard's season.

title: Beathag Clachair is born at Doire mhin
body: Beathag Clachair is born to a family of cutters at Doire mhin on the southern road, three generations deep in boundary-stones and byre-lintels, and is quicker than her father's other apprentices at reading a stone's grain before she has seen twenty summers.

title: The bridge at Dùn chrom
body: The masons' fellowship bridges the river below Dùn chrom, joining the southern road to the western without the long way round by Cathair dhearg. The toll is set at half the road-toll, and Cathair dhearg complains.

title: Ceann mhòr begins the seal-oil trade
body: Ceann mhòr on the north-western coast begins rendering seal-oil from the northern rocks and carrying it down to Ros bheag for silver rings. From then on the seal-oil lamps of the western harbours burn the brightest light on Dia-thìr.

title: The bridge at Ceann àrsaidh
body: A bridge is built at the river town of Ceann àrsaidh, the fourth stone crossing of the lowlands. The masons' roll names the forty who built it, all of the fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill, who had learned the craft while the boats lay idle.

title: Herders take the high pastures above Muileann leathan
body: Herding families take the summer pastures above Muileann leathan for the wool the weavers of Inis mhòr prize above any other, holding no right to the handful and never counted in any census, their pastures too high and too far for a road-guard to trouble reckoning them.

title: Inis mhin's headman walks to the wool-fair with a complaint
body: The headman of the small northern harbour of Inis mhin walks the whole distance to the wool-fair at Inis mhòr to lay a complaint against the road-guard's toll, the only time the harbour comes into the rolls this age, and the complaint kept in fuller telling than the harbour otherwise earns.

title: The bridge at Doire mhin
body: The masons' fellowship builds a small bridge at Doire mhin to carry the southern road over a stream that floods each spring. Beside the hearth-sign in the keystone is cut the name of Beathag Clachair, who cut it: the first mason's mark known.

title: Beathag Clachair cuts the first mason's mark
body: Leading her own crossing for the first time, Beathag Clachair cuts her own name beneath the fourth hearth's sign at the small bridge over the stream at Doire mhin: Beathag the mason set this. No mason before her had ever cut a name of his own beside the hearth's, and within two seasons every hearth on the island follows her.

title: Masons of every hearth cut their names beside the sign
body: Within two seasons of Beathag Clachair's bridge at Doire mhin, masons of every hearth begin cutting their own names beside the fourth hearth's sign wherever a fellowship crew finishes a crossing. The masons call it Beathag's mark.

title: The far-off house is rebuilt in stone
body: The waypoint house the carriers call the far-off house, so distant from any town that a traveller is never nearer to it than halfway, is rebuilt in stone after its old timber and turf give out to a western storm, keeping the name a hundred years of true telling had earned it.

title: The far-off house
body: The waypoint house on the site of An Sligeanach Fad' às, the oldest house under the road-peace, is rebuilt in stone. It lies so far from any town that the carriers say one is never nearer to it than halfway, and from the saying it takes its name.

title: A waypoint keeper of the northern road begins serving fire-water
body: A new keeper of the waypoint house the carriers call a waypoint house on the northern road, on the northern road, begins serving a spirit distilled from barley stronger than any small beer sold on that road before. The carriers name it fire-water for the way of it going down and the way of it sitting after.

title: Fire-water on the northern road
body: The house on the northern road, on the site of An Leòmhann Buidhe, begins to serve a spirit distilled from barley that the carriers call fire-water. The Keepers rule that it is not a burning and no concern of theirs. The house's trade doubles.

title: The Keeper rules fire-water no burning of the Law
body: Asked by troubled reeves of the northern road to rule on fire-water under the Small-Burning Law, the Keeper of that generation answers that a fire kept in a man's own belly is no burning the Law was written to answer for, and that the Hall will rule on drink the day it rules on food. The waypoint house's trade doubles within the season.

title: Beathag Clachair dies at Doire mhin
body: Beathag Clachair dies at seventy at Doire mhin, having cut her mark on four further crossings, and is buried at her own asking at the foot of the bridge that carries her name. Masons of the fellowship keep, for a long while after, the habit of laying a chip of grey stone on her grave in passing.

title: Caol mhòr in the north-west
body: The fisher-families of the north-west gather at Caol mhòr under a headman of their own, and send tolls to Cathair dhearg only in the years the road-guard comes to take them. Little is written of the north-west in this age, and most of it is complaint of that.

title: Ros bheag's merchants arm two boats against raiders
body: The sting-sworn merchants of Ros bheag pay from their own purses to arm and crew two boats against raiders taking dried fish from the western strands. The raiders move north before either boat catches one at sea, and the coast keeps a wariness it had not kept before.

title: Seal-oil from Ceann mhòr
body: Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast begins to trade seal-oil down the western coast to Ros bheag for silver rings, and its beacons burn it. For many generations the seal-oil lamps of the western harbours are the brightest light on Dia-thìr.

title: The high pastures of Muileann leathan
body: Herding families take the high pastures above Muileann leathan in the north and keep sheep there for the wool of Inis mhòr. They hold no right to the handful, have never held one, and are not counted in the census of hands.

title: The second sighting off Baile chrom
body: Two boats of Baile chrom tell of something vast moving beneath their keels in the north-western water, the second such telling the coast remembers since Ruairidh Liath's reign. One boat does not come home, and Baile chrom keeps its old wake for both losses together.

title: Baile chrom keeps one wake for both lost boats
body: One of the two boats of Baile chrom that felt the sea breathe under them does not come home, nor is any wreck found. The harbour keeps the wake it kept for the earlier loss for both losses together.

title: Inis mhin on the northern shore
body: Inis mhin, a fishing harbour on the northern shore, comes into the rolls for the first time when its headman goes to the wool-fair of Inis mhòr to complain of the road-guard's toll. The complaint is written down in full, and it is all that is written of the town in this age.

title: Sliochd Raghnaill sails the round of the offshore islands
body: Boats of Sliochd Raghnaill sail from Seann Tarr round the whole ring of the offshore islands, Eilean ruadh, Eilean dhearg and Eilean fhada among them, and come home within one season, the first crew of the age known to have made the whole round.

title: Families take sheep to summer on Eilean ruadh
body: Coastal families begin carrying sheep over to Eilean ruadh each summer for its grazing, building turf shelters against the weather and bringing the flocks home before the autumn storms. Later herders keep patching the same shelters rather than building anew.

title: The raid on the western strands
body: Raiders from the north-western waters take a season's dried fish from the strands of the north-western coast. The sting-sworn merchants of Ros bheag pay for two armed boats to watch the strands, and the raiders move north.

title: The second sighting
body: Two boats of Baile chrom tell of something vast moving beneath them in the north-western water, the second such sighting remembered. One boat does not come home. The wake that Baile chrom keeps for the first loss is kept now for both.

title: Round the islands
body: Boats of Sliochd Raghnaill sail from Seann Tarr round the offshore islands, Eilean ruadh, Eilean dhearg and Eilean fhada among them, and come home in one season. No crew of the age goes further from the coast than the islands, and none is known to have wished to.

title: Summer herders on Eilean ruadh
body: Families from the coast take sheep over to Eilean ruadh for the summer grazing and bring them back before the storms. They build turf shelters there, which later herders use again.

title: Anna Ruadh
body: Anna Ruadh of the house of Tormod takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. She walks the whole circuit of the roads, the first ruler to do so since Mòrag nan Rathad, and she walks it twice.

title: Anna Ruadh asks the reeves how the roads stand
body: At her first councils Anna Ruadh asks the reeves how the roads stand between one seat and the next. When none can tell her past his own district, she says she will go and see. The reeve of Cathair dhomhain tells her a hall is better kept from a hall.

title: Anna Ruadh sets out with a dozen of her household
body: Anna Ruadh leaves the red hall in spring with a dozen of her household and no more baggage than a carrier takes, no litter and no guard beyond a well-off traveller's, the first ruler to walk the whole circuit since Mòrag nan Rathad.

title: Anna Ruadh at Am Buabhall Fortanach
body: On her first circuit Anna Ruadh stops at the house on the site of Am Buabhall Fortanach, where the War of the Roads was ended, and eats the jugged buffalo like a carrier. The keepers of the house tell of it still.

title: Anna Ruadh's second circuit
body: Anna Ruadh walks the whole road circuit a second time in her middle years, slower than her first walking, stopping longest where keepers who fed her as a young queen feed her again grey-haired; at Am Buabhall Fortanach she sleeps a night under the same roof for the only time in either circuit.

title: Anna Ruadh at the sunny house
body: On the eastern road Anna Ruadh lodges at the house on the site of An Taigh-òsta Grianach and grants its keepers a toll of their own for the upkeep of the road to Cnoc leathan, Slighe Cnoc leathan. No other waypoint house on the island holds a royal charter.

title: Anna Ruadh takes the sunny house's charter to stone
body: The keeper of the sunny house on the road to Cnoc leathan, who has mended the stretch out of her own household's stores for three generations, asks Anna Ruadh that the new charter be cut in stone rather than skin, since a fire can lose a skin but never a stone, and the queen has it cut before she leaves the district.

title: Anna Ruadh at Ceann mhin
body: At Ceann mhin on the south-eastern coast Anna Ruadh hears the quarrel of the fishers and the carriers over who may carry dried fish up to the mountain, and rules that both may. The fish going inland is doubled, and its price at Dùn ìseal halved.

title: An old fisher of Ceann mhin judges the queen fair to the fish
body: Years after Anna Ruadh's ruling that both fishers and carriers might carry the dried catch inland, an old fisher of the strand, asked which side the queen had truly favoured, answers that she had favoured the fish, which was more than either household carrying it had thought to do.

title: Dried fish doubles inland after the ruling at Ceann mhin
body: Two years after Anna Ruadh ruled that fishers and carriers alike might carry dried fish up-country, the fish going inland has doubled and its price at Dùn ìseal has fallen by half. Both sides claim the doubling as proof they were right.

title: The contest at Ceann leathan in stone
body: Anna Ruadh gives the road-guards' contest at Ceann leathan a stone-walled field, and for its prize a silver ring from the red hall. Fighters come to it from all the south, and the losers are fed at the crown's cost.

title: Fearchar Ruadh wins the stone field at Ceann leathan
body: A mason's apprentice named Fearchar Ruadh of Doire mhin takes the silver ring at Anna Ruadh's new stone-walled contest field, and eats the crown's meal at the same board as every man he beat under the queen's own new law, a custom he is said never afterward to have forgotten at any table.

title: A wood-watcher in the red hall
body: Anna Ruadh keeps a wood-watcher from Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag in her household at Cathair dhearg to read the omens of the hall. So the rite of the wood-watchers, the rite of Macha, goddess of sovereignty and of horses, first comes to the capital. The Keeper sends a protest from Dùn ìseal, and the rolls give no answer.

title: The wood-watcher reads a message home before it comes
body: In Anna Ruadh's household at Cathair dhearg the wood-watcher out of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag reads the crossing of three geese and tells the queen, unasked, that a message she had given up waiting for will come within the week; an answer to a year-old letter reaches her on the sixth day, and no one in the household troubles him with idle questions after.

title: The Keeper protests the wood-watcher in the red hall
body: The Keeper at Dùn ìseal sends a protest up the road Anna Ruadh walked, asking by what right a hall built on the Binding keeps an omen-reader who answers to no measure of the vein. No answer is remembered.

title: Cathair dhomhain and the wood-watchers
body: The shrine at Cathair dhomhain, proud of its strict keeping of the Law, will take no wood-watcher, and its people say that the capital has given its omens to folk who sit in trees. From this the rivalry of the two towns takes a turn in matters of faith that it never loses.

title: Cathair dhomhain doubles its own strictness in answer
body: Cathair dhomhain's shrine, stung by the capital's wood-watcher, doubles its own cutter's visits to the Keeper's measure without being asked, and for a hundred years after a Cathair dhomhain man swearing an oath is known on the roads by how exactly he keeps to its letter.

title: Anna Ruadh has the toll rolls read at her bedside
body: In her last winter Anna Ruadh has the toll rolls of the sunny house and of Slighe Cnoc leathan read aloud to her twice, as if to be sure the charter still stands as she had it cut, and asks after no other matter of state.

title: Death of Anna Ruadh
body: Anna Ruadh dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried at Dùn dhearg among the house of Ìomhar and the kings of her own house. Her son Coinneach Bàn takes the hall.

title: The council keeps the hall in Coinneach Bàn's name
body: After Anna Ruadh's death the council at Cathair dhearg keeps the red hall three years in her son's name before Coinneach Bàn, at seven-and-twenty, takes it in his own.

title: Coinneach Bàn
body: Coinneach Bàn rules long and quietly from Cathair dhearg. In his reign the clerks of the hall begin to copy the rolls for the provinces, so that each province seat has its own copy of the laws. Several of those copies survive where the first writings are lost.

title: Coinneach Bàn begins the copying of the provincial rolls
body: Coinneach Bàn, choosing a clerk's work over his mother's roads, has every province seat send its own laws to Cathair dhearg to be copied fresh, and reads each copy through himself before it is shelved, so that within a decade a province's own clerks trust the capital's copy of their rolls sooner than the damp-spoiled skins in their own keeping.

title: A second clerk keeps the unstruck preface
body: Before the knife reaches the Keepers' roll, the clerk Seumas Bàn sends for has already made a copy of the count of his own house for his own hand; it is that unstruck copy, kept quietly through the rest of the age, and not the scraped preface, that answers for the fact today.

title: Seumas Bàn keeps the flame
body: Seumas Bàn of Sliochd Mhuirich is chosen Keeper. Reading the Hall's roll at Dùn ìseal he finds that more than half the Keepers of the age were of his own house, and has the fact struck from the preface. The unstruck copy survives.

title: Seumas Bàn reckons two Keepers in three of his house
body: Going beyond the count of names, Seumas Bàn reckons how many of the remaining Keepers married into Sliochd Mhuirich or fostered a child of it, and finds the true share near two in every three.

title: The rites counted at Dùn ìseal
body: Seumas Bàn has the clerks of the Hall list every rite on the island that burns the handful and every one that lays claim to the vein, that the council may know what it keeps.
